## Definitions and pinned conventions

### The sheaf strata

The following conditions form the sheaf-theoretic hierarchy used by the roadmap:

| Condition | Role here |
| --- | --- |
| quasi-coherent | arbitrary degree-one datum for an affine linear scheme |
| finite presentation | base-change-stable finiteness condition |
| finite locally free | dualizable quasi-coherent objects and finite geometric bundles |
| invertible | constant rank one, agreeing with Tau Ceti's existing object |

Define a finite locally free sheaf at the present API boundary by

```math
\mathrm{IsFiniteLocallyFree}(\mathcal E)
\;:\!\!\Longleftrightarrow\;
\mathcal E\text{ is locally free and finitely presented}.
```

L0 proves that this is equivalent to being locally free on a Zariski cover with finite bases, to
having finite-projective affine modules, and to being dualizable in `QCoh(X)`. Its rank is bundled
as a locally constant function `X \to \mathbb N`; fixed-rank constructions use the full
subcategory on which it is constantly `r`.

### Two related total-space constructions

For a quasi-coherent module `F`, follow Stacks Project §27.6 and define

```math
\mathbf V_{\mathrm{lin}}(\mathcal F)
=
\mathrm{Spec}_X
\mathrm{Sym}_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal F).
```

It is contravariant in `F` and represents linear functionals:

```math
\mathrm{Hom}_X(T,\mathbf V_{\mathrm{lin}}(\mathcal F))
\simeq
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal O_T}(f^*\mathcal F,\mathcal O_T).
```

A quasicoherent linear scheme is intrinsically an affine morphism `p : V \to X` together with a grading

```math
p_*\mathcal O_V = \bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\mathcal A_n.
```

whose coordinate algebra is freely generated by `A_1`. This is expressed by an isomorphism of
graded algebras

```math
\mathrm{Sym}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathcal A_1)\cong\mathcal A,
```

including compatibility with multiplication and the unit. Morphisms preserve the grading. The
equivalent affine-module-scheme presentation supplies zero, addition and scalar multiplication
and retains the condition that the canonical map `Sym^gr(A_1) → A` is an isomorphism. Prove the
correspondence of grading-preserving and module-structure-preserving morphisms on these objects.
An arbitrary affine module scheme need not satisfy this recognition condition: over `F_p`,
`Spec(F_p[t]/(t^p))` is a module scheme but its coordinate algebra is not freely generated in
degree one. For finite bundles, local linear trivializations provide the equivalent recognition
condition.

For a finite locally free sheaf of sections `E`, define the geometric total space

```math
\mathbf V(\mathcal E)
=
\mathbf V_{\mathrm{lin}}(\mathcal E^\vee)
=
\mathrm{Spec}_X
\mathrm{Sym}_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal E^\vee).
```

It is covariant in `E`, Zariski-locally an affine space with linear transition functions, and
represents sections:

```math
\mathrm{Hom}_X(T,\mathbf V(\mathcal E))
\simeq
\Gamma(T,f^*\mathcal E).
```

The names `linearSpec` and `totalSpace` record the variance and the dualization directly in the
public API.

### Relative-Spec convention

Relative Spec is contravariant in quasi-coherent commutative algebras and commutes with arbitrary
base change.

## Layers

Each layer has one discharge-gated milestone and the companion API needed to make it usable.

### L0A — sheaves of modules

Construct the symmetric monoidal closed structure on `X.Modules` from presheaf tensor product and
sheafification, with a natural comparison identifying the tensor object and tensor maps with
that sheafification construction. Expose the tensor--Hom adjunction, evaluation, coevaluation,
and restriction formulas. For internal Hom, construct the canonical stalk comparison
`Hom(E,F)_x → Hom(E_x,F_x)`; prove it is an isomorphism for finitely presented `E`, without
asserting this for unrestricted sources. Make module pullback a strong symmetric monoidal functor
with coherent identity and composition comparisons.

**Milestone:** a symmetric monoidal closed category of sheaves of modules, with internal Hom
characterized by the tensor--Hom adjunction.

### L0B — quasicoherent and finite locally free sheaves

Prove that quasicoherence is an `ObjectProperty.IsMonoidal` and obtain the symmetric monoidal
structure on `QCoh(X)` from Mathlib's generic full-subcategory machinery. Internal Hom from a
finitely presented source preserves quasicoherence. Construct the canonical comparison
`f* Hom(E,F) → Hom(f* E,f* F)`: it is an isomorphism for a finitely presented source and flat
`f`, or for a finite locally free source and arbitrary `f`. Finite presentation alone does not
justify a nonflat base-change isomorphism (see [Stacks, tag 0C6I](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0C6I)).
For finite locally free `E`, construct

```math
\mathcal H\!om(\mathcal E,\mathcal F)
\cong
\mathcal E^\vee\otimes\mathcal F.
```

Package `FiniteLocallyFreeSheaf X`, prove closure under isomorphism and arbitrary pullback, construct
the bundled locally constant rank and rank loci, construct direct sums, and identify rank one with
the existing `InvertibleSheaf X`. Prove that finite local freeness is monoidal and that these
objects form a rigid category. On affine schemes, restrict `tildeEquiv` to finite projective
modules and compare global sections, tensor, dual and rank.

**Milestone:** a quasi-coherent sheaf is finite locally free if and only if it has a left/right dual
in the symmetric monoidal category `QCoh(X)`; the categorical dual agrees with
`Hom(E,O_X)`, and the canonical double-dual map is an isomorphism.

### L0C — polynomial operations

Construct symmetric and exterior powers, their rank formulas and their compatibility with affine
comparison and pullback. Define the determinant object for arbitrary locally constant rank and the
determinant functor on each fixed-rank subcategory

```text
determinant (r : ℕ) : FinLocFree_r(X) ⥤ InvertibleSheaf(X).
```

The construction is also functorial on the core of all finite locally free sheaves.

**Milestone:** tensor, dual, symmetric powers, exterior powers and fixed-rank determinant have
coherent pullback comparison isomorphisms.

### L1A — relative Spec

Define quasi-coherent commutative `O_X`-algebras using the L0 monoidal structure. Construct
`Spec_X(A) \to X` by affine-local spectra and gluing. Prove the functor-of-points universal
property, recover `A` from the pushforward of the structure sheaf, and prove compatibility with
restriction to opens and arbitrary base change.

Expose named functors

```text
relativeSpec : QCAlg(X)ᵒᵖ ⥤ AffSch/X
affineFunctions : AffSch/X ⥤ QCAlg(X)ᵒᵖ
```

and state the functor-of-points equivalence naturally in the test scheme and the algebra.
The carrier of `affineFunctions(V)` is the actual `p_* O_V`: its unit and multiplication are
those on regular functions, and its morphism on `g : V → W` pulls back regular functions along
`g`. The universal property's test-scheme map pulls back algebra maps using the coherent
pullback-composition comparison and the structure-sheaf comparison; its algebra map is
precomposition with the pulled-back algebra morphism.

### L1B — the relative-Spec anti-equivalence

**Milestone:** construct the anti-equivalence

```math
\mathsf{QCAlg}(X)^{\mathrm{op}}
\simeq
\mathsf{AffSch}_{/X}.
```

with the named functors above, explicit unit and counit, triangle identities, affine-base
normalization, and pseudofunctorial compatibility under `Y \to X`.

**Companion results:** relative spectra of symmetric algebras, affine localization, products and
fiber products of affine `X`-schemes, and affine computations through `tildeEquiv`.

### L2A — structured linear schemes

Use `GradedObject` and commutative monoid objects to define nonnegatively graded quasicoherent
algebras `GradedQuasicoherentAlgebra` with graded algebra morphisms. Construct
`gradedSymmetricAlgebra` and its full
subcategory of objects freely generated in degree one. Apply relative Spec while retaining this
grading. On `V_lin(F)`, construct zero, addition and scalar multiplication and prove the affine
formulas and the equivalence with the module-scheme presentation satisfying the canonical
symmetric-algebra isomorphism condition above. The recognition theorem and its morphism
correspondence concern precisely these free-degree-one objects.

Export the affine graded-ring interface for every L2A graded quasicoherent
algebra: take sections degree by degree on affine opens, construct the native
graded multiplication/unit and direct-sum underlying algebra, and prove the
localization, affine-restriction and arbitrary-base-change comparisons.
Prove these maps preserve finite generation and generation in degree one,
and give the symmetric-algebra comparison on affine modules. This is the
shared input interface for StableReduction Layer2's relative Proj and
[SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.3](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/779),
as well as L2A's relative Spec; those consumers
use this graded object and its affine ring charts rather than a second
category of graded quasicoherent algebras.

**First milestone:** the degree-one functor and `linearSpec` are quasi-inverse equivalences

```math
\mathsf{QCoh}(X)^{\mathrm{op}}
\simeq
\mathsf{LinearSch}(X).
```

This equivalence is presented by named `linearSpec` and `degreeOne` functors with objectwise unit
and counit isomorphisms, and its forward functor is identified with `linearSpec`.

### L2B — geometric vector bundles

Define geometric vector bundles as the full subcategory of structured linear schemes whose
degree-one piece is finite locally free. Since the ambient morphisms are already graded, its
morphisms are fibrewise linear. Restricting to finite locally free sheaves and dualizing gives

```math
\mathsf{FinLocFree}(X)
\simeq
\mathsf{GeomVB}(X).
```

Define `totalSpace` through `linearSpec(E^∨)`, identify it as the forward functor of this
equivalence, and prove the section-valued universal property as a natural isomorphism in both the
test scheme and the bundle. Both equivalences are natural under base change. Prove
the following dictionary as natural isomorphisms:

| Sheaf side | Geometric side |
| --- | --- |
| pullback `f^*E` | base change `Y\times_X V(E)` |
| global section | section of `V(E)\to X` |
| module fibre `E_x\otimes k(x)` | affine-space scheme `Spec_{k(x)} Sym((E_x\otimes k(x))^∨)` |
| direct sum | fibre product over `X` |
| zero and addition | zero section and fibrewise addition |
| dual, tensor, internal Hom | corresponding geometric bundles |
| exterior/symmetric powers, determinant | corresponding geometric bundles and determinant line |

For the fibre row, the induced equivalence on `k(x)`-rational points identifies those points with
the vectors of `E_x\otimes k(x)`.

## Worked instances

- Through `tildeEquiv`, a finite projective `R`-module `M` gives
  `Spec(Sym_R(M^\vee)) \to Spec R`.
- The free sheaf on `Fin r` (universe-lifted in Lean) gives Mathlib's `AffineSpace` and represents
  `r`-tuples of sections. Compare the universal property with `AffineSpace.homOfVector` and
  `AffineSpace.homOverEquiv`, and its affine normalization with `AffineSpace.SpecIso`.
  For rank one, recover `Γ(T,O_T)` with test-scheme maps given by pullback of regular functions.
  A free-bundle map with matrix `A` over `Γ(X,O_X)` acts on section vectors over `T` by the
  matrix obtained by pulling each entry of `A` along `T → X`.
- `InvertibleSheaf.trivial X` gives the trivial geometric line bundle.

## Cross-cutting acceptance criteria

- Every construction has restriction, affine-local computation and pullback comparisons. Prove
  arbitrary-base-change isomorphisms for relative Spec, symmetric/exterior powers and finite
  locally free bundle operations. For internal Hom, the general base-change and stalk statements
  are comparison maps; the base-change isomorphism requires a finitely presented source and flat
  base change, or a finite locally free source and arbitrary base change, and the stalk
  isomorphism requires a finitely presented source.
- Every opaque construction has a characteristic equation identifying its underlying object with
  the intended Mathlib or earlier-roadmap construction.
- Every equivalence exposes its functors, unit, counit, and naturality, and identifies its
  essential-image model with the intrinsic target category.
- The variance distinction `F \mapsto V_lin(F)` versus `E \mapsto V(E)` is visible in names and
  theorem statements.
- Fixed-rank statements explicitly assume constant rank; otherwise rank remains locally constant.
- Public APIs have extensionality and simp lemmas that keep covers, gluing data, and affine
  equivalences behind the implementation boundary.
- The worked instances above compile against the public interface.

## Relations to existing roadmaps

`JacobianChallenge` supplies the present rank-one object `InvertibleSheaf`, finitely presented
sheaves, and later the divisor--line-bundle dictionary. This roadmap generalizes its sheaf object to
all finite ranks and supplies the tensor/dual and geometric-total-space infrastructure that its
Picard theory needs. The Picard scheme and Jacobian remain governed by `JacobianChallenge`.

`AlgebraicCurves` supplies curve-specific divisors and Riemann--Roch. The vector-bundle theory here works over arbitrary schemes; `AlgebraicCurves` supplies the
curve-specific degree theory.

## Successor roadmaps — motivation only

The completion of L0--L2 supplies the algebraic vector-bundle theory required by three natural
successors.

### 1. Projective, Grassmann, and flag bundles

A separate roadmap should construct relative projective bundles, Grassmann bundles, and flag
bundles together with their quotient-classifying universal properties. Its main geometric outputs
are the universal quotient bundles and the flag-bundle input for the splitting principle.

### 2. Chow groups and characteristic classes

Building on those classifying constructions, a further roadmap should construct cycles, rational
equivalence, Chow homology/cohomology, Cartier-divisor actions, and the projective bundle formula;
then define Chern classes and prove naturality, the Whitney sum formula, and the splitting
principle.

### 3. Cohomological realization and the Hodge Conjecture interface

A further roadmap should construct analytification, topological vector bundles and Chern classes,
Betti and algebraic de Rham cohomology, the cycle-class map

```math
\mathrm{cl}_X^p :
\mathrm{CH}^p(X)
\longrightarrow
H^{2p}(X^{\mathrm{an}},\mathbb Z(p)),
```

and compatibility between algebraic and topological Chern classes. For a smooth projective complex
scheme it should prove that algebraic cycle classes have Hodge type `(p,p)`.

Together with the merged [Hodge structures roadmap
#49](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/49) (merged 13 August 2026), this supplies
the interfaces for the following formulation of the Hodge Conjecture:

```math
\mathrm{im}\!\left(
  \mathrm{cl}_X^p : \mathrm{CH}^p(X)\otimes\mathbb Q
  \longrightarrow H^{2p}(X^{\mathrm{an}},\mathbb Q(p))
\right)
=
\mathrm{Hdg}^p(X),
```

where `Hdg^p(X)` is the rational subspace of Hodge classes: type `(0,0)` after the Tate twist,
equivalently type `(p,p)` in untwisted degree `2p`. The Hodge-structures roadmap provides the
linear-algebraic target; the future realization roadmap builds the geometric cohomology,
comparisons, and cycle-class map that populate it. The present roadmap supplies the algebraic
vector-bundle input to that programme.

## References

- The Stacks Project, [Relative spectrum as a functor](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01LQ)
  and [Vector bundles](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01M1).
- EGA II, §1; EGA I, the affine-morphism/quasi-coherent-algebra correspondence.
- R. Hartshorne, *Algebraic Geometry*, II.5.
- D. Huybrechts and M. Lehn, *The Geometry of Moduli Spaces of Sheaves*, §2.2.
TauCetiRoadmap/AmenableGroups:
# Roadmap: amenable groups

Amenability makes averaging possible when normalized counting is unavailable. Its
finitely additive form rules out paradoxical decompositions, the phenomenon behind
Banach–Tarski. This roadmap develops invariant means as a usable theory, then proves
the discrete Følner and non-paradoxicality characterizations.

The primary definition applies to arbitrary topological groups. The subgroup,
extension, directed-colimit, Følner and Tarski layers below concern discrete
groups. The locally compact characterization is a separate analytic branch.
Euclidean Banach–Tarski, Property (T), and constructions of nonamenable groups
without nonabelian free subgroups are outside scope.

The README is definitive. [Suggested.lean](Suggested.lean) gives suggested,
non-exhaustive signatures, with `sorry` for unproved targets. The suggested home is
`TauCeti/GroupTheory/Amenable/`, with general-purpose material under
`TauCeti/Topology/`, `TauCeti/MeasureTheory/` and `TauCeti/Algebra/Group/Action/`.

## Conventions and primary definition

Let `G` have `[Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] [IsTopologicalGroup G]`. No separation,
local compactness, countability or generation hypothesis is part of the definition.
Let `UCB(G)` be the bounded real-valued functions satisfying

```text
∀ ε > 0,  ∀ᶠ u in 𝓝 1,  ∀ x ∈ G,  |f(ux) - f(x)| < ε.
```

Equivalently, `sup_x |f(u*x) - f x| → 0` as `u → 1`. This implies continuity.
Use the closed real subspace of
[`BoundedContinuousFunction G ℝ`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Topology/ContinuousMap/Bounded/Basic.html#BoundedContinuousFunction)
specified by this condition. Prove that it is exactly bounded uniform continuity
for Mathlib's
[`IsTopologicalGroup.rightUniformSpace`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/IsUniformGroup/Defs.html#IsTopologicalGroup.rightUniformSpace).
Its entourages compare `(x,y)` through `y*x⁻¹`. Do not infer an `IsUniformGroup`
instance: the left and right uniformities of a general group can differ.

The action on functions is

```text
(L_g f)(x) = (g • f)(x) = f(g⁻¹x),        L_g L_h = L_(gh).
```

A **mean** is a real linear functional `m : UCB(G) →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ` such that
`f ≥ 0 ⇒ m(f) ≥ 0` and `m(1)=1`. A mean is left invariant if
`∀ g f, m(L_g f)=m(f)`. **Amenability** is existence of such a mean.
Continuity is a consequence, not an extra assumption. In discrete layers,
“amenable group” means this definition with the discrete topology; provide
equivalent topology-free statements through Layer 2.

Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette (BDHV), Appendix A.3 and Definition G.1.4, call this
function condition *left* uniform continuity and explicitly warn that the names
are reversed elsewhere. Their topological groups are Hausdorff by the convention
at the start of Appendix A. The definition here also makes sense without that
assumption; comparisons with their results retain their Hausdorff hypothesis.
BDHV use complex-valued functions, with `‖f(ux)-f(x)‖` in the same condition.
Layer 1 proves compatibility by `mℂ(f)=m(Re f)+i m(Im f)`; positivity for a
complex mean concerns real nonnegative functions.

## Layer 1: UCB, means and transport

Develop the function space before defining invariant means on it.

1. Prove the equivalence of the neighborhood, supremum-norm and right-uniform-space
   conditions above. Give coercion and extensionality lemmas, constant functions,
   evaluation bounds, addition and scalar multiplication. Prove closure under
   pointwise multiplication, absolute value, `min` and `max`, and under uniform
   limits. Equip the space with the inherited supremum norm, order and complete
   real normed-space structure. The unital algebra and vector-lattice operations
   must agree with their pointwise interpretations.
2. Construct `L_g` as a real linear isometry equivalence. Prove its pointwise
   formula, identity, composition, inverse, order and constant preservation, and
   norm-continuity of `g ↦ L_g f` for each fixed `f`. Conjugation continuity is
   needed when checking that `L_g` preserves UCB. Prove that right translations
   preserve UCB and commute with `L_g`. Inversion identifies this space with the
   space defined using `f(xu)` and exchanges left and right translation.
3. Give means extensionality, evaluation on constants, monotonicity,
   `inf f ≤ m(f) ≤ sup f`, `|m(f)| ≤ ‖f‖∞`, `‖m‖=1`, and continuity.
   The infimum/supremum are over the nonempty group. Prove
   `|m(f)-m(h)| ≤ ‖f-h‖∞` and compatibility with uniform limits. Bundle the derived
   continuous linear functional using Mathlib's operator API. Prove convexity of
   means and of invariant means. State shared positivity and normalization lemmas
   for the ordered normed function spaces used again in Layers 2 and 7.
4. Put means in the weak-* dual unit ball. Prove that normalization, positivity
   and each equation `m(L_g f)=m(f)` define closed subsets. Evaluation at a point
   shows that the space of means is nonempty. Establish its compactness, the
   finite-intersection criterion for invariant means, and the criterion that any
   weak-* cluster point of approximately invariant means is invariant. Specify
   approximate invariance as `m_i(L_g f)-m_i(f) → 0` for every `g,f`, along a
   nontrivial filter.
5. For a continuous homomorphism `φ : G →* H`, prove that pullback
   `f ↦ f ∘ φ` maps `UCB(H)` to `UCB(G)`, preserves constants and positivity,
   is norm-contracting, and intertwines `L_g` with `L_(φ g)`. It is an isometry
   when `φ` is surjective. Deduce transport of amenability along surjective
   continuous homomorphisms and equivalence along a group isomorphism whose two
   directions are continuous. Provide identity and composition compatibility.
6. Prove the real/complex correspondence stated above, including restriction,
   complexification, inverse laws, normalization, invariance and operator norm
   one. Retain the real space as the primary API.

Reference: [BDHV](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/bachir.bekka/KazhdanTotal.pdf),
Appendix A.3 and G.1, especially Definition G.1.4.

## Layer 2: discrete means, contents and finite groups

For a discrete group prove that UCB is all bounded functions, with the same norm,
order, constants and translations. Use the discrete instance of bounded continuous
functions.

For a set `X`, use `AddContent ℝ≥0∞ (Set.univ : Set (Set X))` with total mass one
for a finitely additive probability on all subsets. Prove the bridge to a
real-valued nonnegative set function `ν` with `ν(∅)=0`, `ν(X)=1` and
`ν(A ∪ B)=ν(A)+ν(B)` for disjoint `A,B`. All values are at most one and finite,
so the conversions using `ENNReal.ofReal` and `toReal` are inverse. Supply finite
disjoint-union, complement, difference, monotonicity and finite subadditivity
lemmas, pushforward along a map, and invariance under a `MulAction G X`.

Prove the mutually inverse correspondence between means on bounded real functions
on `X` and these probabilities:

```text
ν(A) = m(1_A),        m(c₁·1_{A₁} + ⋯ + cᵣ·1_{Aᵣ}) = c₁·ν(A₁) + ⋯ + cᵣ·ν(Aᵣ).
```

The reverse construction must prove independence of the finite disjoint
presentation, positivity and the supremum-norm bound. Prove uniform approximation
of every bounded real function by finite-range functions, then construct and prove
uniqueness of the continuous extension. Prove naturality under
pullback/pushforward and equivariance, so left-invariant means correspond exactly
to left-invariant probabilities.

Conclude the discrete characterization of the primary definition. Also prove that
amenability of an underlying abstract group implies amenability with any group
topology, by restricting its mean to UCB.

For `[Finite G]`, normalized counting gives
`m(f) = (Nat.card G : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ x, f x`, using a `Fintype` instance to write the
sum. Prove positivity, normalization and invariance by the permutation `x ↦ g*x`.
Give the matching content `ν(A)=|A|/|G|`, independence of the chosen `Fintype`
instance, and the trivial-group case. Finite groups with any group topology then
follow from the restriction result.

References: [Garrido](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~garrido/amenable.pdf),
Definitions 1.12–1.13 and Theorem 1.15, used here **in discrete scope**;
[BDHV](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/bachir.bekka/KazhdanTotal.pdf), G.1.
Neither finite additivity nor the domain of all subsets can be replaced by
countable additivity on a sigma-algebra.

## Layer 3: equidecompositions and the free-group obstruction

For `[Group G] [MulAction G X]`, say `A ∼_G B` when an `Equidecomp X G` has source
`A` and target `B`. Prove equivalence with finite families `A_i` partitioning `A`
and elements `g_i` such that the pairwise disjoint sets `g_i • A_i` partition `B`.
Use `Finpartition` and the `Equipartition` bridge described above, including
conversion laws for source, target and the induced bijection. Empty pieces may be
removed without changing the relation.

Develop reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, restriction to subsets, disjoint
finite unions, transport by equivariant bijections and transport of the acting
group along an isomorphism. Define `A ≼_G B` by equidecomposability with a subset of
`B`; prove its preorder laws and the equidecomposition Schröder–Bernstein theorem
`A ≼_G B ∧ B ≼_G A ⇒ A ∼_G B`. Its proof must retain a finite set of acting
elements when constructing the bijection; an arbitrary set-theoretic bijection
does not suffice.

A **paradoxical** subset `S ⊆ X` is nonempty and admits disjoint `A,B` with
`A ∪ B=S` and `A ∼_G S ∼_G B`. Thus the empty set is not paradoxical in this API.
Prove equivalence with disjoint subcopies `A,B ⊆ S` each equidecomposable with `S`,
without requiring that they cover `S`; retain the nonemptiness hypothesis in that
version. Give invariance under equidecomposition and equivariant bijections.

An invariant content assigns equal values to equidecomposable sets, by finite
additivity. Prove that a finite-valued such content with `ν(S)>0` excludes a
paradoxical decomposition of `S`. In particular, an invariant probability rules
out paradoxicality of the whole space. Specialize using Layer 2 to prove the
easy implication for amenable discrete groups.

For `F₂ = FreeGroup (Fin 2)`, let `a,b` be the two generators and `W(c)` the
reduced words whose first letter is `c`, for `c=a,a⁻¹,b,b⁻¹`. Establish the
prefix, disjointness and cancellation API, including

```text
F₂ = {1} ⊔ W(a) ⊔ W(a⁻¹) ⊔ W(b) ⊔ W(b⁻¹),
F₂ = W(a) ⊔ a·W(a⁻¹) = W(b) ⊔ b·W(b⁻¹).
```

These exhibit two disjoint subcopies. Apply the subcopy-to-partition theorem to
obtain a paradoxical decomposition of the entire group, including its identity.
Conclude that `F₂` is not amenable.

Reference: [Garrido](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~garrido/amenable.pdf),
Definition 1.1, Theorem 1.2, Corollary 1.3, Definition 1.4 and Proposition 1.5(1).

## Layer 4: discrete closure theory

All groups in this layer carry the discrete topology. Prove the following
using Layers 1–2, with formulas for the maps on means and their compatibility.

1. **Subgroups.** If `H ≤ G` and `G` is amenable, then `H` is amenable. Choose
   representatives for the right cosets `H*t`, choosing `1` for `H` itself, and
   an `H`-equivariant retraction `r : G → H`, satisfying `r(h*x)=h*r(x)`. Pull a
   bounded function on `H` back along `r`, and average using a mean on `G`. Prove
   the retraction construction, boundedness, positivity, normalization and
   invariance. This is not restriction of a probability to `H`, which can have
   mass zero.
2. **Quotients and images.** Prove amenability of `G/N` for every normal subgroup
   `N`, and of the range of every homomorphism out of an amenable group. Include
   the surjection formulation, the quotient-by-kernel isomorphism and transport
   compatibility, reusing `QuotientGroup` and `MonoidHom.range`.
3. **Extensions.** If `N ◁ G`, `N` and `G/N` are amenable, prove that `G` is
   amenable. For bounded `f`, define
   `q=xN ↦ m_N (n ↦ f(x*n))`, and average this function with `m_(G/N)`.
   Prove independence of the representative, the norm bound and the translation
   formula before applying the quotient mean. Give the equivalent
   surjective-homomorphism theorem with amenable kernel.
4. **Finite products.** Prove binary product closure, the iterated-mean formula,
   and closure for products over a finite index type, including the empty
   product. Identify subgroup and quotient maps used in the extension proof.
5. **Directed unions.** For a nonempty directed family `H_i ≤ G`, let
   `H = ⋃ i, H_i`. If every `H_i` is amenable, prove that the subgroup `H` is
   amenable; in particular `G` is amenable when the union is all of `G`.
   Restrict bounded functions on `H` to `H_i` and apply a mean there. For each
   finite family of invariance equations, directedness puts the finitely many
   acting elements in one `H_i`. Use Layer 1's compact space of means and
   finite-intersection theorem.
6. **Directed colimits.** For a nonempty directed preorder `I`, groups `G_i` and
   homomorphisms `φ_ij` satisfying identity and composition laws, prove that their
   group colimit is amenable when every `G_i` is. The maps need not be injective.
   Reuse `GrpCat.FilteredColimits.colimitCoconeIsColimit`, the forgetful functor's
   preservation of filtered colimits, and `Types.jointly_surjective_of_isColimit`
   to represent every element by a stage. Prove that the canonical images are a
   directed family of subgroups covering the colimit. Each image is a quotient
   of its stage, so image closure and directed unions apply. State and prove the
   same result for any small filtered diagram in `GrpCat` and any specified
   colimit cocone: a cocone over two objects contains both image subgroups.
   Supply transport along the unique colimit isomorphism. Relate the directed
   preorder specialization to Mathlib's `DirectLimit` group construction by its
   universal property.

Finite subsets of `G` lie in finitely generated subgroups; those subgroups form a
directed family with union `G`. Prove these connecting lemmas for Layer 6.
Using Layer 3, also deduce that a discrete group containing a subgroup isomorphic
to `F₂` is nonamenable.

References: [Garrido](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~garrido/amenable.pdf),
Proposition 2.2; [BDHV](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/bachir.bekka/KazhdanTotal.pdf),
Proposition G.2.2 for quotient, extension and directed-union principles.
Subgroups of amenable topological groups need not be amenable; the subgroup
theorem here is for discrete groups.

## Layer 5: Følner criteria for arbitrary discrete groups

Use Mathlib's `IsFoelner` and `maxFoelner` as the Følner API. The abbreviation
`HasFoelnerSets G` directly names `NeBot (maxFoelner G Measure.count)` for the
left regular action on `G`. It installs the measurable space `⊤` locally, so
every subset is measurable even when `G` is uncountable. Prove the discrete
characterization `amenable_iff_hasFoelnerSets`:

```text
Amenable G ↔ HasFoelnerSets G.
```

Obtain the explicit filter characterization `amenable_iff_maxFoelner_neBot`
by unfolding the abbreviation.
Here `NeBot` excludes the bottom filter, for which all eventual conditions are
vacuous. Prove the counting-measure specialization `hasFoelnerSets_iff`
with only `[Group G]`, without topology or countability hypotheses. For a finite
set `F` write `gF={g*x | x∈F}`; the specialization states

```text
HasFoelnerSets G ↔
  ∀ K ⊆ G finite,  ∀ ε > 0,  ∃ F ⊆ G finite,  F ≠ ∅  ∧  ∀ g ∈ K,  |gF △ F| < ε·|F|.
```

Derive `amenable_iff_exists_finset` for discrete groups by composing
`amenable_iff_hasFoelnerSets` with `hasFoelnerSets_iff`.
Cardinalities in inequalities and ratios are coerced to `ℝ`. Use `Finset`, the
pointwise action and `symmDiff`; prove bridges to finite `Set`s and counting
measure. Develop preservation under group isomorphisms, monotonicity in the test
set and tolerance, the symmetric-difference triangle bound, and
`|gF \ F|=|F \ gF|`, hence `|gF △ F|=2|gF \ F|`.

### Amenability implies the finite-test condition

Build the following analytic and finite-combinatorial steps.

* For finite `K` and `δ>0`, construct a finitely supported function
  `p : G → ℝ` with `p≥0`, `∑ p=1`, and
  `∑_(g∈K) ‖L_g p-p‖₁ < δ`. Give the finite-support probability API, its
  inclusion in `ℓ¹(G)`, translation isometries and the pairing with bounded
  functions. Use `lp (fun _ : G ↦ ℝ) 1` for `ℓ¹(G)` and `lp.single` for point
  masses `δ_y`.
* Prove this approximation from a mean by separating zero from the norm closure
  of the convex set `{(L_g p-p)_(g∈K) : p is a finite-support probability}` in
  the finite product of `ℓ¹(G)` spaces, with the sum norm. For a continuous real
  linear functional `Λ` on that product, let `f_g(y)=Λ(ι_g δ_y)`, where `ι_g`
  is the inclusion of the `g`-th factor, and prove `|f_g(y)| ≤ ‖Λ‖`, so each
  `f_g` is bounded. Evaluating a putative strict separator at point masses gives
  a positive lower bound, uniform in `x`, for the finite sum
  `∑_(g∈K) (f_g(g*x)-f_g(x))`; an invariant mean gives that sum mean zero, a
  contradiction. Build the closure and separation connections explicitly.
* For `F_t={x : p(x)>t}`, prove the layer-cake identities
  `∫₀∞ |F_t| dt=1` and
  `∫₀∞ |gF_t △ F_t| dt=‖L_g p-p‖₁`. Since `p` has finite support, these are
  finite weighted sums over the breakpoints of its values; provide that finite
  formulation and the weighted-average argument. Taking `δ<ε` yields a level
  with `F_t` nonempty and total boundary less than `ε|F_t|`, hence the required
  bound for every `g∈K`. Handle `K=∅` by a singleton.

### Filters, nets and the converse

For the counting-measure specialization, prove that finite nonzero counting
measure means a finite nonempty set, and convert the `ℝ≥0∞` ratios of `IsFoelner`
to the real ratios above.

As a concrete directed net, index by pairs `(K,n)` with `K : Finset G` and
`n : ℕ`, ordered by inclusion and the usual order. Choose witnesses with error
`1/(n+1)`. Prove `IsFoelner G Measure.count atTop (fun i ↦ (F_i : Set G))`
and that this filter is nontrivial. Conversely a nontrivial Følner filter of
finite nonempty sets satisfies all finite tests, by intersecting finitely many
eventual conditions. Include reindexing along `Tendsto`, cofinal subnet and
eventual-equality compatibility using the existing filter API.

Use `IsFoelner.amenable` to obtain an invariant `ℝ≥0∞`-valued set function,
bundle it as the normalized `AddContent` of Layer 2, and then obtain a
functional mean. Spell out the analytic content: extend the nontrivial filter
to an ultrafilter, take limits of densities in the compact interval `[0,1]`, and
pass finite sums and the boundary estimate to these limits. For finite nonempty
`F`, let `m_F(f)=|F|⁻¹ ∑_(x∈F) f(x)`, and prove the functional estimate

```text
|m_F(L_g f) - m_F(f)| ≤ ‖f‖∞ · |g⁻¹F △ F| / |F|.
```

For each fixed ultrafilter refining the Følner filter, prove that the weak-* limit
of these averaging functionals corresponds to the density-limit content formed
using that same ultrafilter. Conclude the characterization by the nontrivial
counting-measure Følner filter and its finite-test corollary.

For `[Countable G]`, prove equivalence with a sequence of finite nonempty sets
`F_n` such that, for every `g`, `|gF_n △ F_n|/|F_n| → 0`. Construct an increasing
sequence of finite test sets covering `G`, without requiring an infinite group,
and use error `1/(n+1)`. The reverse implication uses finite intersections of
eventual conditions and needs no countability. The sets `F_n` need not be nested
or exhaustive.

References: [Garrido](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~garrido/amenable.pdf),
Definition 3.1, Definition 3.3, Lemma 3.4 and Theorem 3.6;
[BDHV](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/bachir.bekka/KazhdanTotal.pdf),
Theorem G.3.1 for approximate invariance and G.5.1–G.5.2 for Følner sets and
the level-set argument.

## Layer 6: integers and abelian groups

For the additive group `ℤ`, take `F_n={0,…,n}` with cardinality `n+1`. Prove
`|(k+F_n) △ F_n| ≤ 2*|k|` for every integer `k` and natural `n`, and hence that
the ratio tends to zero. Use `IsAddFoelner` and the additive counterparts of the
discrete API, or transport through `Multiplicative ℤ` with explicit compatibility
lemmas. This proves amenability of `ℤ` by Layer 5.

For a finitely generated abelian group `A`, choose finitely many generators and
construct the surjective homomorphism from a finite product of copies of `ℤ`
sending the standard generators to them. Prove the universal-property,
surjectivity and additive/multiplicative transport lemmas needed for this map.
Finite-product and quotient closure then prove amenability of `A`.

Finally, apply the directed union of finitely generated subgroups from Layer 4
to prove amenability of every abelian discrete group, with no rank or torsion
restriction. Supply the additive API for `AddCommGroup` and its multiplicative
equivalent for `CommGroup`. The one-way topology bridge of Layer 2 also
gives the corresponding abelian topological-group example.

References: [Garrido](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~garrido/amenable.pdf),
Example 3.5 and Proposition 2.3; [BDHV](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/bachir.bekka/KazhdanTotal.pdf),
Example G.5.4 for the integer intervals.

## Layer 7: locally compact Hausdorff groups and Haar L∞

Assume `[LocallyCompactSpace G] [T2Space G]`, in addition to the topological-group
hypotheses, and use the Borel measurable space and a regular left Haar measure
`μ`. The canonical `Measure.haar` is an allowed choice. No sigma-compactness,
second countability or sigma-finiteness is a standing hypothesis.

Here **Haar L∞** means Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.Lp ℝ ∞ μ`: equivalence classes
modulo global Haar-almost-everywhere equality, with the essential-supremum norm.
Prove that `L_g` descends to a positive unital linear isometry on this space and
that the canonical map `UCB(G) → L∞(G,μ)` is a positive unital equivariant linear
isometry. The latter uses positivity of Haar measure on nonempty open sets to
identify the supremum and essential supremum of a continuous function.

Prove

```text
G amenable  ⟺  ∃ M : L∞(G, μ) → ℝ linear, positive, unital and left invariant.
```

Restriction along the UCB inclusion proves the reverse implication. Build the
forward implication by the following smoothing theory.

1. Prove the measurability and Fubini statements needed for convolution without
   adding sigma-finiteness of all of `G`. As connecting targets, prove that a global
   `L¹` function is zero almost everywhere outside a sigma-compact set, using
   regularity and finite-measure level sets. Put any countable collection of
   such supports into a sigma-compact open subgroup, adjoin a compact identity
   neighborhood, and justify restricted integrals and translated-coset
   calculations there. Prove agreement with ambient integrals and independence
   of the subgroup chosen. Kernels can be chosen within one such open subgroup.
   Sigma-compactness does not imply second countability. On the chosen subgroup,
   prove for the restricted Haar measure that every Borel set differs from a
   Baire set by a subset of a Baire Haar-null set, using
   [Haar completion regularity (Fremlin, *Measure Theory*, §443M)](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/chap44.pdf#page=29).
   Here the Baire sigma-algebra is generated by continuous real-valued functions.
   Use these representatives and null envelopes, together with compact-support
   approximation, to prove almost-everywhere strong measurability and Fubini for
   the scalar integrands. Do not assume `Borel(G × G) = Borel(G) ⊗ Borel(G)` or
   install a product-measurable multiplication instance without proving it. For
   the UCB-valued orbit integral, prove essential separability using continuity
   on sigma-compact supports.
   Prove that inversion and right translation preserve Haar-null sets. Use
   `c(g)=(MeasureTheory.Measure.modularCharacter g : ℝ)` for right translation.
   Supply the Haar pushforward and integral formulas for regular measures; where
   the existing pushforward lemma assumes `InnerRegular`, derive the `Regular`
   version from `isMulLeftInvariant_eq_smul_of_regular` and regularity under a
   homeomorphism. Do not infer global `InnerRegular` merely from `Regular`.
   Record `c(g)>0` and `c(g⁻¹)=c(g)⁻¹`, and prove continuity of `c` using a
   nonzero nonnegative compactly supported continuous test function and the
   integral transformation formula.
   Prove the inversion formula
   `μ.map Inv.inv = μ.withDensity (fun x ↦ (Measure.modularCharacter x : ℝ≥0∞))`.
   Its strictly positive finite density gives the null-set equivalence needed
   for representatives in the smoothing construction.
2. Develop `L¹` convolution, with
   `(h*k)(x)=∫ y, h(y)*k(y⁻¹*x) ∂μ` almost everywhere, its associativity and norm
   bounds, and preservation of nonnegative integral-one functions. Prove `L¹`
   continuity of translations and construct nonnegative integral-one kernels
   `h_U` supported in shrinking identity neighborhoods with `‖h*h_U-h‖₁→0` for
   every `h∈L¹`. These are nets. Use compactly supported continuous approximation.
3. For `h∈L¹(G,μ)` and `φ∈L∞(G,μ)`, construct the actual bounded continuous
   function `C_h φ(x)=∫ y, h(y)*φ(y⁻¹*x) ∂μ`. Prove independence of
   representatives, membership in UCB, `‖C_h φ‖∞≤‖h‖₁‖φ‖∞`, linearity,
   positivity when `h≥0`, and `C_h 1=(∫h)1`. Prove the mixed associativity
   identity `C_h(C_k φ)=C_(h*k) φ`, viewing `C_k φ` in L∞ by the canonical inclusion.
4. For an invariant UCB mean `m` and nonnegative integral-one `h`, prove
   `m(C_h ψ)=m(ψ)` for `ψ∈UCB`, using a Bochner integral of the norm-continuous
   translation orbit. Associativity and the preceding approximate identity give
   `m(C_h φ)=lim_U m(C_(h*h_U) φ)=lim_U m(C_(h_U) φ)`. Thus this value is
   independent of the normalized `h`. Fix one `h₀` and define
   `M(φ)=m(C_(h₀) φ)`. Prove positivity, normalization, continuity and invariance.
   For the last property, use the integral formula
   `∫f(x*g)dμ(x)=c(g)∫f dμ` from the preceding Haar pushforward target.
   Thus BDHV's convention `Δ(g)` is `c(g)⁻¹`. Prove
   `C_(h₀)(L_g φ)=C_(q_g)φ`, where
   `q_g(z)=c(g)*h₀(z*g⁻¹)` is again nonnegative of integral one.
5. Prove independence of amenability from scaling `μ` by a positive real
   constant, and compatibility of the characterization with the discrete case.

Also prove the correspondence between these L∞ means and finitely additive
probabilities on the **Borel sets** satisfying

```text
ν(gA) = ν(A),        μ(A) = 0  ⟹  ν(A) = 0.
```

Use `AddContent` on `{A | MeasurableSet A}`. Its values on nonmeasurable sets are
not part of the specification or of the equivalence: restrict to the subtype of
measurable sets, or quotient extensions by agreement there. Define
`ν(A)=M([1_A])`; conversely integrate Borel simple functions, approximate bounded
measurable representatives uniformly, and use null annihilation to descend
through almost-everywhere equality. An essentially bounded representative can
be truncated on a null set. Prove inverse laws on the specified domains,
including naturality of translations. Completion of the Haar measurable space
gives the same correspondence by extension across null sets.

[BDHV](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/bachir.bekka/KazhdanTotal.pdf), Theorem G.3.1
(i) and (v), is the principal reference. Its Section C.5 calls `A` locally Borel
when `A ∩ B` is Borel for every Borel `B` of finite Haar measure, and locally null
when all those intersections have measure zero. A function is locally measurable
when inverse images of Borel sets are locally Borel. The book uses functions
bounded outside a locally null set, modulo equality outside a locally null set.
This is not definitionally Mathlib's global `Lp`, and `L∞=(L¹)*` needs
measure-theoretic hypotheses not assumed here; the smoothing targets above prove
the global version directly. Prove using a countable finite-measure exhaustion
that, for sigma-finite Haar measure, locally Borel sets are Borel and locally null
sets are null. This gives agreement of the function and quotient conventions in
that case; a separate local-L∞ carrier is not a target.

As an example, let `G` be a compact Hausdorff group and `μ = TauCeti.haarProb G`,
the compact-group roadmap's Layer 0 target. By `TauCeti.haarProb_def` it is a
positive multiple of `Measure.haar`, hence a regular left Haar measure. Prove that
`M(φ)=∫ φ dμ` is a left-invariant mean on `L∞(G,μ)`, and that its restriction
along the UCB inclusion is an invariant UCB mean, so `G` is amenable. Prove that
for a finite discrete group `M` restricts to Layer 2's normalized counting. This
example concerns the given compact topology, not the underlying discrete group.

## Layer 8: Tarski's alternative for the whole discrete group

Prove for every discrete group, without countability assumptions,

```text
G amenable  ⟺  G is not paradoxical for its left regular action.
```

This is the **whole-group, left-regular-action form of Tarski's alternative**:
exactly one of an invariant finitely additive probability on all subsets and a
finite paradoxical decomposition exists. The forward implication is Layer 3. The
converse is required work, with the following proof dependencies made explicit.

1. Negating the finite-test Følner condition gives finite `K` and `ε>0` such that
   each finite nonempty `F` has some `g∈K` with
   `|gF △ F|≥ε|F|`. Put `S={1}∪K`. By the difference identity of Layer 5,
   `|SF|≥(1+ε/2)|F|`. Prove this uniformly for all finite `F`, including the
   empty set.
2. Prove iteration of this expansion and choose a natural `n` with
   `(1+ε/2)^n≥2`. Thus the finite set `D=S^n` satisfies `|DF|≥2|F|` for every
   finite `F`. Supply the finite-set multiplication and cardinality lemmas.
3. Apply the existing infinite-index Hall theorem to the neighbor sets
   `N(x,i)=D*x`, indexed by `(x,i)∈G×Fin 2`. For a finite set of indices `A`,
   its projection `F` satisfies `|A|≤2|F|≤|DF|=|⋃_(a∈A) N(a)|`.
   Obtain an injection `j : G×Fin 2 → G` with `j(x,i)∈D*x`.
4. Choose a multiplier from the finite set `D` for each value of `j`. For each
   copy `i`, its multiplier fibers give a finite equidecomposition from `G` to
   the image of `j(-,i)`. Prove the two images disjoint, convert the resulting
   subcopies to a partition by Layer 3, and obtain paradoxicality. With
   Layer 5, this proves nonamenability implies paradoxicality.

The assertion concerns the whole group, not every nonempty subset. Reference:
[Garrido](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~garrido/amenable.pdf),
Theorem 1.11 specialized to `X=E=G`, and Theorem 1.15(iii) in discrete scope.
A proof reference for this alternative is Ceccherini-Silberstein–Grigorchuk–de la
Harpe, [*Amenability and paradoxical decompositions for pseudogroups and for
discrete metric spaces*](https://people.tamu.edu/~grigorch/publications/zCGH.pdf),
Theorem 7, specialized to the left regular action; its relative-subset clause is
outside this target. Its §III.1, Theorem 35, gives the matching method; the
one-sided Hall theorem already in Mathlib suffices for the injection used here.

## Dependencies and completion

The dependency order is `1 → 2 → 3`, `1–3 → 4`, `1–2 → 5`, `4–5 → 6`,
`1–2 + compact-group roadmap Layer 0 → 7`, and `3 + 5 → 8`. Layer 7 does not
gate the discrete layers. Every connecting construction listed in a layer is
part of that layer's completion.

The completed theory is exercised by these targets: amenability of the trivial
group and of finite groups (Layer 2), nonamenability of `F₂` and of every
discrete group containing it (Layers 3 and 4), amenability of `ℤ` and of every
abelian discrete group (Layer 6), and amenability of every compact Hausdorff group
with its given topology (Layer 7); and the transport theorems for the real/complex
mean correspondence and group isomorphisms (Layer 1), the mean–content
correspondence (Layer 2), the counting-measure Følner filter (Layer 5) and the Haar
L∞ characterization (Layer 7).

The [Lean 3 invariant-mean development in mathlib PR #16574](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib3/pull/16574),
its Lean 4 successor [mathlib4 PR #7395, *Amenable monoid actions*](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/7395),
and the associated [Amenable Groups discussion](https://leanprover-community.github.io/archive/stream/113489-new-members/topic/Amenable.20Groups.html)
are predecessor sources. Neither PR was merged. Both are by the same author; the
Lean 4 PR defines amenability of a monoid action through finitely additive
invariant set functions on measurable sets, rather than through functional means
on a group. Before copying or adapting their code, coordinate with the author and
obtain agreement. If coordination is impossible, verify that the licence permits
the intended reuse and discuss the plan on Lean Zulip.

## Principal references

* Alejandra Garrido, [*An introduction to amenable groups*](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~garrido/amenable.pdf),
  especially §§1–3. Use the explicit discrete and null-set qualifications in this
  roadmap when applying its formulations.
* Bachir Bekka, Pierre de la Harpe and Alain Valette,
  [*Kazhdan's Property (T)*](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/bachir.bekka/KazhdanTotal.pdf),
  Cambridge University Press, 2008, Appendix G; also Appendix A.3 for uniformity
  and Haar conventions and C.5 for L∞. Definition and theorem numbers refer to the
  linked manuscript; its page numbers differ from the published edition.
* Tullio Ceccherini-Silberstein, Rostislav Grigorchuk and Pierre de la Harpe,
  [*Amenability and paradoxical decompositions for pseudogroups and for discrete
  metric spaces*](https://people.tamu.edu/~grigorch/publications/zCGH.pdf),
  Proceedings of the Steklov Institute of Mathematics **224** (1999), 57–97,
  especially Theorems 7, 25 and 35.
TauCetiRoadmap/BanachSpaceTheory:
# Banach space theory

Build the geometry and duality of Banach spaces, from weak compactness and bases to
approximation, tensor norms, summing operators and finite-dimensional geometry. The
depth milestones are James's theorem, Pietsch domination and factorization,
Grothendieck's inequality, local reflexivity and Dvoretzky's theorem. Each sits inside
a usable theory of spaces, operators and their constructions.

## Scope and conventions

Spaces are over `𝕜 = ℝ` or `ℂ`, expressed with `RCLike` where appropriate; completeness
is a hypothesis, not part of the meaning of normed space. The local geometry in B7
is over `ℝ`. All duals are continuous duals `StrongDual 𝕜 E`; reflexivity means
surjectivity of `NormedSpace.inclusionInDoubleDual`, not algebraic reflexivity.
Use `WeakSpace 𝕜 E` and `WeakDual 𝕜 E`, with explicit transport between topologies.
Weak convergence in a dual is different from weak-star convergence.

Operators are `ContinuousLinearMap`; subspaces and quotients use Mathlib's
`Submodule` and normed quotient constructions. A Banach subspace is closed.
Compactness and relative compactness must be distinguished: the latter means
compact closure in the stated ambient topology. A Schauder series converges along
initial segments; an unconditional series converges along the net of finite sets.
Use `SchauderBasis`, `UnconditionalSchauderBasis` and `SummationFilter` accordingly.

The prerequisites are Mathlib's Hahn–Banach theorem, Banach–Alaoglu theorem,
uniform boundedness, open mapping theorem, Bochner integration and finite-dimensional
linear algebra. Supply the additional constructions below in Tau Ceti. This roadmap
owns general Banach-space tensor norms and absolutely summing operators.
[Operator ideals](../OperatorTheory/OperatorIdeals/README.md) owns general approximation
numbers and finite-rank approximability, as well as Hilbert-space Schatten ideals,
trace norms and singular values; B4 owns the nuclear/trace-class comparison.
[Operator theory](../OperatorTheory/README.md) owns
the Hilbert-space spectral theory. C*-tensor norms are outside this Banach-space
scope. B5 consumes SelfAdjointSpectralTheory Part B's generic scalar-measure
integration, regularity and bounded continuous-approximation layer
(SA-B81–84 and SA-B58), which is independent
of PVMs, representations and this roadmap's bidual comparison.

## B1. Duality and weak topologies

Develop annihilators and preannihilators, order reversal, annihilators of sums and
intersections, and the double-annihilator theorem: `(Fᗮ)_⊥` is the norm closure
of a subspace `F ≤ E`, while `(G_⊥)ᗮ` is the weak-star closure of a subspace
`G ≤ E*`. For a
closed subspace `F ≤ E`, identify `(E/F)*` isometrically with `Fᗮ`, and `F*` with
`E*/Fᗮ`; construct restriction, quotient and inclusion maps and prove their naturality.
Develop the adjoint of a bounded map using `ContinuousLinearMap.precomp 𝕜 T`,
its norm, kernels, ranges and composition.
For a bounded operator between Banach spaces, with both domain and codomain
complete, prove the closed-range theorem: `range T` is norm closed iff
`range T*` is norm closed. Separate the unconditional identities
`ker T*=(range T)ᗮ`, `ker T=(range T*)_⊥`, and
`closure(range T)=(ker T*)_⊥` from the closed-range conclusion
`range T*=(ker T)ᗮ`. Give the incomplete-domain counterexample
`c₀₀⊂ℓ²` with its ℓ² norm: inclusion has dense proper range,
while its adjoint is surjective by extension to the completion.

Extend the existing canonical bidual embedding by its naturality under bounded
maps, Goldstine's theorem (its closed unit ball has weak-star dense image in the
bidual unit ball), and norming by the dual unit ball. Prove the bipolar theorem for
absolutely convex sets and the weak/norm closure agreement for convex sets; over
complex scalars convexity still means real convexity. Include the finite-convex-
combination form of Mazur's lemma for weakly convergent sequences.

Give weak and weak-star continuity criteria by evaluation, boundedness consequences
of weak boundedness, and the weak-star metrizability of a dual unit ball when the
predual is separable, reusing `WeakDual.metrizable_of_isCompact` and
`WeakDual.isSeqCompact_closedBall`. Specify an actual compatible metric from a dense sequence in
the predual unit ball and prove independence of the chosen sequence at the topology
level. Do not impose separability on Banach–Alaoglu or Goldstine.

## B2. Weak compactness and reflexivity

Prove the following with reusable intermediate separation, compactness and
subsequence lemmas.

* **Eberlein–Šmulian:** a subset of a normed space is weakly compact iff it is
  weakly sequentially compact. Also prove the relative version, where subsequential
  limits may lie in the ambient space. No separability assumption is allowed.
* **Reflexivity:** a Banach space is reflexive iff its closed unit ball is weakly
  compact. Establish invariance under bounded linear equivalence, inheritance by
  closed subspaces and quotients, and equivalence with reflexivity of the dual.
* **James:** for a nonempty weakly closed subset `A` of a Banach space, weak
  compactness is equivalent to attainment on `A` of the supremum of `|f|` for every
  continuous linear functional `f`. Attainment includes existence of a finite
  maximum. Deduce reflexivity iff every functional attains its norm on the closed
  unit ball. Develop the separable reduction and finite norming sets needed in the
  proof; keep completeness as an explicit hypothesis of the theorem.
* **Krein–Šmulian:** a convex subset of the dual of a Banach space is weak-star
  closed iff its intersection with every closed ball centered at zero is weak-star
  closed. Include the linear-subspace criterion using just the unit ball.
* **Bishop–Phelps:** for a Banach space, norm-attaining continuous linear
  functionals are norm dense in the dual. For a nonzero Banach space, support
  points are dense in the boundary of a nonempty closed convex set, and support
  functionals are norm dense in the dual when that set is also bounded.
  A support functional is nonzero and its real part attains its supremum on the
  set; a support point is such an attaining point. Treat the zero space separately.
* **Milman–Pettis:** every uniformly convex Banach space is reflexive. Develop the
  modulus of convexity, passage to closed subspaces and invariance of reflexivity
  under equivalent norms. Include the standard uniform convexity estimates for
  `Lᵖ`, `1 < p < ∞`.

For a bounded operator, weak compactness means relative weak compactness of the
image of the unit ball. For `T : E →L[𝕜] F` with `E` normed and `F` Banach,
prove the Gantmacher criterion
`T**(E**) ⊆ J_F(F)`, weak compactness iff weak compactness of the adjoint, stability
under sums and bounded compositions, and compact implies weakly compact.
Use the identity on an infinite-dimensional reflexive space to separate the two.

## B3. Schauder bases and classical spaces

The basis-constant, perturbation, duality and convergence results in this
milestone concern Banach spaces. Coordinate and finite-projection identities
retain the weaker hypotheses of Mathlib's basis API.

Extend Mathlib's basis and coordinate maps with coefficient uniqueness, basis
constants, equivalent norms making a basis monotone, subsequences and block bases
as bases of their closed spans, and equivalence of bases by two-sided inequalities
on finite linear combinations. Build the induced continuous linear equivalence of
closed spans. Prove the small perturbation theorem: if `(bₙ)` is a Schauder basis
and `∑ ‖bₙ*‖ ‖bₙ−cₙ‖ < 1`, then `(cₙ)` is an equivalent basis, via the bounded
invertible operator sending `bₙ` to `cₙ`. Give its norm and inverse-norm estimates.

A basis is shrinking when its coordinate functionals span a norm-dense subspace of
the dual. It is boundedly complete when every scalar sequence with bounded initial
partial sums gives a norm-convergent series. Develop the dual basic sequence on its
closed span, the shrinking/boundedly-complete duality, and James's basis criterion:
a Banach space with a Schauder basis is reflexive iff that basis is both shrinking
and boundedly complete. Do not equate an ordinary Schauder expansion with `tsum`
using the unconditional filter.

Use `UnconditionalSchauderBasis ℕ 𝕜 E` for sequence-indexed unconditional
bases; construct its conversions with a `SchauderBasis` whose expansion also
converges along `SummationFilter.unconditional ℕ`. Reuse
`SchauderBasis.nnnormProjBound` and `UnconditionalSchauderBasis.nnnormProjBound`
as basis constants. For unconditional bases, give the equivalent uniform bound on finite coordinate
projections and on signed coordinate multipliers, suppression and permutation
invariance, and extension of bounded scalar multipliers. Construct the canonical
bases of `c₀` and `ℓᵖ`, `1 ≤ p < ∞`, identify `c₀* = ℓ¹` and `(ℓᵖ)* = ℓᑫ` for
`1 < p < ∞`, and identify `(ℓ¹)* = ℓ∞`. Use Mathlib's sequence-space models and
give isometric equivalences rather than introducing competing spaces.
Use `C₀(ℕ,𝕜)` (`ZeroAtInftyContinuousMap`) for `c₀`, and `lp` for `ℓᵖ`;
prove the dual identifications using the corresponding scalar integral/series
pairings, including `lp.dualPairing` at conjugate exponents.

Prove Schur's theorem for `ℓ¹`. Exhibit the unit-vector sequence in `c₀` as weakly
null but not norm null, the nonreflexivity of `c₀` and `ℓ¹`, and reflexivity of `ℓᵖ`
for `1 < p < ∞`. These examples also distinguish shrinking from bounded completeness.
Construct the Haar basis of `Lᵖ([0,1])`, `1 ≤ p < ∞`, with the constant first
vector, unnormalized ±1 functions on successive dyadic intervals, and increasing
dyadic levels. Its initial projections are averages on the successively refined
dyadic atom partitions; construct these contractions, their composition law and
convergence on `Lᵖ`, first on dense step functions. For unconditionality, prove
the scalar Bellman estimates for `p > 2` and
`Φ_p(x,y)=(x+y)^(p−1)((p−1)x−y)`, for `x,y ≥ 0`:
`((p−1)^(p−1)/p^(p−2))Φ_p(x,y) ≤ (p−1)^p x^p−y^p`, and
`Φ_p(|x+a|,|y+εa|)+Φ_p(|x−a|,|y−εa|) ≥ 2Φ_p(|x|,|y|)`
for real `x,y,a` and `ε=±1`. Integrate the midpoint inequality inductively
over each split dyadic atom to obtain the signed-transform bound `p−1`.
Use orthogonality at `p=2` and finite-atom Hölder duality at conjugate
`q>2` for `1<p<2`. Thus the real Haar sign-transform bound is
`max(p,p/(p−1))−1`. Deduce the complex bound twice that value by real/imaginary
parts, and hence unconditionality over both fields.

## B4. Approximation and Banach tensor products

The approximation-property equivalences and stability results below concern
Banach spaces. Algebraic tensor norms are defined for normed spaces; completed
tensor/operator identifications, nuclear operators and scalar-unit isometries
use Banach factors. In particular the target `F` is complete in the operator
identifications involving `E* ⊗ε F` and `E* ⊗π F`.

Define the approximation property by uniform approximation of the identity on
each norm-compact subset by bounded finite-rank operators. The `λ`-bounded
approximation property adds `‖T‖ ≤ λ`; BAP means such a finite `λ` exists and MAP
means `λ = 1`. Prove MAP implies BAP implies AP. Under a bounded linear
equivalence `U`, transport `λ`-BAP to `λ‖U‖‖U⁻¹‖`-BAP; AP and BAP
are invariant under these equivalences, while MAP is preserved by isometric
equivalences. For a bounded projection `P` onto a closed subspace, prove
inheritance of AP and transport `λ`-BAP to `λ‖P‖`-BAP. Prove BAP from
a Schauder basis with its basis constant. Prove MAP for
`c₀`, `ℓᵖ` and `Lᵖ([0,1])`, `1 ≤ p < ∞`, using the explicit projections.

Prove Grothendieck's equivalence: `E` has AP iff every compact operator `F → E`
from every Banach space is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators. Include
the compact-disk construction and the fact that a relatively norm-compact set is
contained in the closed convex hull of a null sequence.

Use distinct normed type synonyms of Mathlib's binary `TensorProduct 𝕜 E F`
for the projective and injective norms, and
`UniformSpace.Completion` for the completed
tensors. Give norm-preserving pure-tensor comparisons with the finite-family
`PiTensorProduct` interfaces. On the algebraic tensor product define the projective norm by the infimum of
`∑ ‖xᵢ‖ ‖yᵢ‖` over finite decompositions and the injective norm by
`sup {|∑ f(xᵢ)g(yᵢ)| : ‖f‖ ≤ 1, ‖g‖ ≤ 1}`. Prove they are norms over `ℝ` and `ℂ`,
the elementary-tensor equality, and `ε ≤ π`. Construct their completions, their
dense algebraic embeddings, the maps induced by bounded maps in both variables,
and symmetry, associativity and scalar-unit isometries with coherence on pure
tensors. The injective tensor product preserves isometric embeddings; the
projective tensor product preserves metric quotient maps.

Prove the norm-preserving universal property of the completed projective tensor
product for bounded bilinear maps into a Banach space, and its dual identification
with bounded bilinear forms. Prove that every completed projective tensor is a
norm-convergent series `∑ xₙ⊗yₙ` with `∑ ‖xₙ‖‖yₙ‖ < ‖u‖π+ε` for each
`ε>0`, by successive finite-tensor approximations. Identify the injective completion `E* ⊗ε F` with the
operator-norm closure of finite-rank maps `E → F`. Construct the canonical map
`E* ⊗π F → (E →L[𝕜] F)` and its range with quotient norm: nuclear operators.
Prove completeness, rank-one norm, the ideal inequality and the series
representation `T x = ∑ fₙ(x)yₙ` with `∑ ‖fₙ‖‖yₙ‖ < ∞`; the nuclear norm is the
infimum over those representations. Use the range submodule of the canonical map
as the underlying algebraic carrier, with a separate normed type synonym carrying
the quotient norm and a contractive forgetful map into bounded operators.
Prove the kernel closed. Reuse OperatorIdeals OI-A01 and
OI-A25–OI-A28 for approximation numbers and finite-rank approximability.
Connect AP to tensors: a Banach space `E` has AP iff
`F ⊗π E → F ⊗ε E` is injective for every Banach `F`. Prove that
`E* ⊗π F → (E →L[𝕜] F)` is injective if `E*` or `F` has AP; distinguish
this hypothesis-dependent tensor identification from the always-defined
quotient-norm nuclear carrier. Build the finite-rank tensor approximation and
separation/compact-set arguments for these comparisons.
Keep the nuclear norm distinct from operator norm. On Hilbert pairs, construct
its isometric identification with OperatorIdeals OI-B29–OI-B30's trace-class
gauge. Construct the compact Schmidt series from the existing compact
self-adjoint theorem, reusing Mathlib's
`ContinuousLinearMap.orthogonalComplement_iSup_eigenspaces_eq_bot` and
Tau Ceti's `exists_hilbertBasis_forall_hasEigenvector` in
`TauCeti.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Spectrum`. For compact `T:H→K` on
complete real or complex Hilbert spaces, apply these to `T†T`. Order the
positive eigenvalues `λ_j` with multiplicity and put `s_j=√λ_j`.
Prove only finitely many eigenvalues exceed
any positive threshold, and choose the associated finite or countable
orthonormal families `(e_j),(f_j)`, with `f_j=s_j⁻¹T e_j` and
`s_j>0` nonincreasing, tending to zero in the infinite-rank case. Prove
`Tx=∑ s_j⟪e_j,x⟫f_j`, vanishing on ker T, and operator-norm convergence
of its finite truncations. Zero-pad the singular-value sequence in the
finite-rank case and prove `s_n=a_n(T)` with the zero-based OI convention:
the rank-n truncation gives the upper bound and, below the rank, a kernel
vector on an (n+1)-dimensional singular span gives the lower bound;
at or above finite rank both sides are zero. A finite trace-class
gauge implies compactness by the OI approximation-number criterion.
The summable Schmidt series gives the nuclear-norm upper bound. For the
reverse inequality, use OI's gauge subadditivity and rank-one norm on
partial nuclear sums, operator-norm continuity of each `a_n`, and Fatou
for the series of approximation numbers. This also pins the rank-one norms.

Identify `(E ⊗ε F)*` with integral bilinear forms: those forms whose induced
linear functional on algebraic tensors is bounded for `ε`, with norm the least
such bound. Prove evaluation, completeness, rank-one formulas, and bounded
functoriality in both factors. Compare currying into `F*` and the forgetful map
to bounded bilinear forms; do not conflate the integral and ordinary bilinear norms.

## B5. Function spaces and weak compactness

This milestone uses Banach spaces and finite measure spaces. For compact Hausdorff
`K` with its Borel measurable structure, develop the Banach-space duality between `C(K,𝕜)` and
finite regular scalar Borel measures, with the total-variation norm, evaluation
measures and the weak-star topology. Use the submodule of
`MeasureTheory.VectorMeasure K 𝕜` with finite regular variation, normed by
`(ν.variation Set.univ).toReal`; compare with native `SignedMeasure` and
`ComplexMeasure`. Use native `VectorMeasure.variation_smul` for scalar
closure and norm homogeneity, with SA-B83's regularity comparisons.
Construct the norm and Dirac maps; write
`M(K)` for this normed measure submodule. Consume `VectorMeasure.integral`
for its integration pairing, using `ContinuousLinearMap.mul ℝ 𝕜`
over any `RCLike 𝕜`. Consume
SelfAdjointSpectralTheory SA-B81–82's 𝕜-linearity and scalar-integral
comparison, SA-B83’s finite absolute-continuity regularity lemma, and
SA-B84’s generic scalar-measure uniqueness for injectivity. Prove this normed
dual identification, continuous-function evaluation and the variation norm. Use
`VectorMeasure.variation`, native scalar Radon–Nikodym
derivatives and `RealRMK.rieszMeasure`. Construct positive and negative parts
of real bounded functionals using `Λ⁺(f)=sup{Λ(g):0≤g≤f}` for `f≥0`;
prove additivity, boundedness and extension to a positive linear functional.
Apply RMK to those parts. For general RCLike-valued functionals, restrict to real-valued
functions and represent their real and imaginary parts. Reconstruct the
measure using SA-B81 and extend from real tests using 𝕜-linearity. Build the
Radon–Nikodym density construction below before proving norm equality: at
ν=|μ| it gives μ=ν.withDensityᵥ h and ‖h‖=1 ν-a.e. The integral bound proves
‖Λ_μ‖≤ν(K). For the reverse inequality, choose a measurable representative of
conj(h) bounded by one everywhere, apply SA-B58 to approximate it in L¹(ν)
by continuous functions with the same bound, and use SA-B82's pairing identity.
Their integrals against μ tend to ν(K), hence ν(K)≤‖Λ_μ‖. This uses only
native signed Radon–Nikodym theory and SA-B81–84/58, independently of the dual
identification. Prove surjectivity by the RMK parts construction, then transport
completeness from the strong dual through this onto linear isometry. Export the
resulting isometric dual equivalence and its weak-star evaluation laws.
For nonempty `K`, prove that the extreme points of its dual unit ball are
exactly `λδ_x`, `|λ|=1`, by splitting variation on measurable sets and
using regularity; handle empty spaces separately.
Prove the Banach–Stone theorem in its operator form: a surjective linear
isometry `C(K,𝕜) → C(L,𝕜)` is `f ↦ h · (f ∘ φ)`, where `φ : L ≃ₜ K` and
`h : C(L,𝕜)` has pointwise modulus one; include uniqueness and the converse.
Construct `φ` and `h` from the adjoint action on extreme Dirac functionals,
with `h=T1`, and prove continuity of `φ` via evaluation of continuous functions.

For a finite measure `μ`, prove the Dunford–Pettis weak compactness criterion:
a subset of `L¹(μ)` is relatively weakly compact iff it is norm bounded and its
integrals `∫_A ‖f‖ dμ` are uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to `μ`:
for every `ε>0` there is `δ>0` such that `μ(A)≤δ` implies all these integrals
are at most `ε`. Relate this to native `UnifIntegrable` at exponent 1, and the
bounded version to `UniformIntegrable`; transport representatives of `Lp`
classes explicitly. Relate this
to the uniform tail-integral criterion. Build the truncation, Radon–Nikodym and
weak-closure arguments, and prove weak sequential completeness of `L¹(μ)`.

An operator is completely continuous if weakly convergent sequences have
norm-convergent images. Prove equivalence to taking weakly compact sets to
norm-compact sets. The Dunford–Pettis property of a space means that every weakly
compact operator from it to any Banach space is completely continuous. Prove the
criterion `fₙ(xₙ) → 0` when both sequences are weakly null in the space and its
dual, and prove the property for `C(K)` and `L¹(μ)`. Supply the connecting
constructions: for a weakly null sequence of regular scalar measures `(νₙ)`,
form the finite regular measure `ν=∑ 2^(−n−1)|νₙ|`. Prove that
for every finite regular positive ν `g↦ν.withDensityᵥ g` is an
isometric embedding `L¹(ν)→M(K)` with closed range, consuming native
`Measure.variation_withDensityᵥ` and SA-B82's pairing identity
`⟨f,ν.withDensityᵥ g⟩=∫fg dν`. For ℂ, identify the generic density below with native
`ComplexMeasure.rnDeriv` using SA-B81’s real/imaginary compatibility;
consume native `integrable_rnDeriv`. For ℝ consume native
`SignedMeasure.absolutelyContinuous_iff_withDensityᵥ_rnDeriv_eq` and
`SignedMeasure.totalVariation_eq_variation`. For general RCLike 𝕜,
for `[SigmaFinite ν]` and `|μ|≪ν`, construct the integrable density
`h=rnDeriv(re μ,ν)+I·rnDeriv(im μ,ν)` from SA-B81’s signed parts.
Prove `μ=ν.withDensityᵥ h` using their absolute continuity and SA-B81’s
reconstruction, and specialize to the same native ℝ and ℂ derivatives.
Consume `Integrable.withDensityᵥ_eq_iff` for a.e.-uniqueness and
`Measure.variation_withDensityᵥ` for
`|μ|=ν.withDensity (fun x=>‖h x‖ₑ)` under these same hypotheses; for μ∈M(K), ν=|μ| is finite by definition, hence σ-finite;
prove |h|=1 ν-a.e. Use these derivatives to transfer weak
nullity to the densities in the displayed dominating-measure construction.
Uniform integrability of those densities and bounded convergence of the weakly
null continuous functions then prove the `C(K)` sequence criterion.
Construct the isometric duality `(L¹(μ))*≃L∞(μ)` by the integral pairing,
with indicator tests and Radon–Nikodym densities giving surjectivity and the
essential-bound norm equality. Reuse native scalar `Lp 𝕜 ∞ μ` star and
the Hölder `HSMul` product at exponents ∞,∞,∞ for pointwise multiplication,
construct its unit, and prove its commutative C*-algebra laws over
`ℂ`. Reuse Mathlib's `gelfandStarTransform` to identify it with `C(K_μ,ℂ)`;
construct the real-linear isometries
`selfAdjoint (Lp ℂ ∞ μ) ≃ Lp ℝ ∞ μ` and
`selfAdjoint C(K_μ,ℂ) ≃ C(K_μ,ℝ)` for the real version.
