### Graphs, networks, and orientations

**Undirected graphs** use `G : Graph α β`, with actual vertices `V(G) ⊆ α` and edges `E(G) ⊆ β`.
Vertex and edge finiteness are independent hypotheses on these subtypes, not the ambient types; use subtype `Fintype` instances for finite sums.
A **finite graph** has finite `V(G)` and finite `E(G)`.
Walk endpoints and separators belong to `V(G)`; deleting edges counts identities in `E(G)`, including separate parallel edges.
Loops are allowed.
Use `G.toSimpleGraph : SimpleGraph V(G)` for properties insensitive to loops and parallel edges, and `Graph.ofSimpleGraph` to state and prove the simple-graph corollaries.
Simple-graph statements carry decidability instances exactly where the Mathlib definitions they mention require them; proofs may reason classically.

A weighted multigraph is `G` together with nonnegative capacities `c : E(G) → K`; zero capacities retain the edge in the graph.
Its cut capacity sums over actual crossing edges, once per edge, so parallel capacities add and loops contribute zero.
For the pair-capacity interface, a nonnegative `c : Sym2 V → K` has simple support graph with adjacency `v ≠ w ∧ 0 < c(s(v,w))`.
Diagonal capacities are allowed and ignored by both the support graph and cuts.
Aggregate a weighted multigraph to pair capacities on `Sym2 V(G)` by summing capacities of all edges joining each pair of distinct vertices and setting diagonal values to zero.
This aggregation preserves weighted cuts, not individual edge identities or unweighted edge-disjoint paths.

**Directed networks** are terms, not typeclass instances.

- **Coefficients.** The finite-bound theory is parameterized by a linearly ordered additive commutative group `K`, expressed by `[AddCommGroup K] [LinearOrder K] [IsOrderedAddMonoid K]`.
  It must not assume a unit, multiplication, division, an Archimedean property, topology, or order completeness; in particular, the same theory applies to `ℤ`, `ℚ`, and `ℝ`.
  The minimum-cut theory of Targets 4.1 and 4.3 and Milestone 9 never subtracts and is stated over a linearly ordered cancellative additive commutative monoid, `[AddCommMonoid K] [LinearOrder K] [IsOrderedCancelAddMonoid K]`, so that `ℕ` and `ℝ≥0` are instances alongside these groups; Target 4.2, and the submodularity of the signed upper cut bound `U` that Target 4.1 also proves, use the group.
  The definition and elementary closure lemmas for submodularity use the weaker assumptions specified in Target 4.1.
- **Carrier.** A network `N : Network K V` carries an arrow type `N.Hom v w` for every ordered pair of vertices, in a universe independent of the vertex universe, as for `Quiver.{v}`.
  Each arrow has lower and upper bounds `ℓ, u` in `K`, with a proof of `ℓ ≤ u`; bounds may be negative, and all bounds are finite.
  Parallel arrows, arrows in opposite directions, loops, and zero capacities are allowed; the total arrow type is the dependent sum of the arrow types over ordered pairs of vertices.
  The carrier and bound-order invariant need no finiteness; targets requiring finite vertices or arrows use `[Fintype V]` or `[∀ v w, Fintype (N.Hom v w)]`, respectively.
  An ordinary network is the specialization `ℓ = 0` of this same structure, constructed from nonnegative upper capacities; provide a constructor and simplification lemmas, not a second network type.
  Define arrow assignments, excess, and cut capacity against an explicit arrow family `Hom : V → V → Type`, with bounds as separate parameters where needed; the network bundle exposes these definitions and the bounded-assignment types through abbreviations, so bundled and unbundled networks share the same objects and theorems.
  Abbreviations ignoring a network's lower bounds, such as its ordinary flow type, say so in their names.
  A `Quiver` term is never a parameter.
  **Why:** instance search for `Fintype (Hom v w)` does not see through `Quiver.mk`.
- **Sums.** Every network sum is a `Finset.sum` in `K`; the finite theory requires no infinite sums or infinite capacities.
- **Directed walks.** Use Mathlib's [`Quiver.Path`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Combinatorics/Quiver/Path.html#Quiver.Path), with the quiver argument supplied explicitly from the arrow family, as in `@Quiver.Path V ⟨N.Hom⟩ s t`.
  Networks and orientations share this carrier and reuse its length, composition, vertex-list, and transport API; add the missing simple-path and cycle predicates using `Quiver.Path.vertices`.
  Strong connectivity is Mathlib's [`Quiver.IsStronglyConnected`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Combinatorics/Quiver/ConnectedComponent.html#Quiver.IsStronglyConnected) with the same explicit quiver argument.
  Abbreviations may expose these operations through the network or arrow family.
  **Why:** several quivers then coexist on `V` without competing instances or vertex-type synonyms.

**An orientation** of `G : Graph α β` orders the ends of each edge, with one directed arrow per edge identity and no additional arrows.
A loop gives one directed loop; it has a unique ordered pair of ends.
Its directed walks use the resulting arrow family on `V(G)`.
Simple-graph orientations use the existing `TauCeti.DoubledQuiver.Orientation H`, whose carrier contains exactly one dart from each reversed pair, and its `OrientedQuiver`.
The bidirected network has zero lower bounds and one arrow in each direction for every nonloop edge and one loop arrow for every loop, with the original edge's capacity on each arrow.
Milestone 1 identifies both constructions with the existing simple-graph interfaces and supplies their transport lemmas.

**Namespaces.** Undirected multigraph declarations extend `Graph`.
Simple-graph declarations extend `SimpleGraph`, following [#33355](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/33355) and [#42494](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42494) for connectivity; orientation results extend the existing Tau Ceti orientation namespace.
`Suggested.lean` keeps stand-ins for proposed definitions outside the Mathlib namespaces.
**Why:** the prototype namespace avoids name conflicts with additions to Mathlib.

### Paths, separators, and connectivity

**Undirected walks** are `G.Walk u v`, an inductive type indexed by the ambient vertex type, with constructors `nil` at any point and `cons e h p` for `h : G.IsLink e u v`; a walk therefore retains the identity of each traversed edge, and a loop is traversed in only one way.
Every vertex on a walk of positive length is an actual vertex; reachability requires actual vertices as endpoints, so a zero-length walk at a point outside `V(G)` witnesses nothing.
**Why:** a walk is then determined by its vertex sequence and edge identities, which is all the connectivity and flow targets use; a direction of traversal around a loop is extra data that would double every loop walk and loop cycle.
The bidirected quiver has one arrow `s → t` per edge `e` with `G.IsLink e s t`; Target 1.1 identifies its paths with walks between actual vertices for use in the flow reductions.
Undirected and directed paths have no repeated vertices.
An undirected cycle is a positive-length closed walk with no repeated vertices apart from its endpoints and no repeated edge identities.
Thus a loop is a one-edge cycle and two distinct parallel edges form a two-edge cycle; traversing the same edge out and back is not a cycle.
Directed cycles have positive length and no repeated vertices apart from the coinciding endpoints.
Path families are finite and contain distinct paths, except for the explicitly repeated capacitated packings of Target 5.1.
Edge-disjointness concerns identities in `E(G)` for a multigraph, unordered edges for a simple graph, and actual arrow identities in a network.
Internally vertex-disjoint paths between distinct terminals may share only those terminals.
In particular, a family cannot count the same single-edge path repeatedly merely because it has no internal vertices.

A local vertex separator for distinct terminals `s, t` excludes both terminals and destroys reachability after deletion.
The local vertex form of Menger therefore assumes that `s` and `t` are nonadjacent; in the directed case, there must be no arrow from `s` to `t`.
**Why:** adjacent terminals can satisfy deletion-based vertex reachability for every `k`, exceeding their internally disjoint path count.
Milestone 5 also gives the adjacent-terminal version, counting all direct parallel edges, and its simple-graph specialization.

For vertex-disjoint paths between sets `A` and `B`, separators may meet `A ∪ B`.
Paths have one endpoint in each set, their interiors avoid `A ∪ B`, and the paths are disjoint including endpoints.
A vertex in `A ∩ B` contributes a permitted zero-length path and must belong to every separator.
There is no prescribed pairing of the endpoints.
For the edge-disjoint set-to-set version, require `A` and `B` to be disjoint; paths may share endpoints.

Multigraph reachability is defined by walks.

Use natural-number thresholds, coerced where an upstream predicate takes `ℕ∞`.

### Flows and bounded circulations

Write `δ⁺(S)` for arrows leaving a vertex set and `δ⁻(S)` for arrows entering it.
An ordinary `PseudoFlow` is an arrow assignment with proofs of `0 ≤ f ≤ u`; a `Flow s t` adds zero excess away from distinct terminals and nonnegative excess at `t`.
Use incoming-minus-outgoing `excessAt`, with capacities, assignments, excess, and value in `K` and all sums finite.
Flow value is `excess f t`, equivalently `−excess f s`.
**Why:** demand has positive excess, supply has negative excess, and the same additive calculus serves ordinary flows and signed bounded assignments.
Define excess on arbitrary assignments and conservation independently of `Flow`.
A cut is a source side `S` with `s ∈ S` and `t ∉ S`, of capacity `u(δ⁺(S))`.
Arrows entering the source or leaving the sink are allowed.

A bounded assignment satisfies `ℓ ≤ f ≤ u` arrowwise, with no conservation or sign restriction.
Prescribed excess means `excess f = b`; a bounded circulation is the case `b = 0`.
Keep this equality-based interface, and also express interval excess by `a v ≤ excess f v ≤ b v` on the same bounded assignments.
Vertex constraints are separate parameters, not fields of `Network`; Target 8.3 relates equal-endpoint intervals to exact prescribed excess.
A bounded `s–t` assignment has zero excess away from distinct terminals, with value `excess f t` of either sign.
The prototypes call bounded terminal assignments `BoundedFlow`, exact-excess assignments `Realizes`, and interval-excess assignments `RealizesWithin`.
Ordinary `Flow` is the zero-lower-bound, nonnegative-value specialization of bounded terminal assignments, sharing their assignments, excess, and bound calculations.

For every feasible assignment `f` with finite bounds on `N`, its residual network has the same vertex type, arrow type `N.Hom v w ⊕ N.Hom w v` from `v` to `w`, zero lower bounds, and upper capacity `u e − f e` on a forward arrow and `f e − ℓ e` on a reverse arrow.
The arrow type is independent of `f` and retains zero-capacity arrows; augmenting paths lie in its positive-capacity subnetwork.
**Why:** fixed arrow types avoid path transport after every augmentation, while the sum tags distinguish forward capacity from cancellation even with antiparallel original arrows.
For ordinary flows `ℓ = 0`, so reverse residual capacity is `f e`.
For finite bounds, the source-side cut bound is `U(S) = u(δ⁺(S)) − ℓ(δ⁻(S))`; its corresponding lower bound on terminal value is `L(S) = ℓ(δ⁺(S)) − u(δ⁻(S)) = −U(Sᶜ)`.
Ordinary directed cut capacity is the case `ℓ = 0` of `U`; undirected weighted cuts retain their existing nonnegative-capacity conventions.

## 3. Flows and max-flow/min-cut

### 3.1. Finite flows and assignment decomposition

Derive weak duality from the excess calculus of [Target 1.3](#13-excess-calculus-subnetworks-bounds-and-residual-updates): the value of every feasible flow is at most the capacity of every terminal-separating cut.
Every target in this section concerns ordinary flows, with zero lower bounds and nonnegative value.

1. **Residual augmentation.** Augmenting along a simple augmenting `s–t` path by its minimum residual capacity preserves feasibility and increases flow value by that positive amount.
   Use the common residual update of Milestone 1 and derive the corresponding bounded-circulation cycle augmentation lemma.
2. **Nonnegative assignment decomposition.** Every nonnegative arrow assignment on a finite quiver, without any conservation hypothesis or capacity data, is a finite sum of positively weighted simple directed paths and directed cycles, with equality on every original arrow.
   Each path starts at a vertex of negative original excess and ends at one of positive original excess, with no excess restriction on internal vertices.
   A walk of weight `q` contributes `n • q` to each arrow it traverses `n` times, using natural-number scalar multiplication without a multiplicative unit.
   State the supply and demand identities: the total weight of paths starting at a supply vertex is minus its original excess, and the total weight ending at a demand vertex is its original excess.
   Permit empty path and cycle families, include loops as cycles, and prove that every component assignment is bounded arrowwise by the original assignment.
   Bound the total number of weighted components by the number of arrows with positive original value; this bound precedes any expansion of integer weights into unit paths.
   If the original assignment takes values in an additive subgroup `H`, choose every coefficient in `H`.
   **Suggested proof:** cancel cycles, then peel maximal paths from the acyclic support, removing a support arrow at each step.
   Derive the ordinary `s–t` flow decomposition and the cycle-only decomposition of nonnegative zero-excess assignments as corollaries.
   For a pseudoflow conserved away from the terminals with negative excess at the designated sink, use terminal exchange to obtain paths in the opposite direction.
   These statements require nonnegative arrow values; general signed circulations use the nonnegative residual difference of [Target 8.4](#84-residual-adjustments) for cycle adjustments.
3. **Acyclic flows.** Every ordinary flow has an acyclic flow of the same value: a flow whose assignment is arrowwise no larger and whose support contains no directed cycle; in particular it uses no loop and at most one of any two opposite arrows, and every arrow value is at most the flow value.
   Preserve values in an additive subgroup.
   A decomposition without cycle components need not have acyclic support: unit flows along `s → a → b → t` and `s → b → a → t` together contain the cycle `a → b → a`.
   **Suggested proof:** repeatedly cancel a support cycle by its minimum arrow value, strictly shrinking support; then use path decomposition to bound each arrow value by the total flow value.
4. **Max-flow/min-cut.** There exist a feasible flow and a terminal-separating cut with equal value and capacity.
   Prove the equivalent optimality criteria: maximum flow, no augmenting `s–t` path, and existence of a cut attaining equality.
   Develop shortest-path augmentation as a reusable terminating relation on feasible flows: a step chooses any positive-residual `s–t` path of minimum arrow length and augments by its full bottleneck capacity.
   Prove that the relation is well-founded in the direction of successive augmentations, from any initial feasible flow, and that a flow has no successor exactly when it is maximum.
   Supply the existence of a shortest augmenting path whenever any augmenting path exists, preservation of feasibility, and strict increase of value at each step.
   These statements hold over every coefficient group `K` in the conventions; executable path search and complexity bounds are not targets.
   **Suggested proof:** residual distances do not decrease under shortest-path augmentation, and repeated saturation of a tagged arrow forces progress in those distances; finiteness of the residual graph gives termination independently of coefficient discreteness, Archimedeanness, or completeness.
5. **Integrality.** Capacities in an additive subgroup `H` of `K` admit a maximum flow whose arrow values are in `H` and whose value equals the minimum cut capacity.
   **Why:** residual capacities and augmentations preserve additive-subgroup membership.
   Natural-number capacities in `ℤ`, `ℚ`, or `ℝ` are the case `H = AddSubgroup.zmultiples 1`; state that case with `ℕ`-casts and give the explicit coercion lemmas between the three coefficient types.
6. **Termination for cyclic capacity subgroups.** For capacities in `AddSubgroup.zmultiples d` with `0 < d`, every flow value is at most the total capacity leaving the source, which is a multiple `m • d`, and a flow with arrow values in the subgroup has value `n • d` with `n ≤ m`.
   Augmentation from such a flow keeps the arrow values in the subgroup by item 5 and increases the value by at least `d`, so the relation "`g` has larger value than `f`" is well-founded on flows with arrow values in the subgroup, and every sequence of augmentations starting from one terminates, whatever the choice of augmenting paths; no Archimedean assumption is needed.
   State the integer specialization, where every flow has arrow values in the subgroup for `d = 1`, and the rational specialization, with the lemma that finitely many rational capacities lie in the subgroup generated by the reciprocal of a common denominator `D`, for `d = 1 / D`.
   No such assertion is made for capacities outside a cyclic subgroup, where augmentation sequences can fail to terminate; there item 4 relies on the shortest-path rule.

- A nonnegative assignment with two supply vertices, two demand vertices, and a cycle, verifying arrowwise reconstruction and the supply and demand weight identities.

## 5. Menger's theorem

### 5.1. Path–separator duality

All versions assume finitely many actual vertices.
Edge-disjoint versions also require finite edge or arrow sets; vertex versions do not, except that adjacent-terminal Menger requires finite direct terminal edges or arrows.
Give every version for multigraphs and directed networks, with `SimpleGraph` and `Digraph` corollaries through [Target 1.1](#11-undirected-walks-isomorphisms-and-representation-bridges), retaining actual edge or arrow identities in path witnesses.

For every version, prove **attainment and weak duality**: some admissible path family or packing has size equal to a separator's cardinality or specified weight, and every admissible family or packing has size at most every separator's cardinality or weight.
For adjacent terminals, add the correction `m` below to the separator size in both statements.
**Why:** numerical connectivity invariants alone supply neither attaining witnesses nor their optimality certificates.

- **Local edge Menger:** for distinct terminals `s, t`, use pairwise edge-disjoint `s–t` paths and sets of edge or arrow identities whose deletion destroys `s–t` reachability.
- **Local vertex Menger:** for distinct nonadjacent terminals, use internally vertex-disjoint paths and terminal-excluding vertex separators, following the [directed adjacency convention](#paths-separators-and-connectivity).
- **Vertex-capacitated Menger:** under the same terminal assumptions and with capacities `c : V → ℕ`, a **packing** is a finite indexed family of `s–t` paths, repetitions allowed, in which each nonterminal vertex `v` occurs in at most `c v` members counted with repetition.
  A terminal-excluding vertex separator `X` has weight `∑ v ∈ X, c v`.
  The local vertex Menger statements are the case `c = 1`: a packing is then a family of distinct internally vertex-disjoint paths, since two members sharing an internal vertex would exceed its capacity and the adjacency hypothesis excludes members without internal vertices.
- **Adjacent terminals:** let `D` be the set of all edges joining distinct terminals `s,t`, and let `m = |D|`.
  In the directed version, `D` consists exactly of arrows `s → t`; arrows `t → s` are retained and do not contribute to `m`.
  After deleting all of `D`, a terminal-excluding vertex separator of size `k` and a family of `k + m` internally vertex-disjoint paths in the original graph attain equality, for some `k`.
  The attaining family includes all `m` distinct one-edge paths; weak duality bounds every internally vertex-disjoint family by `|X| + m` for every separator `X` after deleting `D`.
  The simple-graph corollary has `m = 1` and hence `k + 1` paths, including for the single-edge graph where `k = 0`.
- **Set-to-set Menger:** use vertex-disjoint `A`–`B` paths and vertex sets meeting every such path, with the [overlap convention](#paths-separators-and-connectivity).
  Also give the edge-disjoint version for disjoint terminal sets, with edge or arrow separators and shared endpoints allowed.
- **Vertex-capacitated set-to-set Menger:** for arbitrary terminal sets `A, B` and capacities `c : V → ℕ`, a packing is a finite indexed family of `A–B` paths with repetition, whose interiors avoid `A ∪ B`, such that each vertex `v`, including endpoints, belongs to at most `c v` members counted with repetition.
  A separator may meet the terminal sets and has weight `∑ v ∈ X, c v`.
  Recover vertex-disjoint set-to-set Menger at `c = 1`; for `v ∈ A ∩ B`, a zero-length path may be repeated up to `c v` times, and every separator contains `v` even when `c v = 0`.
  Include empty terminal sets and zero capacities.

To obtain vertex versions without finite edge or arrow sets, use simplification or one arrow per inhabited `Q v w`, then lift paths by choosing actual edges or arrows.

## 7. Ear decompositions and strong orientations

### 7.1. Ear decompositions as data

An open ear in a multigraph is a positive-length path adding unused edge identities, with distinct endpoints already present and all internal vertices new.
A closed ear is an undirected cycle adding unused edge identities and meeting the existing subgraph at exactly its base vertex.
Single-edge open ears, one-edge loop ears, and two-edge closed ears using distinct parallel edges are allowed.
The unused-edge condition is required for both kinds, including loops.
For a closed ear in a simple graph it follows from the cycle and vertex-intersection conditions, since every cycle edge has a new endpoint; prove this implication for the transported interface.
An ear decomposition is **data**, not merely a proposition asserting that suitable ears exist.
The multigraph decomposition starts from a single vertex or from a cycle and adds open or closed ears, recording a graph after each prefix on the same ambient vertex and edge types.
Its internal representation is not pinned: an inductive type family indexed by the graph built so far and a finite sequence with a validity proof are both suitable.
The public API must expose the initial cycle or vertex, the number and kind of ears, the `k`-th ear, and the graph after each prefix.
It must identify the zeroth and final graphs, show that each successor prefix adds exactly its displayed ear, provide prefix decompositions and an induction principle following the construction order, and prove edge coverage and preservation of the relevant connectivity property.
A decomposition of `G` has final graph `G`, covering every actual vertex and edge, including loops and all parallel edges.
Transport decompositions of `Graph.ofSimpleGraph H` to the `H.Subgraph` interface and back, preserving the prefix API; this is the simple-graph interface prototyped in `Suggested.lean`.
An open ear decomposition of a simple graph starts from a cycle and has only open ears, expressed as a predicate on the transported data.

### 7.2. Ear characterizations

Prove three characterizations:

1. A finite simple graph with at least three vertices is 2-vertex-connected if and only if it has an open ear decomposition.
   Strengthen existence to start from any prescribed cycle: for each cycle `C` in a 2-vertex-connected finite simple graph, supply an open ear decomposition whose initial subgraph is exactly the subgraph traced by `C`.
   Prove the corresponding prescribed-edge corollary by choosing an initial cycle containing that edge.
   This vertex-connectivity characterization also applies to the underlying simple graph of a multigraph; it does not assert that open ears cover multigraph loops.
2. A finite multigraph with nonempty actual vertex set is 2-edge-connected if and only if it can be built from one vertex by adding open or closed ears.
   Without finiteness assumptions, prove first that 2-edge-connectivity is equivalent to pairwise reachability of the actual vertices and absence of bridges among the actual edges, including the empty-vertex convention for that equivalence.
   Derive the simple-graph ear characterization.
   Reuse Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.isEdgeConnected_two_iff_forall_not_isBridge` for the simple-graph bridge criterion, and prove its agreement with the multigraph criterion under `Graph.ofSimpleGraph`.
   **Why:** `SimpleGraph.IsBridge` can hold for non-edges between components; multigraph bridges concern only actual edges.
3. A network `N` with nonempty finite vertex type and finite arrow types is strongly connected (`N.IsStronglyConnected`) if and only if it can be built from one vertex by adding directed open or closed ears, covering every arrow.

In the directed version, ears are directed paths and cycles of `N` in the sense of the conventions, they retain arrow identities, and the directed decomposition exposes the same prefix API using subnetworks.
Loops are permitted as one-arrow closed ears.
The initial-vertex convention includes the isolated singleton with no ears; relate it to the cycle-starting formulation for strongly connected networks with at least two vertices.

- A disconnected weighted graph whose cut tree contains zero-weight edges.
- On `Fin 4`, the natural-valued function `f(S) = min (|S|, 4 − |S|)`: prove symmetry and submodularity, and prove that no nonnegative real pair-capacity function on the same four vertices has this cut function after casting to `ℝ`.
  Compute every distinct-pair minimum cut value as one, show that a unit-weight path has the correct path-minimum values but its middle edge gives a cut of value two, and exhibit a unit-weight star satisfying both cut-tree properties.
  **Why:** the example distinguishes numerical pairwise values from actual minimum-cut witnesses and exercises symmetric submodularity beyond graph cut capacities.

## Scope boundaries

This roadmap owns graph connectivity, components, separators, cuts, flows, and the representation bridges between `Graph`, `SimpleGraph`, orientations, and networks.
Roadmaps that need `k`-vertex-connectivity for a fixed `k`, such as 3-connectivity in topological graph theory, use `IsVertexConnected k` from here rather than a second connectivity or component theory.
Incidence counts, indegree and outdegree for orientations, the bridge forest, `st`-numberings, the residual component poset of minimum cuts, and the matching and edge-colouring API required by the bipartite targets are in scope.
The roadmap does not develop unrestricted multigraph degree or colouring theory.

The following are outside scope:

- Adapters to the proposed `GraphLike.Walk` and `FlowNetwork` APIs.
- General matching theory beyond the bipartite targets, arbitrary-profit matching, minimum-cost flows and circulations, general-graph edge-colouring, and list edge-colouring.
- Dilworth's theorem, completion of partial orientations to strong orientations (mixed Robbins), Nash-Williams' orientation theorem for `2k`-edge-connected graphs, Edmonds' disjoint arborescences, and the Nash-Williams–Tutte disjoint spanning tree theorems.
- Networks with infinite capacities, multicommodity flows, algorithmic complexity bounds, and algorithms for computing strongly connected components or enumerating cuts.
- Separate developments of infinite graph theory, including Menger's theorem and other extremal results on infinitely many actual vertices, infinite rays and ends, infinite matching and edge-colouring, infinite ear decompositions, and edge-counting or flow theories with infinite edge sets.
- General graph contractions, contractible-edge and wheel theorems, treewidth, drawings, planar embeddings, and surface topology.

## Mathematical references

- Reinhard Diestel, *Graph Theory*, §1.9 and Chapter 3, for bonds, connectivity, Menger, blocks, fans, and ears; see the [author's book site](https://diestel-graph-theory.com/).
- Dimitri P. Bertsekas, [*Linear Network Optimization*](https://www.mit.edu/~dimitrib/LNets_Full_Book.pdf), §1.1.3 and Exercises 2.4–2.6 of §1.2, for bound transformations, feasibility, and rounding.
- Alexander Schrijver, *Combinatorial Optimization: Polyhedra and Efficiency*, Volume A, for flows, cuts, disjoint paths, circulations, and cut trees; see the [author's book page](https://homepages.cwi.nl/~lex/co/).
- Bernhard Korte and Jens Vygen, *Combinatorial Optimization: Theory and Algorithms*, Section 8.6, for the Gomory–Hu construction and the witness-repair step of its correctness proof.
- Jørgen Bang-Jensen and Gregory Gutin, *Digraphs: Theory, Algorithms and Applications*, for directed connectivity, directed ears, and network flows; see the [second edition](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-84800-998-1).
- Dan Gusfield, [*Very Simple Methods for All Pairs Network Flow Analysis*](https://doi.org/10.1137/0219009), SIAM Journal on Computing 19 (1990), 143–155, for the contraction-free cut-tree construction.
- Jean-Claude Picard and Maurice Queyranne, [*On the structure of all minimum cuts in a network and applications*](https://publications.polymtl.ca/5993/), for the residual reachability order and its description of every minimum cut.
- Shimon Even and Robert Endre Tarjan, [*Computing an st-numbering*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3975(76)90086-4), for `st`-numberings and their relation to acyclic orientations; only the existence and structural consequences are targets here.
- András Frank and András Gyárfás, [*How to orient the edges of a graph?*](https://www.renyi.hu/~gyarfas/Cikkek/09_FrankGyarfas_HowToOrientTheEdgesOfAGraph.pdf), for orientation degree bounds; loops in Target 8.8 contribute forced units at their vertices.

The following Mathlib proposals and their review discussions are references for interface design and coordination.
Each entry identifies the part relevant to this roadmap; the conventions and targets specify the required interfaces and their mathematical scope.

- [#33355: vertex connectivity](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/33355): deletion-based `IsVertexReachable`, `IsVertexPreconnected`, and `IsVertexConnected`.

  Mathlib has no walks on `Graph`; these proposals rest on the `GraphLike` hierarchy of [#36743](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/36743).
  The [dart construction in #39053](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/455aa1d6e5c7215f1270da70e328056af9607545/Mathlib/Combinatorics/Graph/GraphLike.lean#L22) splits every loop into a forward and a backward dart, so a graph with one vertex and one loop has two length-one walks there; the [loop-dart discussion](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/36743#discussion_r3191440123) records the trade-off.

# Hamiltonian Floer operations: geometric product and multiplicative PSS

Construct the geometric pair-of-pants product on capped Hamiltonian Floer complexes, its unit and sewing identities, and the multiplicative Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz comparison with GromovWittenTheory G7. The construction includes classical oriented counts on positive spherical-monotone and spherical-c1-zero targets, and the rational virtual punctured application on arbitrary closed symplectic targets. The definitive specification is this README; `Suggested.lean` gives nonexhaustive interface prototypes.

## H0. Scope and prerequisites

The main target is a closed connected boundaryless symplectic manifold (X^(2n),ω), n≥1, with its actual finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth structure. Work componentwise for disconnected targets; the zero-dimensional case has the separate point/count model. Hamiltonians are smooth period-one functions; the contractible one-periodic orbits used as generators are nondegenerate. Their finiteness is the actual clopen-contractible-sector argument of DGF7.C.1. Degenerate Hamiltonians have an invariant homology interpretation through specified nondegenerate perturbations and continuation, not unperturbed generator counts.

There are two geometric coefficient branches. **Classical**: positive spherical-monotone or spherical-c1-zero targets with DGF7.C's actual regular count-dimensional cylinder/PSS package, first mod2 and then oriented integral counts and scalar extensions. This owner proves the additional punctured product/family and sphere-incidence theorems; a cylinder exclusion theorem is not a product exclusion theorem. **Rational virtual**: arbitrary closed symplectic targets, with a coherent punctured Hamiltonian atlas/count package constructed here, including cylinder, plane and comparison families outside DGF's classical hypotheses. G7's rational coefficients are the common comparison coefficients. An integral product in the classical branch is retained; an arbitrary closed integral virtual theory is not inferred from a rational implicit-atlas trace.

Use the following exact prerequisite interfaces and keep their applications distinct.

- [DGFloer, capped classical branch7.C](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/71c960fc2d43fabd27cd77c770128a0271e39225/TauCetiRoadmap/DGFloer/README.md): the cap cover/period datum, cylinders, continuation, ordered orientation conventions and module PSS on its stated positive spherical-monotone and spherical-c1-zero branches. Consume the actual supported complexes and both module inverse homotopies, not a bare isomorphism type. H1–H3 construct the three-ended cap/domain/energy application, and H5 constructs the broader rational virtual extension and its classical overlap.
- [HeegaardFloer F0/F1/F2](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/957): the Banach/Sobolev, punctured linear Fredholm, CZ/relative-Chern/determinant and local curve interfaces at their actual hypotheses. - [AnalyticStableMaps M3](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/987): unforced marked genus-zero stable-map compactness, evaluation and class splitting. H3–H5 construct its attached inhomogeneous, fixed-asymptotic and varying frozen-J application; unforced compactness is not itself punctured Floer compactness.
- [MorseNovikov N1](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/890): exact finite-sublevel Novikov completion, finite convolution, continuous coefficient/period pushforward and finite-orbit module laws. - [GromovWittenTheory G0/G5–G7](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/990): closed stable-map support and invariants, the unit, ordered diagonal/left-dual conventions and quantum ring. - [ImplicitAtlases V0–V7](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/974): the stated atlas, relative virtual complex, H-level trace, specified refinement/concordance, finite cell-like/product and transverse-diagonal machinery. H7 constructs their incidence/PD comparison with G7.

[SymplecticFieldTheory](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/1054) owns contact/Reeb buildings and its contact/full-SFT levels; its count package is distinct from this Hamiltonian application. [FukayaTheory](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/1045) owns the distinct Lagrangian m2 construction.

The primary closed quantum product does not assert a product on every arbitrary-symplectomorphism component, a full extended TFT, SH/Viterbo multiplicativity, or an unrestricted noncompact invariant. Existing DGF atoroidal, arbitrary-seam and Liouville targets remain intact on their hypotheses. An application to those settings requires its own relative cap/reference and no-escape/sewing contracts; it is not an implicit consequence of the closed theorem here.

## H1. Coefficients, caps and degree dictionary before counts

Use DGF's contractible convention: i_(X_H)ω=dH, u_s+J(u_t−X_H)=0, positive ends are inputs, negative ends outputs, A_H(x,D)=∫Dω+∫Hdt, μ=−CZ_HF, μ(constant)=ind(H)−n. For D'−D=B, A increases by ω(B) and μ by 2c1(B). Let S_sph be the spherical Hurewicz image and Γ=S_sph/(kerω∩kerc1). Caps are actual Γ-torsors. The joint kernel, not area alone, preserves equal-energy different-degree classes. Construct class addition, cap gluing and cap/reference changes before matrices.

The Floer ring uses e^B with degree +2c1(B) and valuation ν(B)=−ω(B). For a punctured pair of pants u with input reference caps D1,D2 and output cap D0, put A=D0+u−D1−D2 using the oriented compactification. Its coefficient in the reference-output basis is e^(−A). The raw Fredholm index is

    ind D_u = μ1+μ2−μ0−n+2c1(A).

Thus a rigid coefficient satisfies μ0−2c1(A)=μ1+μ2−n: the product CF_i⊗CF_j→CF_(i+j−n) has degree −n. Define the comparison cochain regrading C^k=CF_(n−k), with differential d_C=d_CF; its product has degree zero and d_C has degree +1. The cap-dependent orientation lines are regraded at the same time. The regrading is an actual construction with sign/shift identities, not a renaming of an unrelated complex.

Let Γ_G be G7's chosen class group with energy and Chern maps. First work over a common class group retaining the classes needed by both constructions. Prove descent to any joint-period quotient and the finite coefficient-summing map, rather than assuming GW invariants are individually cap-quotient classes. The comparison sends q^A to e^(−A): ν(−A)=ω(A). G7's degree +2c1(A) becomes cochain coefficient degree −deg_CF(e^(−A))=+2c1(A). Its energy completion therefore maps in the correct direction. The map is a continuous unital coefficient map only with the actual positive-rescaling period identity and finite-sublevel hypotheses of N1. No t↦1 map on the entire completed Novikov ring is asserted.

General Γ need not have injective valuation, and the resulting graded completed algebra need not be a field. Positive monotonicity has the finite Laurent model before completion; c1-zero has its separate completed integer grading. For arbitrary classes use homogeneous graded pieces and the energy-compatible completion (or the resulting residue grading), not an integer direct sum containing every inhomogeneous infinite series. The PD comparison is H^k(X;Q)→H_(2n−k)(X;Q)→FH_(n−k). Over other rings retain actual orientation, UCT, tensor/base-change and perfect-pairing hypotheses; G7's Q comparison does not prove them automatically.

Fix markers, end coordinates, collars and their changes. Its Euler characteristic is −1 and there is no translation quotient of the entire pair-of-pants domain. # Roadmap: heights, units and S-units of number fields

Dirichlet's unit theorem says that the units of a number field form a lattice of rank `r₁ + r₂ − 1`
modulo torsion, and Mathlib proves it. The height of an algebraic number says how large it is
arithmetically. This roadmap writes the dictionary between the two. A unit's height is the ℓ¹ norm
of its logarithmic embedding, up to the coordinate that embedding drops. The torsion units are
exactly the units of height one. The regulator is bounded above and below by products of heights
of a fundamental system, and the lower bound is sharp enough to choose a fundamental system of
controlled height. The roadmap then carries all of this to `S`-units. It proves the `S`-unit
theorem, builds the `S`-logarithmic lattice and defines the `S`-regulator.

Two pieces of geometry of numbers are needed on the way, and both are built here. The first is a
lattice **basis** controlled by the successive minima, not merely an independent family. The
second applies it to the kernel of an integer matrix. The result is a `ℤ`-**basis** of the integral
kernel of bounded sup norm, at the cost `k!/2^{k−1}` over the Bombieri–Vaaler bound for
independent vectors, with the gcd of the maximal minors. The roadmap also owns a small set of height
estimates that every consumer of heights needs and that no other roadmap supplies:
- the affine height of a tuple,
- bounds for values of linear forms and determinants,
- the `Northcott` instances for projective points and subspaces,
- the projective form of Kronecker's theorem,
- the lower bound for the height away from one at bounded degree.

"Done" means a contributor who needs a fundamental system of units of bounded height, an
`S`-unit group of known rank with an explicit fundamental system, a lattice basis inside dilates of
a convex body, or an integer kernel basis of bounded sup norm finds each one stated in its
natural generality, with its basic API, in Mathlib's vocabulary.

Suggested home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/Height/` for Layers 0–1, beside the height foundation of
[DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence](../DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence/README.md);
`TauCeti/NumberTheory/GeometryOfNumbers/` for Layer 2; `TauCeti/NumberTheory/NumberField/Units/`
for Layer 3; and `TauCeti/RingTheory/DedekindDomain/SUnit.lean` with
`TauCeti/NumberTheory/NumberField/SUnits/` for Layer 4.

## Standing hypotheses and pinned conventions

Work over a field with `[Height.AdmissibleAbsValues K]` wherever the mathematics allows. Layers 0
and 1 are stated at that generality, except where an absolute height forces characteristic zero
or a number field. Layers 3 and 4 are about a number field `K` of degree `d = [K : ℚ]`, with
`r = NumberField.Units.rank K`. Tuples are indexed by an arbitrary finite type, never by `Fin n`
alone.

| Question | Convention |
| --- | --- |
| multiplicative or logarithmic | **Both** for every owned object. The multiplicative one is primary and `logX := Real.log (mulX)`, as in Mathlib. |
| relative or absolute | **Both, distinguished by name.** Over a fixed `K`, `Height.mulHeight` is relative. The absolute height carries the `abs` prefix (`NumberField.absMulHeight₁`) or is DAT's `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight`. Layer 3 states its regulator bounds in the **absolute logarithmic** height `h = absLogHeight₁`, as Bugeaud–Győry do, and its comparisons with `logEmbedding` in the **relative** `logHeight₁`, which is `d · h`. |
| local factor at a place | `⨆ i, v (x i)`, written out, never wrapped in a definition. |
| the affine height | `Height.mulHeightAff x := Height.mulHeight (fun o : Option ι ↦ o.elim 1 x)`, the projective height of `(1, x)`. It is **not** scaling-invariant, and that is its whole purpose. |
| `S` | `S : Set (IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))`, **finite places only**, with the infinite places always present. These are the carriers of `S.integer K` and `S.unit K`. The rank of `S.unit K` is `r + #S`. Bombieri–Gubler 1.5.10 instead includes the archimedean places in `S` and so writes the rank as `\|S\| − 1`. A contributor reading the book translates, and every statement here is in Mathlib's convention. |
| fundamental system | A family `ε : Fin r → (𝓞 K)ˣ` with `Subgroup.closure (Set.range ε) ⊔ torsion K = ⊤`, which is what Mathlib's `closure_fundSystem_sup_torsion_eq_top` says of `fundSystem K`. |
| ℓ¹ norm on `logSpace K` | Mathlib's `‖·‖` on the `Pi` type `logSpace K` is the **supremum** norm. Every ℓ¹ norm is written as `∑ w, |x w|`, and the sup-norm forms are separate statements. |
| declaration names | Statement-named, as in Mathlib. Siegel, Bombieri–Vaaler, Kronecker, Northcott and Dirichlet appear in docstrings, never in identifiers. The exception is a name that is the standard name of an object, such as `Northcott` the typeclass. |

## The build, in layers

### Layer 0: affine heights and the value bounds

**0.1 The affine height of a tuple.** Define
`Height.mulHeightAff (x : ι → K) := Height.mulHeight fun o : Option ι ↦ o.elim 1 x`, with
`logHeightAff` alongside, over any `[Height.AdmissibleAbsValues K]` and `[Finite ι]`. Prove:
- `1 ≤ mulHeightAff x`.
- `mulHeight x ≤ mulHeightAff x` and `mulHeight₁ (x i) ≤ mulHeightAff x`. The second fails for
  `mulHeight`.
- `mulHeightAff (x ∘ f) ≤ mulHeightAff x` for any `f`, with equality for a bijection.
- `mulHeightAff 0 = 1`.
- `mulHeightAff ![x] = mulHeight₁ x`, which is the test that the appended coordinate is the right
  one.
- The non-invariance as a theorem, `exists_mulHeightAff_smul_ne`: over `ℚ`, `![1]` and `![2]` have
  affine heights `1` and `2` and the same projective height.
- The bridge to DAT: for a number field `K` and `f : K →+* AlgebraicClosure ℚ`,
  `absoluteLogHeightAff (f ∘ x) = logHeightAff x / [K : ℚ]` for `x : Fin n → K`. DAT prepends the
  `1` with `Fin.cons`, and this layer appends it with `Option.elim`; the bridge is a reindexing.
(Bombieri–Gubler 1.5.)

**0.2 Values of linear forms and determinants.** Prove:
- `mulHeight₁ (∑ i, a i * x i) ≤ #ι ^ totalWeight K · mulHeightAff a · mulHeightAff x` for
  nonempty `ι`, with its logarithmic form. No bound in the projective heights of `a` and `x`
  exists, because `a ↦ c • a` scales the value and fixes `mulHeight a`.
- `mulHeight₁ A.det ≤ (#n)! ^ totalWeight K · ∏ j, mulHeightAff (fun i ↦ A i j)`, columnwise,
  from the Leibniz expansion and DAT §1.3's signed tuple sum bound
  `Height.mulHeight_sum_sign_comp_le`. Also the corollary `mulHeight₁ A.det ≤ (#n)! ^ totalWeight K · mulHeightAff (entries A) ^ #n`.
- The rejection test `exists_not_mulHeight₁_det_le`: a `1 × 1` matrix has `matrixMulHeight A = 1`
  and determinant its entry.
- Sharpness: `a = x = ![1, 1]` attains the linear-form constant.

**0.3 Arakelov bounds with constant one.** Over a number field, with DAT's `arakelovMulHeight`
applied to the tuple of entries `fun p : m × n ↦ A p.1 p.2`, prove:
- `arakelovMulHeight (fun j ↦ ∑ i, A (j, i) * x i) ≤ arakelovMulHeight A · arakelovMulHeight x`.
- `arakelovMulHeight (entries (A * B)) ≤ arakelovMulHeight (entries A) · arakelovMulHeight (entries B)`.
- Their logarithmic forms.

These need no `Nonempty` hypothesis and carry no cardinality. That is the contrast with DAT's
`matrixMulHeight_mul_le`, whose constant is `(card n) ^ totalWeight K` and which needs a nonempty
inner index. At an infinite place the local factor is the Frobenius norm, and Cauchy–Schwarz makes
it submultiplicative; at a finite place the ultrametric inequality does the same. The
linear-map bound is the one-column case of the matrix bound. Test: over `ℚ`, `A = [1 1]`,
`B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]]` give `matrixMulHeight (A B) = 2` against `matrixMulHeight A = matrixMulHeight B = 1`,
so the sup-norm constant `2 ^ totalWeight K` is attained, while the Arakelov bound holds with
constant `1`.

### Layer 1: Northcott instances and Kronecker's theorem

**1.1 Northcott on projective space.** Over a field with
`[Northcott (Height.mulHeight₁ (K := K))]`, prove `Northcott (Projectivization.mulHeight (K := K) (ι := ι))`
and the `logHeight` instance. Mathlib's `Mathlib/NumberTheory/Height/Northcott.lean` records both
as TODOs. The number-field instances then follow by instance resolution. Route:
- **Normalization.** `Projectivization.exists_rep_apply_eq_one_of_ne_zero` gives a representative
  with a chosen nonvanishing coordinate equal to `1`, and `exists_rep_apply_eq_one` is its
  corollary.
- **Coordinate bound.** `Height.mulHeight₁_div_le_mulHeight`, that
  `mulHeight₁ (x i / x j) ≤ mulHeight x`, is `Height.mulHeight_comp_le` along `![i, j]`.
- **Finiteness.** A bounded-height point is in the image of a finite set of normalized tuples.
  No ring of integers and no ideal norm enter.

There is **no** `Northcott` instance for `Height.mulHeight` on `ι → K`: the whole line `Kˣ • x` has
one height. (Hindry–Silverman B.2.3; Bombieri–Gubler 2.4.9 for `ℙⁿ`.)

**1.2 Northcott for subspaces.** Over a number field, `Northcott` instances for DAT's
`relativeSubspaceHeight`, `relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight` and `subspaceHeight`, and for their
logarithms, on `Submodule K (ι → K)` with **no rank condition**. Route:
- **Absolute height.** For `subspaceHeight` this is DAT's `finite_subspaceHeight_le`.
- **Relative Arakelov height.** `relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight = subspaceHeight ^ [K : ℚ]`, so
  its sublevel sets are those of `subspaceHeight`.
- **Relative sup height.** This needs the **reverse** comparison, because a bound on the smaller
  height must bound the larger one. Prove `relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight_le`: for
  `n = #ι` and `k = finrank K T`,
  `relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight T ≤ (n.choose k) ^ ([K : ℚ]/2) · relativeSubspaceHeight T`.
  It is the upper half of DAT's `arakelovMulHeight_sup_comparison` on the Plücker vector, whose
  index `Set.powersetCard ι k` has `n.choose k` elements and is nonempty because `k ≤ n`. Both
  heights are invariant under scaling, so the representative `relativePluckerPoint` picks does
  not matter. Bound `n.choose k ≤ 2 ^ n` uniformly. Then
  `{T | relativeSubspaceHeight T ≤ B}` lies inside
  `{T | relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight T ≤ 2 ^ (n [K : ℚ]/2) · B}`, which is finite by the
  previous item.
- **Logarithms.** These follow by `Northcott.comp_of_bddAbove` along `Real.log`, as Mathlib
  derives `Northcott (logHeight₁)`.

The rank-free statement is what the typeclass needs, because `Northcott h` quantifies over the
whole domain of `h`. The deliverable is the instance, through which `Northcott.exists_min_image`
produces a subspace of least height with a prescribed property.

**1.3 Kronecker's theorem and the height gap.** Over a field `F` of characteristic zero:
- **Kronecker.** For `x` integral over `ℚ`, `absMulHeight₁ x = 1 ↔ x = 0 ∨ ∃ n, 0 < n ∧ x ^ n = 1`,
  and `absLogHeight₁ x = 0 ↔ …`. The hard direction is DAT's `mahlerMeasure_eq_one_iff` through
  `mahlerMeasure_eq_absMulHeight₁_pow`. The easy direction is the power law
  `absMulHeight₁ (x ^ n) = absMulHeight₁ x ^ n` with `1 ≤ absMulHeight₁`.
- **Tuple power law.** `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight (fun i ↦ x i ^ N) = absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight x ^ N`.
  It is local: `(⨆ i, v (x i))^N = ⨆ i, v (x i ^ N)`.
- **Projective Kronecker.** For a nonzero tuple `x` of algebraic coordinates,
  `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight x = 1` if and only if every ratio `x i / x j` with `x j ≠ 0` is
  zero or a root of unity. The converse direction is a statement about tuples,
  `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight_eq_one_of_forall_eq_zero_or_pow_eq_one`. Its proof: with `N` a
  common order of the nonzero coordinates, `x ^ N` has coordinates in `{0, 1}`, so it is its own
  square, and its height is an idempotent `≥ 1`. (Hindry–Silverman B.2.3.1.)
- **The gap.** `1 < absMulHeight₁ x` for `x` integral over `ℚ`, nonzero and not a root of unity.
  Also, for each `D`, `∃ c > 0` with `c ≤ absLogHeight₁ x` for every such `x` with
  `[ℚ⟮x⟯ : ℚ] ≤ D`. The proof is DAT's bounded-degree Northcott plus Kronecker, and the constant
  is **ineffective**: it is the minimum of a finite set. (Bombieri–Gubler 1.6.15.)
- **Refutation.** The dependence of `c` on `D` is essential: `2 ^ (1/N)` has
  `absLogHeight₁ = (log 2)/N`. State it as "for every `c > 0` there is such an `x` with height
  below `c`". The same family keeps `[ℚ(x):ℚ] · h(x) ≤ log 2`, so it does not bear on Lehmer's
  question.

### Layer 2: a basis from the minima, and Bombieri–Vaaler in the sup norm

**2.1 A basis from the minima** (Cassels, *An Introduction to the Geometry of Numbers*, Ch. V,
Lemma 8; Ch. I, Thm. I). Let `E` be a finite-dimensional real normed space, `L` a discrete
`Submodule ℤ E` and `B` a convex, symmetric set with nonempty interior.

*General form.* For any `ℝ`-independent `a : Fin n → E` with `a i ∈ L` and `n = finrank ℝ E`,
there is a `ℤ`-basis `b` of `L` with
`gauge B (b j) ≤ max (gauge B (a j)) ((∑ i ≤ j, gauge B (a i)) / 2)`. `IsZLattice ℝ L` is a
consequence, not a hypothesis. Route, by induction on `j`, with `V_j = span_ℝ {a i : i < j}`:
1. A basis of `L ∩ V_j` extends by one vector `y` to a basis of `L ∩ V_{j+1}`. This is GoN's
   §0.2.7 `saturated_adapted_basis_of_basis`, applied inside `V_{j+1}`.
2. Write `a j = c • y + w` with `c` a nonzero integer and `w ∈ L ∩ V_j`.
3. If `|c| = 1`, take `b j = c · a j`.
4. Otherwise replace `y` by `y − ∑ round(t_i) • a i`, where `y = c⁻¹ • a j + ∑ t_i • a i`. The
   result still extends the basis, and has gauge at most `½ gauge B (a j) + ½ ∑_{i<j} gauge B (a i)`.

The proof uses `gauge B (r • x) = |r| · gauge B x` for symmetric convex `B`, stated as
`gauge_smul_of_symmetric`. Over `ℝ` a convex symmetric set is balanced: for `x ∈ B` and
`|t| ≤ 1`, `t • x` lies on the segment from `-x` to `x`. Mathlib has no lemma saying so, so state
it as `balanced_of_convex_of_neg_mem`; then `gauge_smul_of_symmetric` is Mathlib's `gauge_smul`.

*Minima form.* In GoN's vocabulary: for `K : ConvexBody E` symmetric with `0 ∈ interior K` and `L`
a full lattice, there is a `ℤ`-basis `b` of `L` with
`b i ∈ (max 1 ((i + 1)/2) · successiveMin L K i) • K` for every `i : Fin (finrank ℝ E)`. Apply the
general form to GoN's `exists_successiveMin_witnesses`. This is strictly more than GoN's
`exists_integral_minimum_flag`, which bounds no vector of the basis.

Further requirements:
- The loss against Minkowski's second theorem is
  `∏_{i<n} max 1 ((i+1)/2) = n! / 2^{n−1}`. State it as `prod_max_one_add_one_div_two`.
- The `max` is forced at `i = 0`, where `λ_0` is attained.
- The general form needs no measure, no closedness and no boundedness. Those enter only in the
  minima form.

**2.2 Integral kernel bases and the minor gcd** (Bombieri–Vaaler 1983, Theorems 1 and 2;
Aliev–Henk 2023, §6; Cassels V Lemma 8). For an integer matrix `A : Matrix (Fin m) ι ℤ` whose rows
are linearly independent over `ℚ`, let `minorGcd A` be the gcd of its `m × m` minors, and let
`k = #ι − m` be the rank of the integral kernel `ker A = {x : ι → ℤ | A *ᵥ x = 0}`.

*Owned here.*
- **The arithmetic identity.**
  `minorGcd A · subspaceHeight (ker A) = √det(A Aᵀ)`, together with
  `linearIndependent_rows_rat_iff : rows independent over ℚ ↔ det(A Aᵀ) ≠ 0`, `0 < det(A Aᵀ)`
  and `1 ≤ minorGcd A`. This turns DAT §2.8's remark on the `K = ℚ` constant into a theorem.
- **Invariance.** `√det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A` is unchanged by `A ↦ U A` for `U ∈ GL_m(ℤ)`
  (`sqrt_det_div_minorGcd_unit_mul`, from `minorGcd_unit_mul` and the Gram determinant's
  `det U ^ 2 = 1`). Classical Siegel's bound `(#ι · max |A i j|)^{m/(#ι−m)}` moves under this
  substitution.
- **The geometric half.** For any lattice `L` in a subspace `V` of `EuclideanSpace ℝ ι`, with
  `cubeSlice V` the slice of `[−1, 1]^ι`, `∏ i, successiveMin L (cubeSlice V) i ≤ covolume L`.
  The `2^k` of GoN's `minkowski_second_upper` cancels the `2^k` of DAT's `siegelProductBallSlice`.
- **An integral kernel basis.** A `Module.Basis (Fin k) ℤ (ker A)`, so a basis of the whole
  integral kernel and not only of a sublattice of finite index, with
  `∏ l, (⨆ i, |b l i|) ≤ k!/2^{k−1} · √det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A`. At `k = 0` both sides are `1`.
- **Sharpness of Siegel's exponent.** The `m × (m+1)` system `B x_i = x_{i+1}` has every nonzero
  integer solution of sup norm at least `B^m`, against Siegel's bound `((m+1)B)^m`.

Assembly of the basis:
1. The covolume of `ℤ^ι ∩ ker A` in its real span equals `subspaceHeight (ker A)`. This is the
   `K = ℚ` case of DAT's `kernelLattice_covolume`.
2. The arithmetic identity rewrites it as `√det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A`. Its proof is DAT's
   `subspaceHeight_orthogonal`, which passes to the row space, and `plucker_cauchyBinet`, which
   computes the rows' Plücker norm as `√det(A Aᵀ)`.
3. The geometric half bounds the product of the minima of the cube slice by that covolume.
4. The minima form of 2.1 converts the minima into a basis. The cube slice's gauge is the sup
   norm, and the loss is `prod_max_one_add_one_div_two k = k!/2^{k−1}`.

*Adapters of DAT's `siegelKernelBasis`, not owned.* At `K = ℚ` DAT's theorem gives a `ℚ`-basis of
the kernel in `ℤ^ι` with `∏ Habs(x_l) ≤ H₂(rowSpace A)`. Dividing each vector by its content keeps
it in the kernel, keeps the family independent, and makes its sup norm equal to its height
(Mathlib's `Rat.mulHeight_eq_max_abs_of_gcd_eq_one`). With the arithmetic identity this is the
sup-norm form of Bombieri–Vaaler's Theorem 2: `ℤ`-independent `x : Fin k → (ι → ℤ)`, each primitive, with
`A *ᵥ x l = 0` and `∏ l, (⨆ i, |x l i|) ≤ √det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A`. Theorem 1 is the smallest
vector of that family: for `m < #ι` a nonzero `x` with
`⨆ i, |x i| ≤ (√det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A)^{1/k}`. State both as corollaries.

The independent family need **not** span `ker A`. For `A = [0, 0, 1]`, the vectors
`(1, 1, 0)` and `(1, −1, 0)` meet the bound `1`, but they span a sublattice of index `2` that misses
`(1, 0, 0)`. The basis milestone is therefore a separate statement, and its factor `k!/2^{k−1}` is
not to be dropped.

### Layer 3: heights of units and the regulator

Throughout, `K` is a number field, `w₀` and `logEmbedding` are Mathlib's
(`NumberField.Units.dirichletUnitTheorem`), and `u : (𝓞 K)ˣ`. Sums over `{w // w ≠ w₀}` use
`open scoped Classical`, since `InfinitePlace K` has no `DecidableEq`.

**3.1 The logarithmic embedding as a height** (Bombieri–Gubler 1.5.12; Bugeaud–Győry 1996, (12)).
The finite local factors of a unit are `1`, so:
- `logHeight₁ u = ∑ w, (mult w · log (w u))⁺`, the sum over all infinite places, which by the
  product formula is
- `2 · logHeight₁ u = ∑ w, |mult w · log (w u)|`.

These are the `S = ∅` case of DAT §4.5's identity and are cited from there. What this milestone
owns is the translation to `logEmbedding`, which drops the coordinate at `w₀`:
- `2 · logHeight₁ u = ∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w| + |∑_{w ≠ w₀} logEmbedding u w|`.
- The two-sided bound `∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w| ≤ 2 · logHeight₁ u ≤ 2 ∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w|`.
- The sup-norm forms `‖logEmbedding u‖ ≤ 2 · logHeight₁ u` and
  `logHeight₁ u ≤ rank K · ‖logEmbedding u‖`.
- The absolute form `absLogHeight₁ u ≤ (∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w|) / d`.
- Both tempting identities, as criteria. `logHeight₁ u = ∑_{w ≠ w₀} (logEmbedding u w)⁺` holds
  **iff `w₀ u ≤ 1`**, and `2 · logHeight₁ u = ∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w|` holds **iff
  `w₀ u = 1`**.
- `finite_setOf_logHeight₁_le`: the units of bounded height are finite. This is Northcott along
  `(𝓞 K)ˣ → K`.

**3.2 Units of height one.**
- `absMulHeight₁ u = 1 ↔ u ∈ torsion K`, with the `mulHeight₁`, `logHeight₁` and `absLogHeight₁`
  forms. From 3.1, `2 · logHeight₁ u` is a sum of nonnegative terms and vanishes exactly when
  every `w u = 1`, which is Mathlib's `mem_torsion`.
- `logHeight₁ u = 0 ↔ logEmbedding u = 0`.
- Kronecker (1.3) removes the unit hypothesis: a nonzero `x : 𝓞 K` has `absMulHeight₁ x = 1` iff
  it has finite order. Such an `x` is a unit.
- Off the torsion the height is strictly above one, and no member of `fundSystem K` is torsion.
  Hence `0 < ∏ i, absLogHeight₁ (fundSystem K i)`.

**3.3 The regulator and the heights of a fundamental system** (Bugeaud–Győry 1996, Lemma 1, case
`S = S_∞`). Write `h = absLogHeight₁`.
- *Hadamard's bound, for every fundamental system* `ε`:
  `regulator K ≤ (2d)^r · ∏ i, h(ε i)`. Also `regOfFamily u ≤ (2d)^r · ∏ h(u i)` for any family,
  and the relative form `regulator K ≤ 2^r · ∏ logHeight₁ (ε i)`. Route: the rows of the
  `logEmbedding` matrix have ℓ¹ norm at most `2 · logHeight₁ = 2d · h` by 3.1, and
  `Matrix.abs_det_le_prod_sum_abs` bounds `|det M|` by the product of the ℓ¹ norms of the rows,
  over any linearly ordered field. For a fundamental system `regOfFamily ε = regulator K` is
  Mathlib's `regOfFamily_div_regulator` at index one. Also prove the positivity of `∏ h(ε i)` for
  every fundamental system.
- *A reduced fundamental system exists*: some fundamental system has
  `∏ i, h(ε i) ≤ (r!)² / (2^{r−1} d^r) · regulator K`, and it can be chosen to satisfy Hadamard's
  bound simultaneously. Route, which is Bugeaud–Győry's and produces exactly this constant:
  1. Let `logBall K = {x : logSpace K | ∑ w, |x w| ≤ 1}`. It is convex, symmetric, closed and
     bounded, and `volume (logBall K) = 2^r / r!` (`MeasureTheory.volume_sum_rpow_le` at `p = 1`;
     by hand at `r = 0`).
  2. Minkowski's upper bound gives `∏ λ_i ≤ r! · regulator K`. `logSpace K` carries the sup norm
     and is not an inner-product space, so state the adapter: transport `unitLattice K` and
     `logBall K` to `EuclideanSpace ℝ {w // w ≠ w₀}` along `WithLp.linearEquiv`. That map preserves
     volume, so it preserves the covolume (`ZLattice.covolume_comap`), and the minima are preserved
     by GoN's `successiveMin_linearEquiv`. Then apply GoN's `minkowski_second_upper`.
  3. Take the basis `b` of 2.1, which costs `r!/2^{r−1}`.
  4. Take units `ε i` with `logEmbedding ε i = b i`. They form a fundamental system because `b`
     spans `unitLattice K`, the whole image of `logEmbedding`
     (`closure_sup_torsion_eq_top_of_span`).
  5. Bound `h(ε i) ≤ (∑ w, |b i w|)/d` by 3.1.
- *Rank zero, as a check.* Both products are empty, and the two bounds agree with Tau Ceti's
  `NumberField.Units.regulator_eq_one_of_rank_eq_zero`, which is consumed and not reproved.

The reduced statement is existential and cannot be made for `fundSystem K` or for every fundamental
system once `r ≥ 2`: a unimodular change of basis then makes the heights arbitrarily large at fixed
regulator. In rank one `GL₁(ℤ) = {±1}`: the fundamental systems are `ζ ε^{±1}` with `ζ` torsion, and they
all have the same height. The
statement `∃ c₁ c₂ > 0, c₁ R ≤ ∏ h(ε_i) ≤ c₂ R` for a fixed field says nothing, so the constants
are part of the target.

### Layer 4: S-integers, the S-unit theorem and the S-regulator

**4.1 The height of an S-integer** (Bombieri–Gubler 1.5.10).
- *Dictionary.* For `v : HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K)` and `x : K`, `FinitePlace.mk v x ≤ 1 ↔
  v.valuation K x ≤ 1` and `FinitePlace.mk v x = 1 ↔ v.valuation K x = 1`. These are
  equivalences because the norm of a prime exceeds `1`. Consequently
  `Set.mem_integer_iff_finitePlace` and `Set.mem_unit_iff_finitePlace`.
- *Height identity.* For `x ∈ S.integer K`,
  `mulHeight₁ x = (∏ w : InfinitePlace K, max (w x) 1 ^ mult w) · ∏ᶠ v ∈ S, max (FinitePlace.mk v x) 1`.
  Also its logarithmic form, a `Finset` form, and the `S`-unit form derived in one line.
- *Characterization.* For `x ≠ 0`, the identity holds **iff** `x ∈ S.integer K`. A single finite
  place outside `S` where `|x|_v > 1` makes the full product strictly larger.
- *The case `S = ∅`.* `Set.mem_integer_empty_iff` (the algebraic integers) and
  `Set.mem_unit_empty_iff` (the units of `𝓞 K`), proved directly, so that the unit identity of
  3.1 is the `S = ∅` case of the display.
- *Tests.* The rational test is DAT §4.1's `mulHeight₁_sUnits_rat`. The rejection test is `1/2` at
  `S = ∅`: its infinite factor is `1` while its height is `2^d`.

**4.2 The S-unit theorem** (Bombieri–Gubler Theorem 1.5.13). Build it under the names and shapes
of mathlib4#40791, so that adopting that PR is a deletion plus an import:
- `Set.unitValuation : S.unit K →* (S → Multiplicative ℤ)`, `unitValuation_ker`, and
  `Set.unit_fg`.
- `Set.unit_finrank_numberField : finrank ℤ (Additive (S.unit K)) = Units.rank K + Nat.card S`
  for finite `S`.
- Beside it, the usable form in the shape of Mathlib's `exist_unique_eq_mul_prod`: a family
  `ε : Fin (rank K + #S) → S.unit K` such that every `S`-unit is uniquely `ζ · ∏ ε i ^ e i` with
  `ζ` torsion and `e` an integer vector.

Route:
1. The kernel of `unitValuation` is the image of `(𝓞 K)ˣ`, by 4.1's `S = ∅` statement. Its rank
   is Mathlib's `NumberField.Units.finrank_eq`.
2. The image has full rank `#S`. For each `v ∈ S`, the class of `v` has finite order in
   `ClassGroup (𝓞 K)`, and a generator of `v ^ orderOf [v]` is an `S`-unit with valuation nonzero
   at `v` and zero at the other places of `S` (`Set.exists_unitValuation_apply_ne_zero`). Only
   this torsion statement about the cokernel is needed. The class number is never computed and no
   map to the class group is built.
3. Rank–nullity over `ℤ`.

Build the fundamental system from the quotient of the `ℤ`-module `Additive (S.unit K)` by
`Submodule.torsion ℤ`, which is free, rather than from a quotient group.

**4.3 The S-logarithmic lattice and the S-regulator.** For a finite `S : Finset (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))`:
- Define `SUnit.logSpace S := ({w : InfinitePlace K // w ≠ w₀} ⊕ S) → ℝ`, and
  `SUnit.logEmbedding S` sending `x` to `mult w · log (w x)` on the left and
  `log (FinitePlace.mk v x)` on the right.
- Prove the product formula for `S`-units,
  `∑ w, mult w · log (w x) + ∑ v ∈ S, log (FinitePlace.mk v x) = 0`.
- Prove the `S`-analogue of 3.1 in `logEmbedding` coordinates:
  `2 · logHeight₁ x = ∑ |logEmbedding S x| + |∑ logEmbedding S x|`, with the two-sided and
  sup-norm comparisons. The rejection test `x = 2` at `S = ∅` is an `∅`-integer but not an
  `∅`-unit, and its sum is `d · log 2`.
- `logEmbedding S (unitOfUnits u) = Sum.elim (logEmbedding u) 0`.
- Define `SUnit.unitLattice S`, the image. Prove it is a **full lattice**:
  - **Discreteness** is Northcott: a bounded embedding is a bounded height by 4.1, and Mathlib's
    `NumberField.finite_setOfPred_logHeight₁_le` finishes (`SUnit.unitLattice_inter_ball_finite`).
  - **Spanning** is Mathlib's `unitLattice_span_eq_top` for the infinite coordinates together with
    the generators of 4.2 at the places of `S` (`SUnit.unitLattice_span_eq_top`).
- **The kernel.** `SUnit.logEmbedding_ker`: the kernel of `SUnit.logEmbedding S` is the torsion
  of `S.unit K`, as `(CommGroup.torsion (S.unit K)).toAddSubgroup`, the `S`-analogue of Mathlib's
  `logEmbedding_ker`. Route: if the kept coordinates vanish, the product formula makes the
  coordinate at `w₀` vanish too, so `logHeight₁ x = 0` by the height identity above, and
  Kronecker (1.3) makes `x` a root of unity. Equivalently, the kernel is the set of `S`-units of
  height one.
- **The quotient.** By the first isomorphism theorem, `SUnit.logEmbedding S` induces a `ℤ`-linear
  equivalence from the torsion-free quotient
  `Additive (S.unit K) ⧸ Submodule.torsion ℤ (Additive (S.unit K))` onto
  `SUnit.unitLattice S` (`SUnit.exists_quotTorsionEquiv_unitLattice`, sending the class of `x`
  to `logEmbedding S x`). It is the bridge from 4.2's quotient to 4.3's lattice.
- **Fundamental systems are bases.** A family `ε : ι → S.unit K` is a fundamental system, meaning
  `Subgroup.closure (Set.range ε) ⊔ CommGroup.torsion (S.unit K) = ⊤` with
  `#ι = rank K + #S`, **iff** `fun i ↦ logEmbedding S (Additive.ofMul (ε i))` is a `ℤ`-basis of
  `SUnit.unitLattice S` (`SUnit.isFundSystem_iff_basis`). The forward direction transports
  generation along the quotient equivalence. The converse lifts a basis to `S`-units and uses
  the kernel statement. In particular 4.2's fundamental system gives a basis.
- Define `SUnit.regulator S := ZLattice.covolume (SUnit.unitLattice S)` and prove
  `SUnit.regulator_pos`.
- **The determinant formula.** For a fundamental system `ε : ι → S.unit K`, an omitted infinite
  place `w'` and any `e : ι ≃ ({w // w ≠ w'} ⊕ S)`, `SUnit.regulator S` is the absolute
  determinant of the matrix whose row `i` is the weighted logarithms of `ε i` at the places
  `e`-indexed by its columns: `mult w · log (w (ε i))` at an infinite place and
  `log (FinitePlace.mk v (ε i))` at `v ∈ S` (`SUnit.regulator_eq_abs_det`). The generic `ι` and
  `e` carry the compatibility with reindexing. Independence of the basis is the
  `GL(ℤ)` invariance of `|det|`. Independence of `w'` is the product formula, which makes the
  columns sum to zero, so deleting any one column gives the same `|det|`. This is the
  `S`-analogue of Mathlib's `regulator_eq_det`, and it is how `regulator_empty` and the worked
  example are computed.
- Prove `SUnit.regulator_empty : SUnit.regulator ∅ = NumberField.Units.regulator K`. This is a
  theorem, not a definitional unfolding: `α ⊕ Empty` is not `α`. Transport the covolume along the
  measure-preserving linear equivalence of the two log spaces.
- **Rank.** `finrank ℤ (SUnit.unitLattice S) = rank K + #S`, from `ZLattice.rank`. Through the
  quotient equivalence, and because quotienting by torsion keeps the `ℤ`-rank, this is 4.2's
  `Set.unit_finrank_numberField`. The two routes must agree. `ZLattice.rank` alone computes only
  the rank of the image. The quotient equivalence is what makes it a statement about `S.unit K`.

## Worked examples (acceptance criteria)

- **Affine height.** `mulHeightAff ![1] = 1` and `mulHeightAff ![2] = 2` over `ℚ`, while
  `mulHeight ![1] = mulHeight ![2] = 1`.
- **Value bound.** Over `ℚ`, `a = x = ![1, 1]` gives `mulHeight₁ 2 = 2 = 2 ^ totalWeight ℚ · 1 · 1`.
- **Kronecker.** `absMulHeight₁ (-1 : ℚ) = 1`, `absMulHeight₁ (2 : ℚ) = 2`; the tuple
  `![1, -1]` has `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight = 1` and `![1, 2]` has `2`.
- **Gap.** For every `c > 0` some `2 ^ (1/N)` has `absLogHeight₁` below `c`.
- **Basis from the minima.** For `L = ℤ⁵ + ℤ·(½,…,½)` and `K` the Euclidean unit ball, every
  minimum is `1`, attained by `e_0, …, e_4`, which span `ℤ⁵`, a sublattice of index `2`. So the
  minima witnesses are not a basis. 2.1 still produces a basis inside the bounds
  `max 1 ((i+1)/2)`, using `(½,…,½)`, of norm `√5/2 ≤ 5/2`, as its last vector.
- **Minor gcd.** The row `[1, 1]` has `det(AAᵀ) = 2`, `minorGcd = 1`, kernel generator
  `(1, −1)` of sup norm `1 ≤ √2`. The row `[2, 2]` has `det = 8`, `minorGcd = 2` and the same bound
  `√2`. This tests rational rescaling of a row, not a unimodular change.
- **Unimodular shear.** `A = [[1, 0, −1], [0, 1, −1]]` has Gram determinant `3`, minors `1, −1, 1`
  and `minorGcd = 1`, so the bound is `√3`. The kernel is generated by `(1, 1, 1)`, of sup norm `1`.
  The shear `U = [[1, 1], [0, 1]]` gives `U A = [[1, 1, −2], [0, 1, −1]]`, again with Gram
  determinant `3` and minors `1, −1, 1`. Classical Siegel's bound moves from `3^2 = 9` to
  `6^2 = 36`.
- **Independent family against basis.** For `A = [0, 0, 1]`, `(1, 1, 0)` and `(1, −1, 0)` meet
  the bound `1` and span a sublattice of index `2` in `ker A = ℤ² × 0`. The basis milestone
  returns `(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)`, inside its bound `2!/2 · 1 = 1`.
- **Regulator, sharp at `ℚ(√2)`.** `r = 1`, `d = 2`, `ε = 1 + √2`, and
  `regulator = log(1+√2)` by Mathlib's `regulator_eq_det` at rank one,
  `h(ε) = log(1+√2)/2`. Hadamard: `log(1+√2) ≤ 4 · log(1+√2)/2`. Reduced:
  `log(1+√2)/2 ≤ (1/2) · log(1+√2)`, an **equality**, so the constant `(r!)²/(2^{r−1} d^r)` cannot
  be lowered at `r = 1, d = 2`.
- **Rank zero.** For `ℚ` and every imaginary quadratic field, both bounds of 3.3 have empty
  products and agree with Tau Ceti's `regulator_rat_eq_one` and
  `regulator_eq_one_of_isTotallyComplex_of_finrank_eq_two`.
- **S-units over `ℚ`.** `S = {2}`: rank `0 + 1 = 1`, fundamental system `{2}`, torsion `{±1}`,
  `SUnit.regulator S = log 2` by the determinant formula: the `1 × 1` matrix at the place `2`
  is `log |2|_2 = −log 2`. The element `1/2` is in `S.unit ℚ`, and its height `2` is carried at
  `2`.

## Ordering

Layer 0 first: 0.1 is used by 0.2, which also uses DAT §1.3's tuple sum bound. Layer 1 needs
only Layer 0's normalization lemmas and DAT §§0.2–0.3, 2.5. Layer 2 needs GoN §§0.2, 1.2, 1.5 and
DAT §§2.5, 2.8; its 2.1 is the input to 2.2's basis and to 3.3. Layer 3: 3.1, then 3.2 (which
also uses 1.3), then 3.3 (which uses 2.1). Layer 4: 4.1 needs nothing from Layer 3 except 3.1's
`S = ∅` identity as a check; 4.2 needs 4.1; 4.3 needs 4.1, 4.2, 3.1 and Kronecker (1.3). The
headline milestones are 3.3, 4.2 and 4.3.

TauCetiRoadmap/Hyperfunctions:
# Sato hyperfunctions and analytic generalized functions

Build the Sato sheaf on every Hausdorff, second-countable real-analytic
n-manifold without boundary, for each finite n, including noncompact and
nonorientable manifolds. Include complex and real structures, hyperforms,
hyperdensities and analytic vector bundles of every fixed finite rank r.
Use the native fixed-model manifold and `VectorBundle` carriers. A space
with varying dimension or rank is an explicitly indexed disjoint union of
such components: construct its sheaf by the product of sections on the
component opens and prove restriction, gluing and all operations componentwise.
In dimension0 use arbitrary complex-valued functions on the discrete space.

Use `TopCat.Sheaf (ModuleCat ℂ)`, its actual morphisms, kernels and derived
cohomology. In dimension1 use the explicit holomorphic quotient and its
restriction maps in `Suggested.lean`, with the canonical embedding
characterized in HF4. In all dimensions use analytic closed-support sheaf
cohomology.

The global smooth-section FS carrier and its compact-current strong dual are
distinct from the LF compact-test carrier and its compact-convergence

## HF0. Closed supports, relative complexes and locality

sheaves `𝓗_S^q(F)` by sheafifying supported cohomology on opens. Prove the
native injective/flabby-resolution comparison, naturality, restriction,
excision and long exact sequences for support inclusions and open triples.
For the purity application construct the degenerate edge comparison: if
`𝓗_S^q(F)=0` for q≠n, prove
`H_Z^(n+j)(W,F)≃H_Z^j(S,𝓗_S^n(F))` for closed Z⊆S, including restriction
and j=0. Also prove the support-truncation implication: if
`𝓗_S^q(F)=0` for q<n, then `H_S^q(W,F)=0` for q<n. Derive both
comparisons from the composed supported-section derived functors, the
bounded-below local hypercohomology filtration and its restriction maps.

Implement closed-support cohomology through the actual sheaf category.
For an open O⊆W let C_O be the sheafification of the free complex-module
Yoneda object corepresenting sections on O. Construct C_(W\S)→C_W and
`Q_S=coker(C_(W\S)→C_W)`. Prove
`Hom(Q_S,F)≃Γ_S(W,F)` and `Ext^q(Q_S,F)≃H_S^q(W,F)` with naturality.
Construct the free-presheaf/sheafification adjunction and its comparison
with the constant-ring `SheafOfModules` carrier for this closed-set support
construction.

Identify derived supports with `Cone(RΓ(W,F)→RΓ(W\S,F))[-1]`. Native
`CochainComplex.mappingCone` has differential `(-d_F a, f a+d_G b)`;
the native shift[-1] changes this to `(d_F a,−f a−d_G b)`. The isomorphism
`(a,b)↦(a,−b)` gives the relative convention

```
A^(p,q)(W) ⊕ A^(p,q−1)(W\S),
d_rel(α,β)=(∂̄α, α|_(W\S)−∂̄β).
```

Use the cone of the ordinary fine Dolbeault resolutions on the two opens.
Prove square zero, cycles, boundaries, complex linearity, resolution
independence, restriction/shrinking, refinement, excision and all product
signs. Build the relative de Rham comparison and type projection. The cup
product for local duality has its specified supports and does not assert
a same-variable product for all hyperfunctions.

Define `or_(M/X)=𝓗_M^n(ℤ_X)` for the real n-codimensional embedding.
Compute its stalks by local Euclidean relative cohomology, identify normal
coordinate generators and sign-of-normal-determinant transitions, and prove
the canonical square pairing `or⊗or≃ℤ_M`. Compare it to the normal-bundle orientation line by these same local
generators. For z=x+iy use normal y before tangent x; its difference
from interleaved complex orientation is `(-1)^(n(n+1)/2)`. Prove coordinate
naturality and use boundary convention `R₀₁=−∂R₁` in relative integration.

Prove **FlasqueLocality** for sheaves of sets and then modules: if every
point has an open neighborhood W on which every restriction F(V)→F(U),
U⊆V⊆W, is surjective, then every open restriction on X is surjective.
Order extensions of a fixed section by their open domains. Glue chains,
apply Zorn, and extend a maximal section across a local flabby neighborhood
to prove its domain is all X. Express the module conclusion using native

locally constant twists from this lemma.

## HF2. Purity, flabbiness and compact duality

**HF2.AnalyticPreparation — Malgrange top vanishing.**

Own **MalgrangeTopVanishing**: for n≥1, every open Ω⊆ℂⁿ and 0≤p≤n,
`H^n(Ω,Ω^p)=0`; equivalently the top-degree smooth Dolbeault operator is
onto. Use the following constructive real-Laplacian route on Ω⊆ℝ^(2n),
with `Δ=Σ_a∂_a²`.

Own the filled-compact exhaustion and harmonic Runge lemma. There are
compact K_j⊂int K_(j+1) exhausting Ω such that Ω\K_j has no relatively
compact connected component. If h is harmonic on a neighborhood of K_j,
then for every m and ε>0 there is H harmonic on all Ω with
`max_(|α|≤m,x∈K_j)|∂^α(H−h)(x)|<ε`. Prove this by Hahn–Banach and the
compact-distribution dual from K5a: a separating distribution T supported
in K_j annihilates every harmonic function on Ω. Its Newton potential
w=E*T satisfies Δw=T and is real analytic off K_j. Here in real dimension
d=2n, use `E=log‖x‖/(2π)` for d=2 and
`E=‖x‖^(2−d)/((2−d)area(S^(d−1)))` for d>2, proving ΔE=δ.
Annihilation of pole kernels and all their derivatives at points outside Ω
makes every jet of w zero there; harmonic-polynomial annihilation and the
convergent exterior multipole expansion make w zero near infinity.
Filledness implies every component of ℝ^(2n)\K_j is unbounded or meets
ℝ^(2n)\Ω: a bounded component contained in Ω would have compact closure
in Ω and would contradict the filled-exhaustion property. Apply analytic
unique continuation on each of these components of ℝ^(2n)\K_j, using
the zero exterior expansion in the unbounded case and the zero jets at
a point outside Ω in the other case. This gives supp w⊆K_j.
Integration by parts against the germ h gives ⟨T,h⟩=0, proving Runge density.
Own the exhaustion, Newton convolution, multipole expansion and harmonic
analyticity/unique-continuation steps with these exact support hypotheses.

For each bounded open O relatively compact in Ω solve Δv=f weakly using
the gradient completion of C_c∞(O), its Poincaré inequality and Hilbert
Riesz representation, with weak identity `∫∇v·∇η=−∫fη`; PDO's interior elliptic regularity gives a smooth
solution on O. On the exhaustion, subtract the global harmonic Runge
approximants to successive differences, with summable errors in the
successive C^j(K_j) seminorms. Prove convergence to a smooth solution of
Δv=f on all Ω, including disconnected Ω componentwise.

For scalar f solve Δv=4f and use
`∂̄(Σ_j(−1)^(j−1)∂_(z_j)v dbar(z)_[j])=f dbar(z₁)∧…∧dbar(z_n)`.
For the holomorphic-first (p,q)-form convention, multiply the corresponding
coefficientwise primitive with dz_I on the left by (−1)^p. This proves
surjectivity, hence closed range, of the stated top Dolbeault operator.
These Euclidean Poisson/Runge inputs form an independent construction
before purity and compact analytic duality.
Dimension0 is treated directly.

**HF2.AnalyticPreparation.FunctionalDuality — FS/DFS transposition.**
Here FS means Fréchet–Schwartz; DFS means a locally convex space
topologically isomorphic to the strong dual of an FS space. Construct the
actual strong-dual identifications and compact Banach-limit description below.
Consume K5a’s global compact-open C^∞ Fréchet carrier for smooth sections
of every finite-rank bundle on a finite-dimensional second-countable
Hausdorff complex manifold. Prove its nuclear Fréchet–Schwartz (FS) property:
embed by a countable chart/frame restriction family as the closed overlap-
compatible subspace of a countable product of local smooth-section spaces,
prove the local nuclear seminorm estimates and prove the restriction map
is a topological isomorphism from K5a’s topology onto that closed compatible
subspace. Construct continuous differentials and
closed kernels on these carriers.
