## Layer 0 Discrete convexity and supporting geometry

### 0.1 Convex height functions and existence

For `h : ℕ → WithTop ℝ`, define the predicate `IsConvexSeq h` by an
order-connected finite domain and monotone real increments on its finite edges.
This is a proposition on a function, not a second type of sequences. A bundled
`ConvexPolygon` contains just a height function and this proof; it does not
require provenance from coefficients or a vertex-walk algorithm. Prove the
discrete chord inequality, supporting-line inequalities and reconstruction from
an anchor and increments.

Define canonical piecewise-affine interpolation on the real interval spanned
by the finite domain. Prove that `IsConvexSeq h` is equivalent to `ConvexOn ℝ`
for this interpolation, for both finite intervals and half-lines; handle empty
and singleton domains explicitly. Integer restriction and interpolation recover
the original heights, and interpolation identifies height equality and order.
The domain for `ConvexOn` is the real interval, not the nonconvex set of integer
points. Existence of an arbitrary convex extension is a useful corollary, but
does not identify a unique interpolation. Keep the discrete predicate available
for coefficient proofs, and use the equivalence to import real convexity results.

Pointwise maxima and nonempty pointwise suprema of convex height functions are
convex, using the conditional-supremum hypotheses explicitly. Pointwise minima
need not be convex.

For an arbitrary height sequence `a`, define `IsLowerConvexEnvelope a h` by
convexity, `h ≤ a`, and greatestness among convex minorants. Prove literal uniqueness.
On `ℕ`, admissibility is the existence of a real affine lower bound:
`∃ c m, ∀ n, c + mn ≤ a(n)`. Prove its equivalence with existence of a convex
minorant and of the greatest one. The empty point set is admissible and has
polygon `∞`. Define a total `lowerConvexEnvelope`, taking the all-`∞` fallback when no
minorant exists; all geometric conclusions require admissibility. The fallback
is not an envelope of the inadmissible input.

For a nonempty admissible sequence the finite domain is the integer convex hull
of its finite indices. The polygon passes through the first finite point and,
when present, the last. Adding a constant translates the height by that constant;
adding `mn` shears it; the construction is monotone in the input. A sequence with
a point and no affine lower bound is called vertical. It has no proper polygon.

### 0.2 Construction, vertices and rationality

Construct the one-sided polygon by minimal slopes from successive contact points.
If the minimal slope is attained at a nonempty finite set of later indices,
move to the largest such index. If the infimum is not attained, or the minimising
indices are unbounded, the remaining polygon is a ray. If no later finite index
exists, it stops. Prove the lower-bound and maximality arguments separately,
including the approximation argument for a nonattained infimum.

Merge collinear pieces when extracting geometric vertices. A last coefficient
lying on a terminal ray need not be a vertex: the slope may not change there.
Interior vertices are genuine strict changes of finite slopes, and occur at
coefficient points. Define maximal finite segments and terminal rays separately.
Truncating the point set preserves the hull up to any retained geometric vertex.

For a finite polygon define its slope multiset from exactly its finite edges.
Its cardinality is the horizontal length and its sum is the endpoint height
difference. A bounded segment with integral endpoint heights has rational slope
whose reduced denominator divides its length. A terminal ray need not have
rational slope, even if all coefficient heights are integers and there is only
one geometric piece.

### 0.3 Supporting values and finite faces

Define `S_a(σ) = inf_n (a(n) - σn)` in `EReal`, with a missing coefficient
contributing `∞`. Prove `S_a = S_h` for an admissible sequence and its polygon,
and recover `h` as the supremum of its affine supporting lines. Where supporting
values are finite, prove concavity. State local piecewise affinity on intervals
where the relevant supporting faces are finite; accumulation can occur at an
endpoint of the domain.

Define a face by contact with a specified supporting line. A finite face has
absolute endpoints `l ≤ u`; its contact indices are exactly `[l,u]`. For a
polygon anchored at `a`, prove
`l = a + #{finite unit slopes < σ}` and
`u = a + #{finite unit slopes ≤ σ}` under the finiteness hypotheses.
A singleton face contributes zero multiplicity. Do not define an infinite face
endpoint by an unguarded natural-number infimum or cardinality.

A nonempty finite polygon has finite faces at every real slope. An infinite polygon whose
finite slopes tend to `∞` does too. More locally, if some later finite slope is
strictly greater than `σ`, the face of slope `σ` is finite and nonempty.
For infinite support, distinguish unbounded slopes, a terminal ray and slopes
strictly increasing towards a finite supremum.

### 0.4 Minkowski sums and common lower bounds

For one-sided polygons use the finite min-convolution
`(h₁ ⊞ h₂)(n) = min_{i+j=n}(h₁(i)+h₂(j))`.
Prove convexity, symmetry and associativity. The singleton at `(0,0)` is the
identity and the empty polygon is absorbing. For nonempty polygons the anchors
add, and their supporting values add in `EReal`. Prove the
common-supporting-slope description of a minimising split. When the relevant
faces are finite, their endpoints add; the splits at the two endpoints are
unique. For finite polygons, slope multisets add.

For later addition estimates, construct the greatest convex minorant of
`min(h₁,h₂)` when admissible. A common convex lower bound of `h₁` and `h₂`
is a lower bound for that envelope, by greatestness in §0.1. The generally
nonconvex pointwise minimum itself is not a lower bound for the polygon of a sum.

### 0.5 Integer-indexed sequences

Give the height-function specification and supporting-value theory on `ℤ` as
well. Existence is equivalent to an affine lower bound on the entire point set.
Prove compatibility with extension by `∞` on negative indices and with integer
translation. A sequence bounded below in its support reduces to the one-sided
construction. No vertex walk starting at a nonexistent first point is asserted
for a genuinely two-sided sequence.

### 0.6 Slope presentations and reconstruction

Provide `ConvexPolygon.FiniteSlopeData` for a nonempty finite polygon: an
initial abscissa in `ℕ`, an initial height, a horizontal length `d`, and
nondecreasing unit slopes indexed by `Fin d`. Length zero represents a singleton;
the empty polygon is separate. Reconstruct heights by cumulative sums on the
specified interval and put `∞` outside it. Conversely, recover the starting
point, length and slopes from a nonempty finite convex height function. Prove
both round trips, including equality of the slope data when heights agree.
Transport this presentation to an integer anchor for the bounded-below domains
of §0.5.

The unit-edge representation enforces the structural edge conditions directly.
Slopes and the initial height belong to an ordered additive group such as `ℚ`
or `ℝ`, not an extended-value type containing slope sentinels. Every actual edge
has horizontal length one. If `d=0`, `Fin d` is empty: the singleton has no
zero-width segment and no dummy slope. Finite slope entries exist only on
`Fin d`, so there are no out-of-support entries to fix. The value `∞` occurs

A finite compressed presentation consists of strictly increasing slopes with positive

```text
extract (heights s) = s
lowerConvexEnvelope (heights s) = heights s.
```

## Layer 2 Coefficients, Gauss values and active indices

### 2.1 Coefficient polygons and elementary operations

Define `a_f(n)=w(coeff n f)` and use `lowerConvexEnvelope a_f` to define
`Polynomial.newtonPolygon` and `PowerSeries.newtonPolygon`, with their explicit

L5 using §1.2's order-valuation comparison; initial forms and ramified substitutions

Polynomial sequences are admissible. A power-series
sequence is admissible exactly when it is restricted at some positive radius;
prove this by passing between an affine lower bound and geometric decay at a
strictly smaller radius. This includes the zero sequence.

For nonzero polynomials prove the anchor, endpoint and slope-cardinality
statements of Convention 4. Compare polynomial and power-series coercions.
Prove scalar multiplication, `X^a` shifts, substitution `X ↦ cX` for `c ≠ 0`,
and isometric scalar extension with compatible valuations. For a polynomial of
degree `d`, reversal reflects the finite graph by `n ↦ d-n`; its slopes are
negated. Multiplication by a nonzero scalar translates heights and preserves
slopes. A nonzero constant or monomial has no finite slopes.

### 2.2 Gauss norms as supporting values

For `r=b^σ`, establish the term dictionary
`‖a_n‖ r^n = b^(-(w(a_n)-σn))` for nonzero coefficients, with the correct
inequality reversals and explicit zero cases. For nonzero `f` with bounded
radius-`r` coefficient terms,
`S_f(σ) = -log_b(gaussNorm norm r f)` is real and equals the supporting value
of its polygon. Boundedness is equivalent to `S_f(σ)>-∞`; nonzeroness excludes
`S_f(σ)=∞`. Restrictedness is stronger than boundedness.

For polynomial inputs the supporting function is concave and piecewise affine
on all of `ℝ`. For a series the same local statement holds in the interior of
its convergence range, with breakpoints at the finite slopes. Prove the
Legendre reconstruction with the extended-valued supporting function, including
its domain; do not apply a real logarithm to a junk or zero Gauss value.

### 2.3 First and last active coefficient

For `r>0`, `f≠0` and `f` restricted at `r`, define `l_r(f)` and `u_r(f)`
from the finite nonempty set of norm-attaining coefficient indices. Prove
their extremal characterisation, strict bounds outside their interval,
monotonicity as the radius increases through restricted radii, and compatibility
with coefficient isometries and order shifts.

If `f` is restricted at some `s>r`, show that the supporting face at
`σ=log_b r` is finite with endpoints `l_r(f),u_r(f)`. Include the polynomial
case at every radius. On compact slope intervals lying strictly inside the
convergence range only finitely many coefficients can be active. The one-sided
derivatives of `S_f` there are `-l_r(f)` on the left and `-u_r(f)` on the right.

The greatest active index makes `f` distinguished of that degree over the
field, using the predicate supplied by RestrictedPowerSeries. The unit
criterion is `u_r(f)=0`, equivalently unique attainment at index zero.
It must not be replaced by a claim about the absence of a terminal polygon ray.

### 2.4 Purity and first breaks

For a polynomial of positive degree and nonzero constant coefficient, purity
of slope `m` means that all finite slopes equal `m`. It is equivalent to the
coefficients lying on or above the line joining the first and last points.
Interior points may lie on that line. In Gauss form all terms at `b^m` are
bounded by the equal constant and leading terms.

Define a first break at `j` by the first segment ending there and a genuine
increase of the slope afterwards, allowing the polynomial endpoint as a
terminal finite segment. Give its coefficient-line criterion: equality at
the endpoint and a supporting line of strictly larger slope after it.
Pointwise strict inequalities beyond `j` alone do not imply a break for an
infinite sequence. At a finite face's right endpoint, translate the resulting
conditions into distinguishedness and then use Layer 4.

### 2.5 Hodge lower bounds and coefficient comparisons

For an admissible coefficient sequence and a convex height function `H`, prove
that coefficient bounds `H(n) ≤ w(coeff n f)` imply `IsBelow H (newtonPolygon f)`.
Specialise to finite and infinite nondecreasing weight sequences from §0.7,
with a chosen starting point and explicit domain. A general admissible bound
`b` gives `lowerConvexEnvelope b ≤ newtonPolygon f`; the raw interpolation of

For the operator application, take coefficient estimates for

Row bounds or weights give a Hodge lower polygon once those estimates are
proved. The sequence-level construction and the implication from coefficient
bounds are owned here; determinant expansions, minor bounds and compactness

The finite-dimensional interpretation fixes the convention. For a full-rank

`χ_U(T)=det(TI-U)`.
Our coefficient polygon of `χ_U` has slopes equal to negatives of root

## Layer 5 Convergence and entire products

### 5.1 The intrinsic radius

Define `R(f)` as in Convention 6. Prove that `0<r<R(f)` implies restrictedness
at `r`, and that `r>R(f)` excludes it. Prove the Cauchy–Hadamard formula in
extended nonnegative reals,
`R(f)⁻¹ = limsup_{n→∞} ‖a_n‖^(1/n)`.

`R(f)=∞`, using the definition supplied by RestrictedPowerSeries §7.2.

For infinitely supported `f`, let
`λ = liminf_{n→∞} w(a_n)/n` in `EReal`, assigning `∞` to zero coefficients.
If the coefficient sequence is admissible, identify `λ` with the supremum of
its finite unit slopes. Then `R(f)=b^λ`, with `b^(+∞)=∞` and `b^(-∞)=0`
in `ℝ≥0∞`. If it is vertical, `λ=-∞` and `R(f)=0`.

slope multiset. Do not take a finite polynomial's largest slope as its radius.

At a finite positive boundary radius no conclusion about restrictedness follows
from the limiting slope alone. Restrictedness at one positive radius does not
bound all slopes: an entire nonpolynomial provides a counterexample.

### 5.2 Convergence in extensions

For a complete isometric extension `L/K`, prove that convergence at a point
of positive norm `r` is equivalent to restrictedness at `r`; use ultrametric
summability and the norm of the individual terms. Deduce convergence throughout
every closed disc at a restricted radius, with the supplied evaluation bound.
Convergence on all points of a closed ball implies restrictedness at its
numerical radius when that radius is attained by the norm of a point.

Define the separate supremum `R_L^{points}(f)` of norms of convergence points.
It is at most `R(f)` and equals it when the positive norms of `L` are dense in
`ℝ_{>0}`. Prove this density for `ℂ_p` using §1.3. Include a discrete-value-group
example where the inequality is strict. These comparisons do not change the
definition of `R(f)`.

### 5.3 Entire factorisation

For an entire nonzero series, the slopes are either a finite polynomial
multiset or tend to `∞` along the finite edges. Its zeros in an algebraically
closed complete extension are finite in every bounded disc, with multiplicity.
Their total support is countable. When infinitely many are listed with
multiplicity, their norms tend to `∞`.

For `f(0)=1`, the canonical polynomials `P_r` tend to `f` in every fixed Gauss
norm as `r→∞`. Prove this using entire polynomial division and the normalised

`f = ∏ (1-X/α)` over its nonzero zeros with multiplicity, with convergence in

from an enumeration of its countable multiset.

Conversely, a family of nonzero elements with only finitely many members in
each bounded ball, counted with multiplicity, defines an entire product with
exactly that zero divisor. Normalised entire functions with the same zero
divisor are equal. Entire units are nonzero constants; over an algebraically
closed field an entire function with finitely many zeros is a polynomial.
Do not extend these global product claims to a finite open disc without new

is asserted on the whole affine line, not on an arbitrary open disc.

## Layer 6 Discrete valuations and formal preparation

### 6.1 Denominators and irreducibility

For an integer-valued additive valuation normalised at a uniformiser, record
the exact slope `(y₁-y₀)/(i₁-i₀)` of a bounded segment. Its reduced denominator
divides the segment length. If a nonconstant polynomial with nonzero constant
coefficient is pure of slope `a/d`, has degree `d`, and `gcd(a,d)=1`, prove
irreducibility over the field. The proof uses the polynomial product theorem
and integrality of the endpoint heights of any factor.

Recover the Eisenstein criterion and compare with Mathlib's
`Polynomial.IsEisensteinAt`. A monic Eisenstein polynomial of degree `d`
has endpoints `(0,1),(d,0)` and slope `-1/d`. Dividing by its constant
coefficient gives constant term one and keeps that slope. Reversal instead
negates it, giving `+1/d`. State both transformations explicitly.

Over a complete coefficient field, use §4.2's pure slope factors. For each
factor of degree `d_m` and slope denominator `q_m`, every
irreducible factor degree is a positive multiple of `q_m`. Consequently there
is at least one factor for each distinct slope and at most `d_m/q_m` factors
within that slope, counted with multiplicity. The case `d_m=q_m` forces
irreducibility of that pure factor; otherwise the polygon alone need not decide.

### 6.2 Ramification consequences

If a nonzero root has base-normalised valuation `a/q` in lowest terms and lies
in a finite extension `L`, prove `q` divides `e(L/K)` using the integral
normalisation on `L`. Combine this with `e≤[L:K]` from §1.3. For local fields
state the conclusion on LocalFieldsRamification's canonical ramification index.
The minimal-polynomial and pure-factor versions are corollaries. Do not require
a finite residue field for the valuation-theoretic divisibility statement.

### 6.3 The preparation contract for Iwasawa theory

Let `O` be a complete discrete valuation ring, `π` a uniformiser, and `f∈O⟦X⟧`
nonzero. Completeness is for the maximal-ideal adic topology. Define
`μ(f)=min_n v_π(a_n)` and
`λ(f)=min{n | v_π(a_n)=μ(f)}`.
Prove the minima exist, using the nonnegative integer values and nonzeroness.
No finite-residue-field hypothesis is imposed.

Supply the public target `exists_pow_mul_distinguished_mul_unit` in the
valuation-ring form consumed by PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras §4.3: for
`O = Valuation.integer (NormedField.valuation (K := K))`, with `K` complete
and ultrametric, `[IsDiscreteValuationRing O]`, and
`[IsAdicComplete (IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal O) O]`, an irreducible `π : O`
and nonzero `f : PowerSeries O` admit

```text
f = PowerSeries.C (π ^ μ) * (u : PowerSeries O) * (P : PowerSeries O),
P.IsDistinguishedAt (IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal O),
u : (PowerSeries O)ˣ.
```

Prove the stronger specification that the exponent is `μ(f)` and
`P.natDegree=λ(f)`, and uniqueness for the fixed uniformiser and monic
distinguished polynomial. The proof removes the common uniformiser power
coefficientwise, then applies Mathlib's ideal-adic preparation theorem.
Give the abstract complete-DVR theorem as well, with the valuation-ring form
as its specialisation, so consumers need not introduce a fraction-field norm
merely to apply preparation.

Prove `μ(fg)=μ(f)+μ(g)` and `λ(fg)=λ(f)+λ(g)` for nonzero formal series.
Use reduction of the normalised series modulo the maximal ideal and addition
of orders in the residue-field power-series domain. This does not require
restrictedness at radius one or a global analytic polygon product theorem.

On embedding `O` in its complete discretely valued fraction field, identify
`μ` with the minimum polygon height and `λ` with the first absolute index
where that minimum is attained. The minimum face may be an infinite ray;
its right endpoint is not used. Its left endpoint includes any order of
vanishing at zero. These are the interfaces consumed by
[PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras §4.3](../PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/README.md).

### 6.4 Comparing formal and normed preparation

Every `O`-coefficient formal series is restricted at `0<r<1`; it need not be
restricted at `r=1`. After removing `π^μ`, the least unit coefficient occurs
at `λ`. For all `r<1` sufficiently close to one, it is the unique dominant
weighted coefficient: the finitely many earlier coefficients have norm less
than one, and later terms acquire the strictly smaller powers of `r`.

Prove that the formal distinguished polynomial is exactly the monic normed
preparation polynomial at those radii, and that the formal unit is a unit of
each such restricted algebra. At radius one, when the series is restricted,
the normed degree is the **greatest** index attaining the minimum coefficient
valuation. It agrees with the formal degree when that index is unique; no
unqualified equivalence of the two notions of distinguishedness is asserted.

The formal polynomial counts the zeros in the open unit disc, with
multiplicity, after passage to a splitting complete extension. The normed
unit-disc polynomial may include additional boundary roots.

### 6.5 A ramified quadratic base-extension check

Over `ℚ₂`, `ξ₂=X²+2X+2` is Eisenstein and irreducible. Over `ℚ₂(i)`, with
`i²=-1`, it factors in the valuation ring `ℤ₂[i]` as

```text
ξ₂ = (X-(i-1)) (X-(-i-1)).
```

Prove the identity, monicity and degree one of both factors, and reducibility.
Give the Lean example in the valuation ring of any complete ultrametric
`ℚ₂`-extension containing such an integral `i`.
For `ℚ₂(i)` identify `i-1` as a uniformiser. In its integer normalisation
`v(2)=2` and the polygon slope is `-1`; in the base `2` normalisation the
slope is `-1/2`. This explains why the base-field irreducibility criterion
cannot be reapplied using the wrong value group after extension.

**Checks.** `X^p-p` has slope `-1/p` and forces ramification index `p` in
the degree-`p` root extension. `Φ_p(X+1)/p` has slope `-1/(p-1)`;
`Φ_p(X)` is flat. For `p+X+X²`, `μ=0` and `λ=1`, whereas the unit-disc
Weierstrass degree is two. For `ΣX^n∈O⟦X⟧`, `μ=λ=0` and the series is
a formal unit, although it is not restricted at radius one. Include the
two linear factors of `ξ₂` above.

**Dependencies.** Layers 1–4 for the polygon, root and ramification statements;
Mathlib DVR and ideal-adic preparation for §6.3; RestrictedPowerSeries for
§6.4. Formal preparation and the algebraic additivity of `μ,λ` are independent
of the entire-series theory. Sources: [Neukirch], [Washington] §7.1, [NSW]
(5.3.1)–(5.3.4).

## Dependency order and completion criteria

```text
Mathlib convexity → Layer 0 ─┐
Mathlib valuations → Layer 1 ├→ Layer 2 → Layer 3
RestrictedPowerSeries ───────┘               │
                                            ↓
shared preparation and evaluation ───────→ Layer 4 → Layer 5
Layers 1–4 ─────────────────────────────→ Layer 6 polygon consequences
Mathlib DVR/adic preparation ───────────→ §6.3 formal preparation
shared restricted-series theory ────────→ §6.4 comparison
```

The polynomial product and root theorems precede slope factorisation. General
Gauss multiplicativity is an input, so there is no cycle through an entire-series
polygon theorem. The finite-extension valuation arguments do not use the
Newton irreducibility criterion they later support.

Completion requires the following interfaces and their checks.

1. A unique generic convex envelope with honest finite-edge slopes, finite
   faces, terminal rays, affine covariance and supporting-value reconstruction;
   canonical `ConvexOn` interpolation; and finite/infinite slope-data conversions
   with normalised round trips, including rational finite presentations.
2. Compatible integer, rational and real valuation normalisations, including
   `ℚ_p`, `ℂ_p`, algebraic extensions and local-field comparisons.
3. Polynomial slope/root multisets and product identities, and the fixed-radius
   first/last-active-index product and perturbation theorems.
4. Canonical disc polynomials, compatible slope factors, analytic multiplicities
   and exact open/closed/sphere counts with their splitting hypotheses.
5. The intrinsic radius theorem with polynomial, vertical and boundary cases,
   and convergence of the entire Weierstrass product in every Gauss norm.
6. Discrete irreducibility and ramification consequences, the complete-DVR
   preparation contract and quadratic check, and the precise formal/normed comparison.
7. Pointwise polygon order, its partial-sum characterisation, and Hodge lower
   bounds from explicit coefficient inequalities, with the Fredholm determinant
   convention and operator-theory ownership boundary preserved.

Consumers should be able to cite these interfaces without reconstructing a
valuation normalisation or restricted-series algebra. In particular, the
Iwasawa preparation target is usable independently of the analytic layers.

# Cyclic cohomology, spectral triples and noncommutative tori

Build the differential and cyclic theory of smooth operator algebras, its
Fredholm-module Chern characters and index pairings, and the spectral-triple
Hochschild-class theorem. Develop the logarithmic trace ideal and Dixmier
traces with their actual generalized-limit hypotheses. The smooth two-torus
is a complete example: its differential calculus, periodic cyclic cohomology,
Fourier spectral triple and Heisenberg-module index connect these constructions.

## Scope, conventions and suppliers

Algebras are complex. The algebraic cyclic theory begins for associative
unital algebras, with nonunital algebras handled by forced unitization and
relative complexes; analytic statements use continuous cochains on complete Hausdorff
locally convex algebras, and smooth dense Fréchet star subalgebras of
C*-algebras. A Fréchet algebra has a complete metrizable locally convex
complex topology with continuous multiplication; its inclusion into the
C*-algebra is injective, continuous and dense. Spectral-invariance and
summability hypotheses are stated separately. Spectral triples here have
separable complex Hilbert space, a self-adjoint densely defined closed D,
compact resolvent and bounded commutators on the specified smooth algebra.

Hilbert products conjugate the first variable. The integer Fredholm index is
kernel dimension minus cokernel dimension. Even grading γ has γ*=γ, γ²=1,
commutes with the representation and anticommutes with F or D; the even
compression goes from the positive to the negative grading. Odd compression
uses `P=(1+F)/2`, and its index is `ind(Pπ(u)P)`. Fix
`√(2i)=1+i` in the odd cyclic pairing and character constants.
Operators multiply in composition order, with the rightmost acting first.
Universal forms have degree one differential and Koszul signs.

Representations of bounded Fredholm modules can be nonunital. Normalize
their compact defects by the doubling construction in N3 before extending
to the forced unitization by `π̃(a,λ)=π(a)+λI`; use relative cyclic/K
classes for nonunital algebras. For a unital algebra represented nonunitally,
the even unit pairing compresses to π(1)H, and the odd unitary is represented
by `π(u)+I−π(1)`. The doubled, unitized cycle defines the index map;
prove agreement with the original compression wherever that compression
is already Fredholm. A compact defect relative to π(A) alone does not
define a compression index on every unitization class.
Full cyclic cochains and the normalized Hochschild mixed complex have the
same cyclic cohomology; normalization removes degeneracies, not the
degree-zero scalar cochain or its even periodicity images.
For unital A the Hochschild and mixed complexes are those of A itself.
For nonunital A use the kernel of restriction from the cochain complexes
of A⁺ to those of ℂ along its scalar-unit inclusion; the algebra
augmentation supplies a splitting in the contravariant direction.
The SBI assertion concerns this relative Hochschild theory. No
H-unitality or comparison with the naive nonunital bar complex is assumed.

`Derivation` for the commutative specialization. For noncommutative
endomorphism-valued derivations consume Tau Ceti's existing
`derivationLieAlgebra ℂ A`, the Lie subalgebra of native `Module.End`
with the associative Leibniz rule; construct the A-bimodule-valued
universal-derivation comparison using commuting left/right actions. Use
`ChainComplex`/`CochainComplex`, kernels, quotients and cohomology APIs.
Use `ContinuousLinearMap.IsFredholm`, `FredholmPackage` and the native
integer index through K4. Do not replace closed operator domains by total
linear maps, or Fredholmness by an opaque extra predicate. N1 owns the
cyclic/mixed-complex structure; ordinary derived categories belong to the
existing homological-algebra developments.

The selected character theory is finite summability and the Dixmier-trace
Hochschild class. Entire cyclic cohomology and fixed-temperature θ-summable
characters are outside scope, as are foliations, the full local index formula,
geometric elliptic-symbol calculus and Standard Model constructions.
[IndexTheory](../IndexTheory/README.md) owns closed-manifold elliptic index
and the Atiyah–Singer theorem; no such theorem is a prerequisite for the
abstract or torus index computations here.

## N1. Universal differential forms and cyclic complexes

Construct completed projective tensors of Hausdorff locally convex
spaces using the seminorms
`π_(p,q)(t)=inf_(t=Σx_i⊗y_i)Σp(x_i)q(y_i)` and Hausdorff completion.
Prove the universal property for continuous bilinear maps into complete
spaces, functoriality, associativity, tensor flip and compatibility with
finite sums. Prove Fréchet completeness/metrizability and its agreement
with BanachSpaceTheory B4's Banach projective tensor. Build completed
bar resolutions and their continuous contracting homotopies for unital
algebras. Identify continuous multilinear cochains with continuous
functionals on the completed tensors by the universal property, using
uniform convergence on products of bounded sets for the cochain topology
on both sides, and prove compatibility of the differentials. In the smooth
circle example prove `C^∞(S¹)⊗̂_π C^∞(S¹)≃C^∞(𝕋²)` using
rapid Fourier decay, including both topologies and inverse-closedness.

For every associative A use its forced unitization A⁺, even when A
already has a unit. Construct universal forms from the kernel of
`multiplication:A⁺⊗A⁺→A⁺`, with
`da=1_ext⊗a−a⊗1_ext`, and their graded tensor algebra. Identify
positive-degree forms with `A⁺⊗A^⊗n`; under this identification
da is `1_ext⊗a`. Prove the derivation universal property, graded
Leibniz rule, d²=0, tensor-word relations and functoriality.
A cycle has an algebra map ρ:A→Ω⁰ which need not preserve an
existing unit, and a closed graded trace. Prove every cyclic cocycle
realized by such a universal-form cycle and every cycle gives a
cyclic cocycle via
`φ(a₀,…,a_n)=∫ρ(a₀)dρ(a₁)⋯dρ(a_n)`.
For unital A separately construct the normalized form quotient
`A⊗(A/ℂ1_A)^⊗n` and its comparison with normalized Hochschild
chains. Do not replace the full cycle construction by this quotient:
`φ(a,b,c)=abc` on ℂ is a cyclic 2-cocycle nonzero on (1,1,1),
requiring a possibly nonunital cycle map and the forced unitization.

For unital A define degree-n cochains as multilinear maps A^(n+1)→ℂ.
For nonunital A apply these formulas to A⁺ and take the relative
complex specified above. A cyclic cochain
satisfies `φ(a_n,a₀,…,a_(n−1))=(−1)^nφ(a₀,…,a_n)`.
Pin the Hochschild coboundary to

`(bφ)(a₀,…,a_(n+1))`
`=Σ_(j=0)^n(−1)^j φ(a₀,…,a_j a_(j+1),…,a_(n+1))`
` +(−1)^(n+1)φ(a_(n+1)a₀,a₁,…,a_n)`.

Prove b²=0 and preservation of the cyclic subcomplex. Construct cochain
pullbacks, addition, scalar multiplication, kernels, boundaries and cyclic
cohomology. For unital A prove the Hochschild comparison with coefficients
in its algebraic dual. In the unital Banach/bounded specialization consume
BanachAlgebras A6's Hochschild differential and cochain API; this
roadmap supplies the cyclic and Fréchet extensions and their comparison.
For unital A, currying the first argument identifies the scalar (n+1)-cochains
with n-cochains valued in A*, using `(aφb)(x)=φ(bxa)`; prove
the differentials agree under this identification.
For locally convex A use continuous multilinear cochains;
prove the finite multiplication/permutation/degeneracy formulas preserve
continuity and compare with continuous-dual tensor formulations. Give
continuous cochains the topology of uniform convergence on products of
bounded sets. Cohomology is the algebraic quotient of continuous cocycles
by continuous coboundaries, with its quotient topology; boundaries are
not replaced by their closure. These quotients need not be Hausdorff.

Construct the cyclic operator, faces, degeneracies, b′ and cyclic norm N.
Prove the cyclic/simplicial identities, Connes B, `B²=0` and `bB+Bb=0`.
On normalized chains `a₀⊗bar a₁⊗⋯⊗bar a_n` pin B to

`Σ_(i=0)^n(−1)^(ni) 1⊗bar a_i⊗⋯⊗bar a_n⊗bar a₀⊗⋯⊗bar a_(i−1)`.

Prove descent through degenerate chains and comparison with the full
cyclic bicomplex. Construct the cyclic total complex with its finite-column
truncations, and prove its cohomology agrees with the cyclic-cochain
complex. Explicitly preserve `HC^(2k)(ℂ)=ℂ` generated by `S^k[τ]`
and `HC^(2k+1)(ℂ)=0`. For a nonzero unital A, reduced cochains
are the kernel of restriction along A's own unit inclusion ℂ→A;
the reduced complex of ℂ is zero. Distinguish this from the relative
forced-unitization theory recovering the full theory of a unital A.
Treat the zero algebra by its zero complexes. Prove the SBI sequence
with `I:HC^n→HH^n`, `B:HH^n→HC^(n−1)` and
`S:HC^(n−1)→HC^(n+1)`, and exactness at every term.
Normalize S as exterior product with the scalar cyclic 2-cocycle
`σ₁(a₀,a₁,a₂)=a₀a₁a₂`. Construct the comparison maps using the
b′ contraction inserting the unit and the cyclic norm N, then normalize
them by the scalar and circle calibrations below; inclusion in a
single unnormalized (b,B) column is not the comparison map.
Define periodic cohomology by the same-parity direct limit under S and
prove its comparison with the direct-sum cochain totalization of the
stabilized (b,B) bicomplex: representatives have finitely many nonzero
components. Pin the scalar comparison: the cyclic degree-2m class
represented by `σ_m(a₀,…,a_(2m))=m!∏_j a_j` on ℂ maps to
the degree-zero functional z↦z in this totalization. Prove its
compatibility with S and N2's pairing. For a normalized cyclic
n-cocycle the homogeneous column comparison has scalar
`c_(2m)=(−1)^m/(2m)!` and
`c_(2k+1)=(−1)^k/((1+i)sqrt(π)(2k+1)!)`.
Prove these maps agree with the full cyclic-bicomplex comparison,
including its lower unit columns, and with N2's closed periodic
Chern chains and both pairings. This pins every odd degree as well as
the degree-one circle class. Prove naturality and periodic homotopy invariance for
polynomial algebra homotopies, and for continuous homomorphisms
`A→C^∞([0,1],B)` in the locally convex theory, with continuous derivatives
and the smooth-function seminorms; construct their transgressions.
Construct matrix Morita invariance and the exterior product by tensoring
differential-form cycles, with
`(ω⊗η)(ω′⊗η′)=(−1)^(deg η deg ω′)ωω′⊗ηη′` and
`d(ω⊗η)=dω⊗η+(−1)^(deg ω)ω⊗dη`. Prove the cochain shuffle
comparison, including `[φ#ψ]=binom(p+q,p)[φ]∨[ψ]` for the
Hochschild cup comparison, graded commutativity sign `(−1)^(pq)` and compatibility
with S and the K-theory exterior product. Work out
ℂ, finite matrix algebras and traces as degree-zero cocycles, and compare
commutative differential-form cycles with their cyclic characters.

## N2. Cyclic pairings with K-theory

Extend a cochain to matrices by
`(φ#Tr)(a₀,…,a_n)=Σ_(i₀,…,i_n)φ((a₀)_(i₀i₁),…,(a_n)_(i_ni₀))`.
Prove cyclicity, compatibility with b,B,S, stabilization and trace
normalizations. For a cyclic cocycle of degree 2m and an idempotent e
use the even pairing

`⟨[e],[φ]⟩=(m!)⁻¹(φ#Tr)(e,…,e)`.

For odd n and invertible u use

`⟨[u],[φ]⟩=(1+i)⁻¹ 2^(−n) Γ(n/2+1)⁻¹`
` ·(φ#Tr)(u⁻¹−1,u−1,…,u⁻¹−1,u−1)`.

There are n+1 alternating arguments. Prove independence of cocycle
representative, stabilization, conjugation, direct sums and smooth
homotopy; prove the compatible periodicity normalization and the product
formula fixing this odd constant. Construct algebraic K₀ by group
completion of finite projective modules, with its stable-idempotent
description, and algebraic K₁ as `GL_∞(A)/E_∞(A)`, where E_∞ is
generated by elementary matrices. Prove the stable commutator/elementary
identification, functoriality and the relative unitization versions.
Prove the pairings descend through these relations, including vanishing
on elementary matrices, before imposing topological homotopy.
For inverse-closed dense Fréchet
subalgebras transport them through K3 to C*-K₀/K₁, proving continuity
and path/transgression estimates needed for topological homotopy.
Nonunital pairings use the relative forced-unitization complex and K
kernels. Prove functoriality and compare idempotents with projections and
invertibles with unitaries using K1–K2's functional-calculus paths and
K3's inverse-closed comparison.

Pin comparison with the normalized mixed complex by its closed periodic
Chern chains. The even components are `ch₀(e)=e` and, for k≥1,
`ch_(2k)(e)=(−1)^k(2k)!/k! · (e−1/2)⊗bar e^⊗(2k)`;
the odd components are
`ch_(2k+1)(u)=(−1)^k k! · u⁻¹⊗bar u⊗bar u⁻¹⊗⋯⊗bar u`,
with 2k+2 factors. Prove `(b+B)ch=0`, the relative-unitization
versions and invariance under stabilization and homotopy. Pair a
finite-support periodic cochain with these chains by the finite sum,
and prove the cyclic-to-mixed comparison gives exactly the displayed
N2 pairings.
For a normalized cyclic cocycle, pin the degree-2k component of
its mixed image to `(−1)^k φ/(2k)!`, and its degree-(2k+1)
component to `(−1)^k φ/((2k+1)!(1+i)sqrt(π))`.
For full cyclic cochains construct the lower components using the
unit/degeneracy comparison; the scalar σ_m class retains the
degree-zero component specified in N1. Prove that evaluating on
the displayed Chern chains gives N2's factorial/Gamma factors.
In odd parity calibrate on the circle cocycle
`ψ(a₀,a₁)=(2πi)⁻¹∫_(S¹)a₀ da₁`: its normalized mixed image
has degree-one component `ψ/((1+i)sqrt(π))`, so its pairing with
the positive winding class is `1/((1+i)sqrt(π))`.

Pin the odd-by-odd product on C(𝕋²): with coordinates (x,y) in
that order and winding unitaries z₁,z₂, require
`[z₁]×[z₂]=q*β`, where q collapses the coordinate circles and
has degree +1 onto the oriented two-sphere. Compare K3's chosen
tautological β with N2's smooth Bott cocycle, whose value is +1.
The product circle cocycle has coefficient `(2πi)⁻²` on dx∧dy;
compute its value on q*β as `1/(2πi)`, equal to the square of
`1/((1+i)sqrt(π))`. This calibrates the odd pairing constant and
the exterior product together, including the ordered suspension sign.

An arbitrary complex cyclic class need not pair integrally. N3 proves
integrality for the normalized Fredholm Chern character. Give the trace
pairing and a scalar multiple of it that has a noninteger value on [1].
Include matrix Morita invariance and the point normalization. For Bott
use the inverse-closed dense Fréchet algebra `𝒮(ℝ²)⊂C₀(ℝ²)` with
ordered coordinates (s,t), orientation ds∧dt and the cyclic cocycle
`φ_B(f₀,f₁,f₂)=(2πi)⁻¹∫_ℝ² f₀ df₁∧df₂`.
Build its continuity, inverse-closedness and K3 comparison. Replace
K3's tautological projection by a smoothly flattened radial pullback
equal to p(∞) off a compact disk, so its difference from p(∞) has
Schwartz entries; prove that the pullback preserves β. Compute
`⟨β,[φ_B]⟩=+1` and the scalar constant-projection contribution zero.
These formulas fix the comparison with the chosen Bott generator and
keep the sign distinct from a separately chosen geometric Chern–Weil convention.

## N3. Fredholm modules and their finite characters

Consume K5–K6's Hilbert-space specialization of KK cycles. For a cycle
whose `(F−F*)π(a)` is compact, construct the self-adjoint replacement
`(F+F*)/2` and its class-preserving compact-perturbation homotopy.
Define even
and odd Fredholm modules with bounded representation π, F*=F,
`[F,π(a)]` compact and `(F²−1)π(a)` compact; even modules carry the
specified γ. Develop unitary equivalence, direct sums, degenerate cycles,
compact perturbation, homotopy and the K4 Fredholm compressions. Build
normalization to F²=1 by first applying functional calculus to replace F
by the self-adjoint contraction `sin(πF/2)`, preserving the essential
values ±1 and its cycle class, and then doubling
on H⊕H with representation π⊕0 and operator
`F′=[[F,sqrt(1−F²)],[sqrt(1−F²),−F]]`.
In even parity use grading `diag(γ,−γ)`. Prove the off-diagonal
terms multiplied by π(a) compact, the cycle homotopy, F′²=1 and
agreement of the index with the original compression wherever that
compression is Fredholm. Extend this normalized cycle to the
forced unitization. Finite-dimensional augmentation suffices when the
defect has finite rank, including the finite kernel in N5; it is not
the general normalization construction. Construct the K6 product
comparison with the unitization conventions specified here,
including the even compression to π(1)H and the odd extension of a
unitary by the identity on the complement of π(1)H.

For normalized F and a chosen dense smooth algebra require
`[F,π(a)]∈S_p` for every a, and continuity of this commutator map
into its Schatten norm or quasi-norm. Prove matrix, sum, algebra-product,
dagger and perturbation estimates. Construct the conditional trace
`Tr′(T)=½Tr(F(FT+TF))` when FT+TF is trace class. Establish its
linearity and the graded commutator identities on its precise domain.
For integer n with the correct parity and n+1≥p define

`τ_n(a₀,…,a_n)=Tr′(π(a₀)[F,π(a₁)]⋯[F,π(a_n)])`,

with γ inserted before π(a₀) in even parity. For the displayed operator
T prove FT+TF trace-class by Hölder and the n+1-commutator identity;
T itself need not be trace-class. Establish
continuity, cyclicity and bτ_n=0. Construct transgressions between
same-parity degrees and smooth homotopies. Normalize the periodic
character by `Ch_n=λ_n τ_n`, where

`λ_n=(−1)^(n(n−1)/2)Γ(n/2+1)` in even parity,

and multiply this by −(1+i) in odd parity. With N2's positive odd
pairing factor, this sign makes the character agree with the index of
compression by P=(1+F)/2. Pin the degree-one calibration on the circle:
for F=2P_Hardy−1 and the positive winding unitary u,
`τ₁(u⁻¹−1,u−1)=2`, while `ind(P_Hardy u P_Hardy)=−1`,
so `⟨[u],Ch₁⟩=−1`. Prove independence of the
sufficiently large same-parity representative and compatibility with S.
For nonexact self-adjoint contraction cycles impose explicitly
`[F,π(a)]∈S_p` and `sqrt(1−F²)π(a), π(a)sqrt(1−F²)∈S_p`,
continuously in a. Prove these bounds give p-summable doubled cycles.
These are additional summability hypotheses, distinct from the compact
defects of an arbitrary Fredholm cycle.
Also prove that the usual bounds `[F,π(a)]∈S_p` and
`(F²−1)π(a)∈S_p`, with their adjoint/continuity bounds, give an
S_(2p)-summable doubled cycle by square-root estimates. Prove the
power-series commutator bounds for the sine replacement, using
p-subadditivity when p<1, before applying these square-root estimates.
Use a sufficiently large same-parity degree n+1≥2p in that case.

Prove the character index theorem: the even pairing with a projection e
is the index of `π(e)F⁺π(e):π(e)H⁺→π(e)H⁻`; the odd pairing with
an invertible u is `ind(Pπ̃(u)P)` on PH, with P=(1+F)/2 and forced
unitization where needed. For a unital algebra acting nonunitally replace
π(u) by `π(u)+I−π(1)`. Construct the trace index identity and its
perturbation/finite-kernel argument before proving integrality. Compare
with K4's native index and, under K5–K6's separable C*-algebra
hypotheses, the KK product. Construct the external product of the two
smooth circle Fredholm modules using N7's Fourier Dirac operator at θ=0.
Prove the two Hardy classes have indices −1 and their unswapped product
is this oriented Dirac class. K5's swapped period reduction gives its
negative class, represented by the reversed grading. For this product
prove `Ch(x×y)=−Ch(x)#Ch(y)` and the graded index-interchange
identity; point factors contribute no additional adapter sign. These
computations concern the explicitly finitely summable point/circle
products. A general KK product is not assumed to have a finitely
summable representative on the given smooth algebra. Work out point cycles,
the circle Hardy/shift compression with index −1 for the forward
shift and +1 for its adjoint, a finite matrix
amplification and a nonsummable compact-commutator cycle. Summability
is a condition on the specified smooth algebra, not automatically on
the whole C*-completion.

## N4. Weak ideals, generalized limits and Dixmier traces

Using OperatorIdeals' singular values, construct the Marcinkiewicz
logarithmic trace ideal

`L^(1,∞)={T compact : sup_(N≥1) (log(1+N))⁻¹ Σ_(j<N)μ_j(T)<∞}`.

Prove its ideal/quasi-norm structure, completeness, adjoint/unitary
invariance, singular-value inequalities, finite-rank and trace-class
inclusions and bounded left/right multiplication. Distinguish it from
`S_(1,∞)={T: sup_(j≥0)(j+1)μ_j(T)<∞}`, supplied by I1's weak L₁
specialization, and construct a diagonal operator in the former but not
the latter. For p>1 write `L^(p,∞)` for I1's weak Schatten space
`sup_(j≥0)(j+1)^(1/p)μ_j(T)<∞`; prove its equivalent partial-sum
description and compare its power/product estimates with the logarithmic
ideal. In particular `T∈L^(n,∞)` implies `|T|^n∈L^(1,∞)`.
For n=1 use the logarithmic ideal itself. Do not replace the logarithmic p=1
ideal by the smaller pointwise singular-value condition.

Construct positive generalized limits on bounded real sequences which
extend ordinary limits and are invariant under integer dilations,
including duplicating entries. Prove existence by positive extension
and an invariant-mean/compactness argument, and develop restrictions,
rescalings and complex linear extension. For positive T define

`Tr_ω(T)=Lim_ω((log(1+N))⁻¹ Σ_(j<N)μ_j(T))`.

Prove additivity on the positive cone with the dilation-invariance
hypothesis, positive homogeneity and extension to a linear trace on
L^(1,∞). Prove unitary invariance, `Tr_ω(AT)=Tr_ω(TA)` for bounded A,
boundedness, vanishing on trace class and its singularity/non-normality.
Give diagonal examples with nonzero trace, zero trace outside trace
class, and dependence on ω. A general positive extension of limits
without dilation invariance is not asserted to give an additive trace.
Call T measurable when all Tr_ω with dilation-invariant ω agree; prove
ordinary convergence of the logarithmic means a sufficient condition.

Prove the logarithmic Hardy–Littlewood/Karamata Tauberian bridge used
here, including its monotonicity/positivity and summation-by-parts
estimates: for positive T∈L^(1,∞),
`lim_(s↓1)(s−1)Tr(T^s)=L` iff the logarithmic partial-sum means
converge to L. Deduce Tr_ω(T)=L and the simple-pole residue formula.
This elementary Tauberian theorem is built here; the Wiener–Ikehara
supplier in ArithmeticDirichletSeries is not a substitute. Work out
the diagonal sequence 1/(j+1) and finite-rank perturbations. N7 owns
the Fourier lattice example using this Tauberian bridge. No general pseudodifferential residue
formula is imposed on arbitrary members of this ideal.

## N5. Spectral triples and the Hochschild class

For a self-adjoint D, compact resolvent means that its bounded inverse
`(D−i)⁻¹` is compact; compare this with the native `(i−D)⁻¹`
convention. Prove compactness of one nonreal resolvent equivalent to
compactness at all nonreal parameters by the resolvent identity.
Construct the compact positive injective operator
`K=(1+D²)⁻¹=((D−i)⁻¹)* (D−i)⁻¹` and apply Mathlib's compact
self-adjoint spectral theorem. Prove its nonzero eigenspaces finite-dimensional,
contained in Dom(D²) and invariant under D. Diagonalize D on each
such space to obtain a complete orthonormal eigenbasis, using ker K=0.
Prove every bounded interval contains only finitely many eigenvalues,
counting multiplicity, and give the graph-domain series criterion
`Σ_j(1+|λ_j|²)|ξ_j|²<∞`.
In this basis define f(D) on
`{ξ:Σ_j |f(λ_j)|²|ξ_j|²<∞}` for Borel f, proving domain,
closedness, adjoint and composition laws and independence of the
eigenbasis. Compare its spectral projections with
SelfAdjointSpectralTheory SA-E and its continuous calculus with H6.
This supplies |D|, sign D, heat operators and inverse powers, including
their kernel conventions, for the compact-resolvent triples here.

Develop spectral triples (𝒜,H,D), their even/odd versions, operator-domain
invariance, bounded commutator extension, graph-norm estimates and
unitary/smooth-algebra transport. Build `[D,ab]=[D,a]b+a[D,b]`
and dagger identities on the common domain before extending boundedly.
Specialize H6's bounded transform to Hilbert spaces and compare the
resulting Fredholm class with N3; prove compactness and the Schatten bounds from stated spectral
summability. Develop resolvent, heat-functional-calculus and truncation
estimates needed for these assertions without invoking manifold
elliptic theory.

Let δ(T) be the bounded extension of `[|D|,T]` for operators preserving
Dom|D|. Define its closed derivation domain, iterated domains and smooth
intersection; prove completeness for graph seminorms, Leibniz, star,
inverse and matrix rules and functional-calculus stability, with
`δ(T*)=−δ(T)*` and the corresponding iterated signs. Regularity
requires both π(a) and `[D,π(a)]` in every δ-domain, with continuous
maps from the selected Fréchet algebra. Establish the commutator and
resolvent estimates used in the character comparison; regularity is
not only smoothness of π(a).

For integer n≥1 of the module's parity, initially invertible D, assume
D⁻¹∈L^(n,∞), F=sign D, and the preceding regularity and bounded
commutators. Prove finite summability in every larger exponent and
construct N3's character. Prove the Hochschild-class theorem: for

`φ_ω(a₀,…,a_n)=λ_n Tr_ω(π(a₀)[D,π(a₁)]⋯[D,π(a_n)]|D|⁻n)`,

with γ inserted in even parity and N3's λ_n, prove bφ_ω=0 and equality
with the Chern-character evaluation on every Hochschild n-cycle.
Develop the trace-ideal/domain estimates, resolvent transgression and
finite truncations that prove the comparison. The cochain can depend
on ω, while its cycle evaluation is independent of ω. State the
character as a periodic cyclic class and its Hochschild image; do not
identify arbitrary representatives as equal cochains.

Extend to finite-dimensional kernel by defining |D|⁻n to be zero on
the kernel and constructing the finite-dimensional augmentation and
character comparison explicitly. Pin the finite-rank corrections and
index contribution; simply writing sign(0)=0 does not make F²=1.
Compare diagonal spectral models with different summability exponents.
This is the Hochschild class of the index character, not the full
local index formula.

## N6. Smooth noncommutative two-tori and differential calculus

For every real θ consume K7's universal rotation algebra
`A_θ=C(𝕋)⋊_αℤ`, with `α(f)(z)=f(exp(2πiθ)z)` and
`U₁=v,U₂=u`. Its presentation has no irrationality restriction.
Construct the commuting coordinate-rotation and D4 dual actions, giving
`β_(z₁,z₂)(U_j)=z_j U_j`, and prove their joint strong continuity.
Construct 𝒜_θ, the rapidly decreasing Fourier series
`Σ_(m,n∈ℤ) a_mn U₁^m U₂^n` with
`U₂U₁=exp(2πiθ)U₁U₂`. Pin the ordered product multiplier to
`exp(2πiθ n m′)` and derive the star multiplier by reversing the word.
Develop rapid-decay seminorms, convergence, complete Fréchet star-algebra
structure, the injective dense map into A_θ and Fourier coefficient
uniqueness. Identify 𝒜_θ with the smooth vectors of the two-torus gauge
action; prove spectral invariance in all matrix levels by differentiating
inverses and applying K3. For every real θ identify the underlying
C*-algebra with K7's rotation crossed product by `U₁=v,U₂=u`.

Construct the canonical faithful trace τ(a)=a_00 and the derivations
`δ_j(U₁^mU₂^n)=2πi n_j U₁^mU₂^n`, n₁=m,n₂=n.
Prove continuity, Leibniz, star compatibility, commuting derivations and
τδ_j=0. Construct the two-dimensional differential calculus, orientation,
closed graded trace and its character

`φ(a₀,a₁,a₂)=(2πi)⁻¹ τ(a₀(δ₁a₁ δ₂a₂−δ₂a₁ δ₁a₂))`.

Prove cyclicity, bφ=0 and gauge/parameter-isomorphism transport. Build
connections on finite projective smooth right modules: ∇_j(ξa)=
(∇_jξ)a+ξδ_j(a), curvature `[∇₁,∇₂]`, Hermitian compatibility,
change of connection and gauge transformation. For a projection e
construct its Grassmann connection and prove the curvature-trace
formula equals `(φ#Tr)(e,e,e)`, including the (2πi)⁻¹ normalization.
Prove independence of connection by transgression. N7 supplies its
identification with an integer Fredholm index; cyclicity alone does not.

Compute continuous periodic cyclic cohomology for all θ:
`HP^even(𝒜_θ)≃ℂ²` with classes Sτ,φ, and
`HP^odd(𝒜_θ)≃ℂ²` with classes
`φ_j(a₀,a₁)=τ(a₀δ_j(a₁))`, j=1,2, with their periodic comparison.
Construct the Fourier resolutions, invariant/noninvariant cochain
contractions and comparisons proving completeness and independence.
Keep periodic cohomology distinct from fixed-degree ordinary cyclic
cohomology. Construct a continuous two-step bimodule resolution and its
comparison with the completed bar resolution, including the continuous
splittings needed to compute cohomology with continuous-dual coefficients.
For irrational θ set `λ=exp(2πiθ)`. The Diophantine condition is that
there exist C>0 and k∈ℕ with `|1−λ^n|⁻¹≤C(1+|n|)^k` for every
nonzero integer n. Prove
`dim H^j(𝒜_θ,𝒜_θ*)=1,2,1,0` for j=0,1,2,≥3 under this
condition, where 𝒜_θ* is the continuous dual. Without this condition
prove H¹ and H² infinite-dimensional and non-Hausdorff in N1's
quotient topology; H⁰ remains ℂ and the two-step resolution gives
vanishing above degree two.
Do not apply the Diophantine hypothesis to the periodic result.

## N7. Fourier spectral triples and Heisenberg indices

Identify L²(A_θ,τ) with ℓ²(ℤ²) by the ordered Fourier basis and use
left multiplication for π. On its tensor product with ℂ² take
`D=−i(σ₁δ₁−σ₂δ₂)`, `γ=σ₃`, with the usual Pauli matrices.
Thus D⁺=−i(δ₁−iδ₂); this pins the orientation of the index and φ.
Construct the closed domain, self-adjointness, compact resolvent,
bounded smooth commutators and regularity. Prove |D| has nonzero
Fourier eigenvalues `2πsqrt(m²+n²)`, with spin multiplicity two per
lattice point and a two-dimensional kernel at (0,0). Combine lattice
points of equal radius when computing eigenvalue multiplicities.
Prove p-summability for p>2 and failure
at p=2. Build the lattice-counting estimates and derive
`Tr_ω(|D|⁻²)=1/(2π)`, with zero on the kernel. More generally prove
`Tr_ω(π(a)|D|⁻²)=τ(a)/(2π)`. For a spin matrix M∈M₂(𝒜_θ),
prove `Tr_ω(π₂(M)|D|⁻²)=τ(Tr₂ M)/(4π)`.
Construct the gauge implementing unitaries commuting with |D|; unitary
invariance makes the trace of every nonzero Fourier mode vanish.
Use `|Tr_ω(AT)|≤‖A‖Tr_ω(T)` for positive T and rapid Fourier
convergence to pass from polynomials to smooth a and spin matrices.
Use N5's
λ₂=−1 and this orientation to compute the Hochschild character φ;
compare the periodic character using N6's basis and its value on [1].

For 0<θ<1 construct the smooth Heisenberg right module on 𝒮(ℝ) with
`(ξU₁)(s)=ξ(s+θ)` and `(ξU₂)(s)=exp(2πis)ξ(s)`.
Build its A_θ-valued inner product, positivity, complete Hilbert module,
finite smooth projective frames and identification with a smooth
Powers–Rieffel projection of trace θ. Prove the frame/trace dictionary
and, for irrational θ, compare its K₀ class with K7's positive-trace
generator. Construct
`∇₁ξ=−2πis ξ/θ`, `∇₂ξ=dξ/ds`, prove the right Leibniz and
Hermitian laws, and curvature `2πi/θ`. Complete the module after
tensoring with L²(A_θ,τ), identify it with the scalar L²(ℝ) model
with its correct norm, and construct the closed coupled Dirac operator.
Its chiral part is `−i(∇₁−i∇₂)=−d/ds−2πs/θ`. Prove its
Gaussian kernel is one-dimensional, adjoint kernel zero and range
closed using the harmonic-oscillator estimates. Thus its index is +1.
Establish the comparison of this coupled compression with N3/K6's
pairing and with the curvature trace, giving φ(generator)=1 and
φ([1])=0. This explicit calculation fixes the sign; changing the
second Clifford generator reverses the orientation.

For irrational θ conclude the joint trace/Chern map takes
`[1]↦(1,0)` and the positive-trace generator to `(θ,1)`, hence
identifies K₀ with the lattice `{(m+nθ,n):m,n∈ℤ}`. Compute the odd
cyclic pairings on U₁,U₂ with N2's constants: the rescaled classes
`ν_j=((1+i)sqrt(π)/(2πi))φ_j` pair as `ν_j(U_k)=δ_jk`.
Construct the two odd Fredholm modules on ℓ²(ℤ): write Se_k=e_(k+1),
`V_±e_k=exp(±2πikθ)e_k`, and let P_H be the projection onto k≥0.
Set `ρ₁(U₁)=S`, `ρ₁(U₂)=V_+`, `ρ₂(U₁)=V_-`,
`ρ₂(U₂)=S` and F=1−2P_H in both modules. Verify the defining
rotation relation, extend the representations to A_θ, and prove the
smooth commutators are Schatten-class using finite-rank shift
commutators and rapid Fourier decay. The positive F-projection is
1−P_H, so compression of S has index +1; the diagonal unitary has
index zero. Compare their periodic characters with ν₁,ν₂ by these
pairings and N6's cohomology basis, and with K7's K₁ generators.
Treat θ=0 as the ordinary smooth torus and compare
with its Fourier/de Rham calculations. Rational parameters retain the
periodic cyclic theorem and Fourier triple; the irrational unique-trace
and K-generator assertions are not imposed on them.

## Sources and API evidence

- Connes, [*Noncommutative Geometry*](https://alainconnes.org/wp-content/uploads/book94bigpdf.pdf),
  Chapter III §§1–3, pp.187–205,216–218,229–231, for cycles, the cyclic
  bicomplex/SBI, torus cohomology and pairings; Chapter IV §1,
  pp.295,299–303, for the conditional trace, character normalization
  and index theorem; IV §2, pp.310–317, for Dixmier traces,
  Tauberian criteria and Theorem8's Hochschild class; IV §6,
  pp.356–362, for the smooth torus and Heisenberg connection.
- N3's odd character coefficient is minus the coefficient printed in
  Connes IV §1, Definition 3, p.302. The positive N2 odd pairing is
  retained; the Hardy compression calculation fixes agreement with
  the kernel-minus-cokernel index and OperatorKTheory K6.
- The ordered Fourier triple, its chosen second Clifford sign and its
  Gaussian chiral calculation in N7 specify the comparison required
  here; they are not left to a convention implicit in the elliptic
  formula of Connes IV §6.
- Mathlib's multilinear, derivation, homological-complex, compact-operator
  and Fredholm APIs fix the foundational vocabulary. Tau Ceti's
  `Algebra/Lie/Derivation/Basic` supplies the noncommutative derivation
  carrier and its Leibniz/inner/conjugation API. Its existing
  `Analysis/Fredholm/{SmallPerturbation,CompactPerturbation,ContinuousFamily}`
  and the K4 index comparisons are suppliers, not private substitutes.
  [Mathlib's Fredholm design discussion](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/144837-PR-reviews/topic/.2341189.3A.20define.20Fredholm.20operators.20between.20TVSs/near/609444718)
  fixes the native operator/index interface.
TauCetiRoadmap/OperatorAlgebraDynamics:
# Operator-algebra dynamics, crossed products, and equilibrium

Develop continuous actions on C*-algebras and their full and reduced crossed
products, induction and imprimitivity, Takai duality, Hausdorff groupoid
C*-algebras, and equilibrium states of quantum systems. Build the analytic
constructions and representation theory that connect these subjects: integrated
forms, Hilbert-module completions, disintegration, modular characterization of
KMS states, and the thermodynamic limit of quantum spin systems.

## Scope, conventions, and dependencies

C*-algebras are complex and may be nonunital. Groups in D1–D4 are arbitrary
locally compact Hausdorff groups; separability and second countability are not
standing assumptions there. Groupoids in D5–D6 are second-countable locally
compact Hausdorff topological groupoids with Haar systems. Equilibrium theory
in D7 allows nonunital algebras except where unitality is specified; the CAR,
Weyl, and spin algebras in D8–D9 are unital.

An action is a homomorphism `G →* (A ≃⋆ₐ[ℂ] A)` with point-norm continuity
`∀ a, Continuous (fun g => α g a)`. A unitary representation is strongly
continuous when every orbit in its Hilbert space is continuous. Mathlib's
`ContRepresentation` makes each operator continuous; it does not impose this
continuity in the group variable. Use Tau Ceti's
`ContRepresentation.IsUnitary` and state strong continuity separately.
Hilbert-space and right Hilbert-module inner products are linear in the second
variable. Use [HilbertModules](../HilbertModules/README.md)'s opposite-algebra
implementation for right modules.

Fix left Haar measure μ. Write `c(g)=Measure.modularCharacter g` in the
convention `∫ f(xg) dμ(x)=c(g)∫ f(x) dμ(x)`. Thus Williams's modular function
is `Δ(g)=c(g)⁻¹`. Formulae involving different groups use their respective
Haar measures and modular functions. Fourier transforms and dual actions use
positive characters: `f̂(χ)=∫ f(g)χ(g) dμ(g)` and
`α̂χ(f)(g)=χ(g)f(g)`.

- [BanachAlgebras A7](../BanachAlgebras/README.md) supplies L¹ convolution,
  vector integration, Haar modular identities, and the support and Fubini
  arguments needed without global σ-finiteness. Its amenability dependency
  is the [AmenableGroups roadmap](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/821).
- [CStarAlgebras C1–C2](../CStarAlgebras/README.md) supplies representations,
  approximate units, multipliers, ideals and quotients; C5 supplies tensor
  products and analytic inductive limits; C6 supplies nuclearity and CP
  approximation, and C7 supplies exactness. [HilbertModules H1–H4](../HilbertModules/README.md) supplies
  adjointable operators, interior tensor products, induction, Morita
  equivalence, and linking algebras.
- [VonNeumannAlgebras V0–V4](../VonNeumannAlgebras/README.md) supplies states,

```
f*(s)     = c(s) α_s(f(s⁻¹)*) .
```

For a representation ρ of A construct the regular covariant representation
on `L²(G,Hρ)`:
`ρ̃(a)ξ(r)=ρ(α_(r⁻¹)(a))ξ(r)` and `λ_s ξ(r)=ξ(s⁻¹r)`.
Prove its strong continuity, nondegeneracy when ρ is nondegenerate, and

is injective on C_c(G,A), using its kernel/vector tests and approximate

Define the full norm as the supremum of the integrated representation norms.
Control universes by a bounded-cardinality family of cyclic representations

by density of units with trivial isotropy, and strong effectiveness by

in the commutant. Require this for the functionals of a Borel set and
its complement. Use SelfAdjointSpectralTheory SA-B14's projection-valued-measure
carrier. Own the measure obtained from these orthogonal decompositions and prove
its range lies in the GNS commutant; consume SA-B44's integration to construct
its L∞ representation, proving descent through the representing measure's
a.e. classes via SA-B50 and `P(B)=0↔μ(B)=0`, using the cyclic GNS
vector's separating property for the commutant. For compact-space commutative
representations consume SA-B59 and SA-B67's supported, possibly degenerate
version. For separable A construct the measurable
fields of cyclic representations and the corresponding direct-integral
GNS identification. Prove the correspondence between orthogonal decompositions and
abelian subalgebras of the commutant, and identify the central measure from
the GNS center with the maximal KMS representing measure. In general prove
the unique maximal representing-measure theorem; for separable A prove the metrizable
version with the unique measure supported on the extreme boundary. Supply
the measurable decomposition and its comparison with the GNS center, not
an unspecified appeal to a simplex predicate.

Define ground states and prove equivalence of: τ-invariance with
nonnegative GNS generator; bounded analytic continuation of correlations
to the upper half-plane; and `−i ω(a*δ(a))≥0` on the generator domain.
Prove that weak-* limits of β-KMS states as β→+∞ are ground states whenever
the limit is a state; unitality guarantees this norm-one condition.
For a self-adjoint matrix Hamiltonian K and `τ_t=Ad exp(itK)`, prove the
unique β-KMS state is `Tr(exp(−βK)·)/Tr(exp(−βK))`, including β=0, and
prove its zero-temperature limit is `Tr(P₀·)/Tr(P₀)`, where P₀ is
the projection onto the lowest eigenspace.

Develop bounded perturbations of faithful normal states using V10's
standard form. If Ω represents ω, define the perturbed vector for bounded
self-adjoint Q by `Ω^Q=exp((log Δω+Q)/2)Ω` and normalize its vector state
to obtain ω^Q. Prove existence of this vector, normalization, the
cocycle/analytic-continuation formula, continuous dependence, the inverse
perturbation law, and its modular characterization. For a β-KMS state,
Q=βP corresponds to subtracting the physical energy P, giving generator
`δ−i[P,·]`. Establish this sign by the finite-dimensional Gibbs calculation
and prove compatibility with the abstract bounded-perturbation construction.

## D8. CAR, Weyl algebras, and free equilibrium states

For a complex Hilbert space h construct CAR(h), generated by an antilinear
map a with `{a(f),a(g)}=0` and `{a(f),a(g)*}=⟨f,g⟩1`. Prove the universal
property, `‖a(f)‖=‖f‖`, functoriality for isometric inclusions, gauge action,
simplicity, and the finite-dimensional identification `CAR(ℂⁿ)≃M_(2ⁿ)(ℂ)`.
Construct the antisymmetric Hilbert Fock space and its creation and
annihilation operators, vacuum state and faithful CAR representation.
Reuse finite-dimensional exterior/Clifford algebra from
[SpinRepresentations](../RepresentationTheory/SpinRepresentations/README.md);
build the Hilbert completion and norm estimates here. Show that finite
subspace inclusions give the CAR inductive limit, including separable
infinite-dimensional h and its matrix stages.

Construct gauge-invariant quasi-free CAR states for every positive
contraction S on h. Define them by vanishing of monomials with unequal
creation and annihilation counts, two-point function
`ω_S(a(f)*a(g))=⟨g,Sf⟩`, and the determinant Wick formula
`ω_S(a(f₁)*⋯a(fₙ)* a(gₙ)⋯a(g₁))=det[⟨gᵢ,Sfⱼ⟩]_(i,j)`.
Prove positivity, norm one, uniqueness,
restriction to subspaces and continuity in the covariance. For a
self-adjoint one-particle Hamiltonian h₀, prove that
`τ_t(a(f))=a(exp(it h₀)f)` is a point-norm continuous action and that its
unique β-KMS state is the gauge-invariant quasi-free state with
`S=(1+exp(βh₀))⁻¹`, interpreting this as bounded Borel functional calculus.
Include negative β, β=0, finite modes, and the occupation-number formula;
derive the KMS identity on analytic vectors and extend by continuity.

For a real symplectic space `(V,σ)` construct the universal Weyl algebra
with `W(f)W(g)=exp(−iσ(f,g)/2)W(f+g)` and `W(f)*=W(−f)`.
Develop symplectic functoriality, linear independence of the Weyl
generators, the canonical trace, and the nondegenerate form's simplicity.
Distinguish the algebraic symplectic data from continuity: a representation
is regular if `t↦π(W(tf))` is strongly continuous for each f. Construct
field operators by Stone's theorem in regular representations, their
invariant domains and the Weyl-to-commutator relation on those domains.
Prove `‖W(f)−1‖=2` for nonzero f. A nontrivial continuous one-particle flow
therefore need not give a point-norm continuous Weyl-algebra action.

For `V=h_ℝ`, `σ(f,g)=Im⟨f,g⟩`, construct the symmetric Hilbert Fock
representation, field operators and vacuum characteristic function
`ω₀(W(f))=exp(−‖f‖²/4)`. For real symmetric covariance forms q require
`q(f,f)≥0` and `|σ(f,g)|²≤q(f,f)q(g,g)` for all f,g, and construct the
quasi-free state with characteristic function `exp(−q(f,f)/4)`.
Prove positivity, uniqueness from the characteristic function, regularity
and Wick's formula. In the gauge-invariant case develop the complex
sesquilinear covariance description; a bounded covariance is represented
by a bounded positive operator C≥I, with `q(f,g)=Re⟨f,Cg⟩`.
For a positive self-adjoint h₀
with `h₀≥εI`, ε>0, and β>0, construct the thermal covariance
`Cβ=coth(βh₀/2)=I+2(exp(βh₀)−I)⁻¹` and state
`ωβ(W(f))=exp(−⟨f,Cβf⟩/4)`.
Prove the strip KMS identities on Weyl correlations, normal extension of
the dynamics in its regular GNS representation, and the modular
characterization there. In this Weyl setting define β-KMS to mean that
the invariant regular state's GNS dynamics extends to a σ-weakly continuous
normal flow and its normal vector state satisfies the W*-strip KMS
condition; prove its Weyl-correlation characterization. Prove uniqueness
among gauge-invariant quasi-free β-KMS states with bounded covariance:
write its occupation covariance as a bounded T=(C−I)/2 and derive
`⟨(exp(βh₀)−1)g,Tf⟩=⟨g,f⟩` for analytic spectral-cutoff vectors g.
Justify differentiating the Weyl KMS correlations to two-point functions,
including cutoff/domain bounds. Spectral cutoffs and the bounded inverse
then force `T=(exp(βh₀)−1)⁻¹` on all vectors. Do not assume the difference
of two positive covariances is positive. A bounded one-argument-invariant
positive form vanishes under the gap, as a consequence of the same spectral
argument; jointly invariant forms do not satisfy that criterion.
The spectral gap makes the thermal bounded covariance formulae defined
for every f∈h. Gapless Bose condensation and interacting
continuum fields are outside this development. Do not apply the
point-norm C*-system theorem to this Weyl flow without its continuity
hypothesis.

## D9. Quantum spin systems and the thermodynamic limit

For a countable site set L and a fixed integer d≥1, construct local matrix
algebras `A_Λ=⊗_(x∈Λ) M_d(ℂ)` and their unital inclusions for finite Λ.
Construct the quasi-local C*-inductive limit, density of local observables,
commutation of disjoint regions, tensor decomposition into a finite region
and its complement, product states and normalized partial-trace
expectations. For `L=ℤ^ν`, ν≥1, construct translations and prove their
asymptotic abelianness. For d=1 prove the scalar specialization has a
unique state, which is β-KMS for every β.

An interaction Φ assigns self-adjoint `Φ(X)∈A_X` to nonempty finite subsets
X of L. Define `H_Φ(Λ)=∑_(X⊆Λ) Φ(X)`, the local inner dynamics, and the
interaction norm

```
Mλ(Φ) = ∑_(n≥0) exp(λn) sup_(x∈L)
          ∑_(X∋x, |X|=n+1) ‖Φ(X)‖ .
```

For some λ>0 assume `Mλ(Φ)<∞`. Prove absolute convergence of the local
derivation `δ(A)=i∑_(X∩Λ≠∅)[Φ(X),A]`, independence of a local support Λ
for A, closability, and that the local algebra is a core for its closure.
Construct the point-norm continuous infinite-volume action; prove that
`Ad exp(itH_Φ(Λ))` converges on each observable uniformly on compact time
intervals as Λ increases to L. Develop comparison estimates under a change
of interaction, restriction, and addition of a bounded local perturbation.
Include finite-range interactions on lattices and on-site product models.

Construct the finite-volume Gibbs states and their extensions using the
normalized trace on the complement. Prove existence of weak-* cluster
points and that every such thermodynamic limit is a β-KMS state. Define
the norm-convergent surface energy
`W_Φ(Λ)=∑_(X∩Λ≠∅, X∩Λᶜ≠∅) Φ(X)` and prove convergence from the interaction
bound. The Gibbs condition is: Ωω is separating in its GNS von Neumann
algebra and, for every finite Λ, the normalized perturbation by
`Q=β πω(W_Φ(Λ))` from D7 factors as
`ω^Q=ω_(Λ,β)⊗ω̃_(Λᶜ)` for a state on the complement. Prove this condition
equivalent to β-KMS. More generally retain the precise sufficient
hypotheses of Bratteli–Robinson Theorem 6.2.18: convergence of the local
dynamics, existence of every surface energy, and the local algebra being
a generator core. The perturbation removes the boundary interaction; its
sign is fixed by D7.

For translation-invariant interactions on `ℤ^ν` build the thermodynamic
variational principle. Define the interaction Banach norm
`‖Φ‖B=∑_(X∋0) ‖Φ(X)‖/|X|`, assume it finite, and use finite boxes or van
Hove nets. Fix for each a∈ℕ_(>0)^ν the partition of ℤ^ν by translates
of the rectangular tile Λ_a. Let n⁻_Λ(a) count tiles contained in Λ and
n⁺_Λ(a) tiles meeting Λ. A net of nonempty finite regions is van Hove
when its volumes tend to infinity and n⁻_Λ(a)/n⁺_Λ(a)→1 for every a.
Prove translation and boundary-neighborhood formulations and their
compatibility with boxes and tile estimates. Construct mean energy
`e_Φ(ω)=∑_(X∋0) ω(Φ(X))/|X|`, mean entropy
`s(ω)=lim |Λ|⁻¹ S(ω|A_Λ)`, and pressure
`p(βΦ)=lim |Λ|⁻¹ log Tr(exp(−βH_Φ(Λ)))`.
Develop finite-matrix entropy and relative entropy
`D(ρ||σ)=Tr(ρ(logρ−logσ))`, with infinity when the support condition
fails, and `0 log0=0` in entropy. Prove positivity for trace-one ρ,σ,
ordinary subadditivity, and the relative-entropy calculus for an arbitrary
positive reference σ used in the monotonicity argument.
Prove strong subadditivity `S(ABC)+S(B)≤S(AB)+S(BC)`. For a concrete route,
build the compression inequality for −log from its resolvent integral and
positive block-matrix Schur complements. On Hilbert–Schmidt matrices form
the positive relative modular operator `L_σ R_(ρ⁻¹)` for invertible ρ,σ.
Construct the partial-trace isometry
`V(x ρ_A^(1/2))=(x⊗1)ρ_AB^(1/2)`, verify its modular compression
identity, and apply the −log inequality to obtain relative-entropy
monotonicity under partial trace. Extend by ε-regularization to the support
cases, then apply monotonicity to ρ_ABC and `1_A⊗ρ_BC` to prove the
stated entropy inequality. Give entropy concavity and the mixture bounds
used to prove affinity of the mean. Supply boundary estimates and all
limit arguments, including strong-subadditivity transfer of successive
entropy increments in lexicographic tile order. Prove independence of the admissible exhaustion,
affinity and upper semicontinuity of mean entropy on translation-invariant
states, convexity and Lipschitz continuity of pressure, and

```
p(βΦ) = sup_(ω translation-invariant state) (s(ω) − β e_Φ(ω)).
```

For the stronger assumption `∑_(X∋0) ‖Φ(X)‖exp(λ|X|)<∞` for some λ>0,
prove equivalence, for translation-invariant states, of maximizing this
functional, the Gibbs condition and β-KMS. The pressure existence theorem
and the equilibrium equivalence have distinct interaction hypotheses.

Finally prove a quantitative high-temperature uniqueness theorem. Set

```
Mλ,d(Φ) = ∑_(n≥0) exp(λn) d^(2n) sup_(x∈L)
            ∑_(X∋x, |X|=n+1) ‖Φ(X)‖ .
```

For d≥2, if this is finite, prove uniqueness of the β-KMS state whenever
`|β|Mλ,d(Φ) < (λ/2)/(1+exp(λ)d³/(d−1))`, by the perturbation/contraction
argument of Bratteli–Robinson Proposition 6.2.45. This is a sufficient
region, not an assertion of a sharp critical temperature. Work out the
interaction norms and resulting bound for finite-range nearest-neighbor
spin interactions, as well as exact Gibbs and thermodynamic formulae for
the on-site model.
