  `ℤ`-span of the basis fails to be unimodular, together with `2`. This is what the lattice
  spinor-genus consumer reads off Jordan data.

  ⚠ That identification is a theorem about the **family**, not about the construction, and neither
  inclusion is automatic: in dimension one `SO(V_p)` is trivial at every prime, so every compatible
  tuple has trivial reference images and never the unit classes, which
  `exists_localSpinorNormImage_ne_unitSquareClasses` records. Openness is what holds for every
  tuple; the value is what an integral family supplies.

**3D. The three adelic point groups.** The index conventions are pinned in Lean rather than written
informally: the finite places are indexed by the primes; the archimedean place is carried by a
product decomposition rather than by a dependent type of places, so that `G(𝔸) = G(ℝ) × G(𝔸_f)` is
a definition and not a theorem; and for a finite set `S` of places with `∞ ∈ S`, `G(𝔸^S)` is the
restricted product over the finite places outside `S`, so that at `S = {∞}` it is `G(𝔸_f)` on the
nose rather than up to an identification. For **each** of `O`, `SO` and `Spin`, relative to a
compatible tuple: finite adelic points, points away from `S`, and full adelic points. Then the
restrictions `G(𝔸_f) → G(𝔸^S)`, the projections out of `G(𝔸)`, and the componentwise maps
`Spin(V)(𝔸_•) → SO(V)(𝔸_•) → O(V)(𝔸_•)` in all three flavours, obtained from 3B's functoriality
applied to `spinToSpecialOrthogonal` and `specialOrthogonalToOrthogonal` with 3C's compatibility.
⚠ All three groups are built and not just `O`. The approximation application in
`OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass` is a theorem about `Spin` transported to `SO`, and its measure
application is about `SO`; constructing only `O` would supply neither interface.

**3E. ⚠ Diagonal points: discrete in the full adeles, not generally discrete in the finite
adeles.** Density in the finite adeles is not a Layer 3 statement at all; it belongs to
`OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`. The diagonal
map is well defined only once one knows that a given rational isometry lies in `U_p` for all but
finitely many `p`, which is a theorem. Both forms are milestones: the **relative** one, for a
tuple satisfying "every element of `O(V)(ℚ)` lies in `U_p^O` for almost all `p`" as an explicit
hypothesis, which is the form the integral lattices roadmap discharges for its lattice
stabilizers; and the **absolute** one, discharging that hypothesis for the stabilizers of the
`ℤ`-span of a chosen basis of `V`, by clearing denominators in the matrix of a rational isometry
and of its inverse. The second exists so the roadmap's own objects rest on something; it develops
no lattice arithmetic. Its carrier is `integralOrthogonalSubgroup`, cut out **as data** by
integrality of the matrix entries of an isometry and of its inverse in the base-changed basis — one
condition alone gives a submonoid and not a subgroup — with its openness, its compactness, and
`eventually_mem_integralOrthogonalSubgroup`, which is `eventually_mem_orth` discharged rather than
assumed. It is also the family 3C's reference-image identification is stated for.

The diagonal map is built for each of the three groups, and for each of the three flavours of 3D:
for `O` and for `Spin` from the two integrality hypotheses of 3C, and for `SO` from `O`'s, since a
rational proper isometry lying in `U_p^O` lies in `U_p^{SO}`. Each comes with its evaluation rule
and its injectivity, and the square `Spin(V)(ℚ) → Spin(V)(𝔸_f) → SO(V)(𝔸_f)` against
`Spin(V)(ℚ) → SO(V)(ℚ) → SO(V)(𝔸_f)` commutes, which lets `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`
speak of "the image of the rational spin points in adelic `SO`" without saying which of the two
routes is meant.

Then, and the contrast is the point: `G(ℚ)` is **discrete in `G(𝔸)`**, the full adeles, once the
real place is included. It is **not** discrete in `G(𝔸_f)`, and the roadmap records the
counterexample rather than leaving the distinction to be discovered: for a split rational
quadratic space of dimension at least three, take integral `u` and `w` and the rational
one-parameter family `t ↦ E_{u,tw}` of 2C; inside any basic finite-adelic neighbourhood of the
identity, a nonzero integer `t` divisible by a high enough power of each of the finitely many
constrained primes gives a transvection that is integral at every other prime and arbitrarily
close to the identity at the constrained ones. So the diagonal image accumulates at the identity.
This supplies the rejection test a density theorem must respect.

**3F. The adelic spinor norm, on `SO`.** The restricted product of the local square-class groups
relative to the reference subgroups `θ_p(U_p^{SO})` of 3C; the theorem that the componentwise local
spinor norms induce a continuous homomorphism `SO(V)(𝔸_f) → ∏' ℚ_p^×/(ℚ_p^×)²` into it,
**together with its evaluation rule**, that the `p`-component of the value is the local spinor norm
of the `p`-component of the argument; and the **adelic spinor kernel** as its kernel. Three things
are pinned here rather than left to an implementer.

- There is no such thing as "the restricted product of the local square-class groups" until the
  reference subgroups are fixed; several inequivalent choices exist, and the one used here is
  `θ_p(U_p^{SO})`.
- ⚠ The domain is adelic **`SO`**, not adelic `O`. The reference subgroups are the images of the
  `U_p^{SO}`, and an improper element of `U_p^O` has no reason to have local spinor norm inside
  `θ_p(U_p^{SO})`, so a map out of adelic `O` would not land in the stated codomain.
- ⚠ The evaluation rule is part of the milestone. A homomorphism into that restricted product with
  no rule relating its components to the local spinor norms is satisfied by the trivial
  homomorphism, and every theorem stated about its kernel would then be a theorem about the whole
  group.

**3G. Double cosets, with the maps stated separately.** The set `G(ℚ) \ G(𝔸_f) / U`, with three
distinct comparison statements rather than one blanket change-of-`U` map, since eventually equal
reference families give canonically equivalent ambient groups but do **not** automatically give a
canonical bijection of double-coset sets: an inclusion `U ≤ U'` of compact opens induces a
surjection of double-coset sets in the corresponding direction; conjugate compact opens induce a
canonical bijection; and a componentwise equivalence carrying one tuple to another transports the
double-coset set along 3B's canonical equivalence. Finiteness of the set is not claimed here.

**3H. Explicit stop point.** RestrictedProducts exports none of the norm-one subgroup,
reduction theory, finite-covolume theorem, strong approximation, or Tamagawa infrastructure. This
roadmap therefore stops after the specialized point groups, diagonals, and adelic spinor norm. It
states no generic finite-covolume or density theorem and no orthogonal application of one.

## Consumer contract for `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`

Layers 0 to 3 expose all three point groups and the spinor-kernel API because one named successor
consumes them: **`OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`**, which owns the orthogonal applications of
strong approximation and of Tamagawa theory, the orthogonal Tamagawa numbers, the mass formula, and
the genus/spinor-genus comparison. None of that is a milestone here, and none of it may be promoted
back into this roadmap. The contract is short, and it is the whole of what the two roadmaps agree
on.

**What this roadmap exports to it**, by exact name: `transvection` and `transvectionLiftHom`, the
root subgroups of 2C; `spinorNorm` with its local table 2F–2G and its localization 2H;
`finiteAdelicOrthogonal`, `finiteAdelicSpecialOrthogonal`, `finiteAdelicSpin` and their away-`S`
and full-adelic forms, with the componentwise maps and the diagonals of 3D–3E; `adelicSpinorNorm`
with its evaluation rule and `adelicSpinorKernel`; `unitSquareClasses` with the reference-image
theorems of 3C; and the double-coset comparisons of 3G.

**What the successor must import before it may state anything**, and may not replace by a local
stand-in: an algebraic-group point functor and the almost-simple-factor API from Reductive Groups;
a generic strong-approximation theorem and the reduction-theory stages from
`AlgebraicGroupStrongApproximation` and `ArithmeticReductionTheory`; a Tamagawa measure, a
finite-covolume theorem, the simply connected semisimple value, and the central-isogeny defect
formula from `TamagawaMeasures`; `ClassFieldTheory.hilbertProductFormula`; and
`GlobalQuadraticForms.hasseMinkowski_equivalent`.

**What it then proves**, listed so that the interface above can be checked against a use: that the
orthogonal root subgroups generate the elementary subgroup of `Spin(V)(K)`; that the
noncompact-place condition of the imported theorem is equivalent to noncompactness of every
almost-simple factor at a place of `S` — ⚠ a noncompact-*place* condition, not a synonym for
indefiniteness, since a positive-definite rational form may satisfy it at a finite place; the
resulting density of the rational spin points in `Spin(V)(𝔸^S)` for `dim V ≥ 3`, dimension two
being excluded because `Spin(V)` is then a one-dimensional torus and the statement is false; that
the closure of the rational spin image inside adelic `SO` is exactly the adelic spinor kernel and
**not** the closure of all rational `O`-points, a rational reflection of nonsquare spinor norm
lying in the larger image and outside the kernel; the orthogonal gauge forms and Tamagawa
measures; and `τ(SO_Q) = 2` for `dim V ≥ 3`, with the low-dimensional values `2` for a nonsplit
binary form, `1` for a split one, and `1` in dimensions one and zero, which are the guard the
integral lattices roadmap's Conway–Sloane normalization records in its own low-rank branch.

⚠ Two ownership facts that a reader of the successor will otherwise get wrong.
`Ш¹(ℚ, SO_Q) = 1` is not a formality: it is the Hasse principle for quadratic forms, consumed by
exact name as `GlobalQuadraticForms.hasseMinkowski_equivalent`, and translating it into a
pointed-set statement is the successor's work, because that supplier defines no `H¹(K, SO(Q))`.
And the central-isogeny computation is instantiated from the imported defect formula, never
restated as a generic Ono ratio.

## Required basic API

"Build the library, don't race to the theorem" applies per object. Each object this roadmap owns
carries the same seven-part checklist, and a milestone is not discharged until all seven exist:
**constructors and the defining characterization**; **extensionality**, that is a usable criterion
for two elements to be equal; **functoriality** in the quadratic space, along isometries;
**base change**, along a field extension for the field-level objects and along a ring map for the
bilinear ones; **comparison lemmas** against the neighbouring object, which is the row below or
above it here; **edge cases**, meaning dimension zero, dimension one, and the degenerate form
wherever a statement is claimed without nondegeneracy; and the **downstream interface**, the
handful of lemmas the consuming layer actually calls.

The objects, in dependency order: `orthogonalDet` and the `specialOrthogonalWithin` interface
(0A); the bilinear-form isometry group and the dictionary (0C); the reflection with its
determinant and conjugation law (0D); `vectorUnit` and the scalar-unit homomorphism, with the
membership theorems that put them in Mathlib's carrier (1B); the Clifford norm and the three
`star`-versus-`reverse` comparison theorems (1A); the spinor norm (1D); `evenUnitaryGroup` with its
membership criterion, its functoriality along an isometry, and its comparison with `spinGroup`
(1F); the local topological point groups (2A, 2B); the transvections and their Spin lifts (2C);
`integralOrthogonalSubgroup` (3E); the compatible compact-open data, `unitSquareClasses`, and the
three adelic point groups (3C, 3D); the adelic spinor norm and the adelic spinor kernel (3F).

## Worked examples (acceptance criteria)

Discharge these alongside their layers. Each catches a vacuous definition, a wrong sign, or a
convention drift.

- The two reflection spellings agree: `B x v / Q v = 2 · B x v / B v v` for `Q v ≠ 0`, and
  `τ_v v = -v` computed from either. The mixed form `2 · B x v / Q v` gives `-3v`, and that is the
  error the convention table warns against (Layer 0D).
- Dimension one, `Q x = a x²` for `a ∈ Kˣ`: `O(Q) = {±1}`, `SO(Q)` is trivial, `-1` is the
  reflection in any `v ≠ 0`, and `θ(-1) = [a]`, which is nontrivial exactly when `a` is not a
  square. ⚠ The scalar has to be carried: for `Q x = x²` one gets `Q v = v²` and `θ(-1) = [1]`,
  so that instance is the degenerate one and tests nothing. With `a` a nonsquare this is the
  acceptance check that the square class detects `-1` and hence that the `reverse` and `star`
  norms of 1A really do differ on `O(Q)` (Layers 0, 1).
- The hyperbolic plane over any `K`: `SO(H) ≅ Kˣ` through the diagonal torus and `θ` on that torus
  is the square class of the parameter, so `θ : SO(H)(K) → Kˣ/(Kˣ)²` is **surjective**, and the
  image of `Spin(H)(K) → SO(H)(K)` is the square-parameter subgroup `(Kˣ)²`, which is `ker θ`. The
  sequence of 1E extended by `→ 1` is therefore exact here over every `K`. ⚠ Whether
  `Spin(H)(K) → SO(H)(K)` is itself onto is a property of `K`, not of `H`: it is surjective exactly
  when every unit of `K` is a square. Over `ℚ` it is **not**, the parameter `2` having no preimage,
  which is `not_surjective_spinToSpecialOrthogonal_hyperbolic_rat`, and what fails there is the
  naive expectation that a central isogeny is onto on `K`-points. Over an algebraically closed
  field the same form is a case of `spinToSpecialOrthogonal_surjective_of_isAlgClosed`, and the
  acceptance proof verifies surjectivity rather than contradicting it (Layers 0, 1).
- The sum of three squares over ℚ: the central map from the norm-one Hamilton quaternions to
  `SO(Q)` is an isogeny of algebraic groups with kernel `±1`, and its image on rational points is
  the spinor kernel, strictly smaller than `SO(Q)(ℚ)`. Stating it as "`SO(Q)(ℚ)` is the quotient of
  `Spin(Q)(ℚ)` by `±1`" is exactly the error the previous item is designed to catch (Layer 1F).
- `O(Q)(ℝ)` for a definite `Q` is compact and agrees with the Euclidean orthogonal group of
  `TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/OrthogonalGroup.lean`; for `Q = x² − y²`, pass to the isometric
  `xy`-model and exhibit noncompactness with the diagonal torus
  `t ↦ diag(t, t⁻¹)`. The acceptance proof must also verify that `u^⊥ / ℝ u = 0` in
  dimension two, so the transvection family of 2C cannot serve as the witness there. In dimension
  at least three the isotropic noncompactness example uses a nontrivial Eichler transvection family
  (Layers 2B, 2D).
- A rational isometry lies in the stabilizer of the standard `ℤ`-span at all but finitely many
  primes, exhibited for one explicit non-integral rational isometry (Layer 3E).
- **Non-discreteness in the finite adeles**: for a split rational `V` of dimension at least three,
  the transvections `E_{u,tw}` with `t` a highly divisible integer accumulate at the identity in
  `SO(V)(𝔸_f)`, so the diagonal image is not discrete there, while it is discrete in `SO(V)(𝔸)`.
  This is the acceptance check for 3E (Layer 3).
- Two compatible tuples differing at one prime give a canonical isomorphism of restricted products,
  computed on coordinates, and the induced comparison of double-coset sets is the one 3G names
  rather than a bijection (Layer 3).
- Dimension four, split against nonsplit, in three forms: `H ⟂ H` over `ℚ`, whose discriminant
  algebra splits and whose `Spin` is `SL₂ × SL₂`, two factors each of `ℚ`-rank one; the sum of
  four squares over `ℝ`, whose discriminant algebra also splits but whose `Spin(ℝ)` is
  `SU(2) × SU(2)`, two factors of real rank zero; and `x² + y² + z² + 2w²` over `ℚ`, whose
  discriminant algebra is the field `ℚ(√2)` and whose `Spin` is one `ℚ`-almost-simple factor. The
  first two test that the split case of 1F asserts absolute rank one and nothing more, and the
  third tests the distinction between split and nonsplit that 1F draws (Layer 1F).
- **Dimension five is symplectic**: for a five-dimensional `Q` the even Clifford algebra has degree
  four, `Spin(Q) = evenUnitaryGroup Q = Sp(C₀, σ)`, and in the split case `Spin₅ ≅ Sp₄`, which is
  not a special linear group of any central simple algebra (Layer 1F).
- **Dimension six is where that stops**: for a split rational six-dimensional `Q`,
  `evenUnitaryGroup Q ≅ GL₄(ℚ)` while `Spin(Q) ≅ SL₄(ℚ)`, so the dimension-five equality is sharp.
  This is the acceptance check that nobody extends `evenUnitaryGroup_le_lipschitzGroup` past
  dimension five (Layer 1F).
- **A positive-definite real form has trivial spinor norm on the whole of `O`**, not all square
  classes: every value of `Q` is a positive real and hence a square. Beside it, a negative-definite
  form of the same rank, where `θ(O)` is all of `ℝˣ/(ℝˣ)²` and `θ(SO)` is trivial. This is the
  acceptance check for the signature split in 2F (Layer 2).
- **The reference images are open but not identified**: `θ_p(U_p^{SO})` is open for every
  compatible tuple, while for a one-dimensional `V` it is trivial at every prime and so is never
  the unit square classes. This is the acceptance check for 3C (Layer 3).

## Ordering and parallelism

The current supplier order is fixed by the portfolio DAG:

    LocalFieldsRamification, QuadraticFormInvariants,
    RestrictedProducts → OrthogonalSpinGroups.

Within this roadmap, Layers 0 and 1 establish the algebraic orthogonal/spin API and exact
spinor-kernel sequence. Layer 2 builds the orthogonal local specialization and transvections.
Layer 3 instantiates imported adelic carriers and maps and constructs the adelic spinor norm.
That is the end of this PR's current scope.

`OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass` branches after Layer 3 and behind Reductive Groups and the
generic successors named in its contract; `AlgebrasWithInvolution` branches after Layer 1 and is
independent of everything adelic. IntegralLattices may consume only the interfaces that have

TauCetiRoadmap/PadicFunctionalAnalysis:
# P-adic functional analysis

Build the functional analysis of nonarchimedean Banach modules and the analysis
of continuous and locally analytic functions on `ℤ_p`. The library supplies
Banach–Tate operator theory, orthonormalisable modules, Mahler and Amice
coordinates, quantitative distribution estimates, and continuous characters
of `ℤ_pˣ` with their specialisation maps. These interfaces serve Fredholm
theory, Iwasawa theory, adic geometry and families of automorphic forms.

The central results are Serre's orthonormalisation theorem; continuous splitting
for Banach spaces of countable type; Amice's basis theorem for analytic stages;
the bounded and unbounded Amice transforms; and the universal character with
coordinate `T=[exp(q)]−1`, where `q=p` for odd `p` and `q=4` for `p=2`.
The coefficient ring may be a Banach–Tate ring rather than a field. Field,
discrete-valuation and characteristic-zero assumptions are imposed locally.

Every milestone and check below is required. This README is definitive;
[Suggested.lean](Suggested.lean) records representative interfaces with real
definitions and admitted theorem targets; it is not an exhaustive checklist.
Suggested homes are `TauCeti/Analysis/Normed/` for the Banach-module and
operator APIs, `TauCeti/RingTheory/Huber/` for the topological comparisons,
and `TauCeti/NumberTheory/Padics/` for measures, analytic stages and characters.

## Scope and ownership

| Area | Supplied here | Supplied elsewhere |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Banach–Tate analysis | Multiplicative pseudo-uniformisers, seminorm gauges, norm comparisons, ring-scalar operator norms and quantitative mapping theorems | Huber rings, pairs of definition and topological open mapping: [AdicSpaces](../AdicSpaces/README.md), Layer 0 |
| Model spaces | Native `C₀`, bounded-family extension, bases, (Pr), matrices, finite coordinates and countable-type splitting | Complete continuity, Fredholm determinants, Riesz theory and spectral transforms: compact operator theory; geometric uses in [LocallyAnalyticDistributions, PR #854](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/854), Layer 4 |
| Restricted series | Their use as analytic charts and coefficient spaces | Carriers, norms, coefficient-model comparisons, evaluation, substitution, translation, Hasse derivatives and Strassmann: [RestrictedPowerSeries][RestrictedPowerSeries] ([PR #919](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/919)), Layers 0–2 and §7 |
| Valuations | Logarithmic gauges on Banach rings and comparison with field valuations | Additive normalisations, `ℂ_p` value group and polygons: [NewtonPolygons][NewtonPolygons] ([PR #926](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/926)), Layer 1; local-field arithmetic: LocalFieldsRamification |
| Measures | Bounded Mahler duality, the integral dual unit ball, `φ,ψ`, character integration and the Amice-coordinate comparison | General clopen measure calculus, weak/strong topologies, finite coordinates, coefficient extension and the measure/completed-group-algebra comparison: [PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras](../PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/README.md), Layers 0–1 |
| Locally analytic distributions | One-variable stages, algebraic union, stage-bounded dual, Amice bijection, norm estimates, point masses and additive convolution | Locally convex limits, strong dual topology, completed tensors, manifolds, `C^r` growth, general distribution operations and geometric Mellin theory: [LocallyAnalyticDistributions](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/854), Layers 0–3 |
| Iwasawa algebra and weights | Character coordinates, adic and normed specialisation, bounded integral-measure functions | Completed group algebra and procyclic coordinate: [ProfiniteProPGroups](../ProfiniteProPGroups/README.md), Layer 9; pseudo-measures, module structure and characteristic ideals: PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras |
| Automorphic applications | Character analyticity, scalar expansions of `κ(cz+d)` and the annular coefficient example | Matrix actions, automorphy-factor cocycles, Hecke operators and classicality: quaternionic modular-form theory |

The gauge contract is consumed by [AdicSpacesPartII §R0.4](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/817);
countable-type splitting and its completed-extension consequence give the
`countable-type-closed-subspace-section` interface in
[AdicSpacesPartIII §R3.6](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/813).
Use §2.4 as the shared Banach-space theorem behind that interface. Part III
retains the geometric application; no second splitting theory is required.
[AdicSpacesPartII §R0.3](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/817)
and LocallyAnalyticDistributions §0.0 supply the completed-tensor carriers and
functoriality; compare their field specialisations before transporting the
split-exactness corollary.
An imported theorem is a dependency and comparison target, not another proof
project. The open-roadmap links below identify the mathematical contracts;
the prototype imports library modules, not another roadmap's `Suggested.lean`.
In particular, neither a second Tate algebra nor a second completed group
algebra is constructed here. Compactness, Fredholm theory and automorphic
operator actions are consumers of this library, not prerequisites for it.

General Hahn–Banach theory, reflexivity, nuclear spaces, geometric weight
spaces and analytic Laurent/Robba-ring libraries are outside the scope.
The particular coefficient ring in §5.6 is a Banach–Tate example motivated by
the boundary-of-weight-space calculations in [LWX].

## Conventions

1. **Native structures.** Use `IsUltrametricDist`, `Module R E`,
   `IsBoundedSMul R E` and `CompleteSpace`. Add `NormOneClass`, `NormMulClass`
   and `NormSMulClass` only where needed. Commutative rings are the default
   for scalar actions on operator spaces and matrix multiplication.
   “Banach module” means these properties on the existing normed module;
   no new `BanachModule` carrier or fundamental typeclass is required.
   `IsBoundedSMul` supplies the contractive inequality
   `‖a • x‖ ≤ ‖a‖ ‖x‖`. A merely bounded action with an extra constant
   is a different hypothesis and does not give the same exact norm identities.

2. **Normed and topological Tate conditions differ.** `NormedRing.IsTate R`
   records a unit `ϖ` with `0<‖ϖ‖<1` and `‖ϖx‖=‖ϖ‖‖x‖`.
   `NormedRing.PseudoUniformizer R` carries the choice for the given norm.
   `TauCeti.Huber.IsTateRing R` instead asserts the topological Huber property
   and existence of a topologically nilpotent unit, with no chosen norm or
   exact scaling law. Use the topological class for topological statements
   and the normed class or explicit multiplicative unit for quantitative ones.
   Neither class includes completeness. The normed condition here excludes
   the zero ring; the topological gauge construction also treats zero and
   non-Hausdorff rings. Section 0.4 supplies the comparison, without a reverse
   instance asserting that an arbitrary existing norm is Tate.

3. **Use `C₀(I,E)`.** The index type is arbitrary and discrete; decay is
   along the cofinite filter. No replacement coefficient carrier or
   countability assumption is introduced. Empty indices and zero modules
   have norm zero. Prove boundedness before using a real supremum.

4. **Orthonormality controls scalar coefficients.** Require
   `‖Σ_{i∈S} a_i e_i‖=max_{i∈S}‖a_i‖` for finite `S`, with empty maximum
   zero. Orthogonality uses `max‖a_i e_i‖` and is weaker over rings.
   A basis additionally has dense span. `IsONable` means linearly isometric
   to a model space; `IsPotentiallyONable` means continuously linearly
   equivalent; (Pr) means a continuous linear retract of such a module.
   Under the complete coefficient-ring and module hypotheses of §2.2,
   `IsONable` is equivalent to existence of an orthonormal basis. A chosen
   basis and a chosen model isometry must be interconvertible; neither is
   chosen globally by typeclass inference.

5. **One operator norm.** Extend Mathlib's infimum of uniform Lipschitz
   bounds with scoped ring-scalar instances and agreement with the field
   API. Continuity implies a finite bound over Tate scalars, but not over
   every normed ring. The norm of an identity or Neumann inverse is one
   only for a nonzero module.

6. **Output index first.** `matrixCoeff u i j=(u(single j 1))(i)`.
   Rows index outputs and columns index inputs; columns are images of
   coordinate vectors. This agrees with Mathlib's `LinearMap.toMatrix`.
   For the input-first notation `b j i=(u(single j 1))(i)` used by
   LocallyAnalyticDistributions, supply a named transpose adapter. Null
   columns in the first convention are null rows in the second. Uniform
   decay over output coordinates, used in compactness criteria, is a
   different condition. The convention and its action/composition formulas
   are fixed in §2.6; compactness itself belongs to CompactOperators.

7. **Analytic stages are coefficient models.**
   `LA_h(E)=C₀(ZMod(p^h)×ℕ,E)` uses natural representatives as centres
   and `w=(x−a)/p^h`. Evaluation is norm-decreasing; injectivity needs a
   theorem. Use RestrictedPowerSeries' field-separation hypothesis, or the
   Amice diagonal for Banach `ℚ_p`-spaces. Re-expansion exists for all
   bounded `ℤ_p`-modules, but need not be injective for torsion coefficients.

8. **Mahler and Amice coordinates differ.** Put `m_h(n)=⌊n/p^h⌋!`.
   The Amice coordinate `c_n` gives Mahler coefficient `a_n=m_h(n)c_n`.
   A dual moment `b_n` is therefore weighted by `‖m_h(n)‖`, not its inverse.
   Module-valued coordinate equivalences are not called scalar bases of
   `C(ℤ_p,E)` unless the coefficient module warrants that assertion.

9. **Name the norm and topology.** The normalisation is `‖p‖=p⁻¹` in
   `ℚ_p`; use normed `ℚ_p` scalar actions for the analytic estimates.
   The distribution carrier here has stage seminorms but no new global
   topology. Integral measures retain their native carrier; field dual norms
   are taken after coefficient extension. The Iwasawa topology is profinite,
   not the coefficient sup-norm topology.

10. **All primes.** Put `q=p` for odd `p`, `q=4` for `p=2`,
    `Δ=(ℤ/qℤ)ˣ`, `γ=exp(q)` and `T=[γ]−1`. At `p=2` the sign factor
    does not split the integral group ring into two rings. A normed-ring
    weight has a topologically nilpotent coordinate; only a multiplicative
    norm makes this equivalent to `‖T_κ‖<1`.

## Existing foundations

Mathlib supplies ultrametric summability, `C₀`, continuous linear maps and
field operator norms, normed quotients, finite-dimensional topology, Mahler's
isometry, continuous additive characters, `AbstractMeasure`, power series,
binomial coefficients and `p`-adic fields. Its current measure API includes
`AbstractMeasure.amiceTransform`, coefficient extensionality, the integral
Amice equivalence and convolution in `Measure/Monoid`. Extend these native
declarations rather than creating parallel transforms or products.

Use `PadicInt.mahlerEquiv` in its existing generality of complete ultrametric
modules with contractive `ℤ_p` action. Use `AbstractMeasure.amiceTransform`,
`coeff_amiceTransform`, `injective_amiceTransform` and `amiceTransformEquiv`
directly; the prototype proves the comparison with `PadicInt.mahlerTerm`.
The scalar-linear refinements, bounded dual norm, range and integral-lattice
comparisons are additional targets.

Follow [Mathlib PR #42865](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42865),
which makes `ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm` depend only on semiring modules,
and the accompanying [Zulip discussion](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/217875-Is-there-code-for-X.3F/topic/compact.20operators.20and.20Fredholm.20determinant/with/572850121).
Keep that definition and its names; Tate scalars supply the boundedness and
normed-space laws that do not hold for arbitrary continuous ring-linear maps.
The local prototype formula is definitionally equal to Mathlib's field norm,
not a competing production norm.

For convolution compatibility follow [Mathlib PR #42836](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42836)'s
`AbstractMeasure.amiceTransformₐ` and `amiceTransformEquivₐ`, using
`Multiplicative ℤ_p` to express additive convolution through the native
monoid-measure API. The earlier Amice proposals
[#23772](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/23772) and
[#23791](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/23791) are related
existing work; use the native `AbstractMeasure` interfaces as the common carrier.
Build required missing results in Tau Ceti in these API shapes and adopt
Mathlib's declarations when available, without waiting for those proposals.

Tau Ceti's `RingTheory/Huber/Basic.lean` supplies `IsTateRing`,
`IsPseudoUniformizer` and `IsTateRing.exists_hasBasis_nhds_zero`.
Its `RingTheory/Huber/Normed.lean` supplies norm-boundedness and
power-boundedness comparisons, and `RingTheory/Huber/OpenMapping.lean`
supplies the topological mapping theorems. Section 0.4 constructs the
unit-ball pair of definition and proves the normed-to-topological Tate
bridge, importing native versions of those comparisons when available.
The topological open-mapping and finite-module APIs supply the topological
facts; the statements below supply their quantitative form. RestrictedPowerSeries
supplies the analytic algebra used in Layers 4–5.
Tau Ceti's `NumberTheory/Padics/PadicIntegers.lean` already supplies
`PadicInt.compactSpace_units` and `totallyDisconnectedSpace_units`; reuse
these instances for the weight-pairing norms.

## Layer 0 Ultrametric Banach modules and Tate gauges

### 0.1 Sums and estimates

Use the native equivalence between summability and cofinite decay in a
complete ultrametric group. Prove boundedness and norm-supremum attainment
for a nonzero null family. Supply the strict bound for a summable family
whose terms have norm `<B`, `B>0`, and equality with a unique dominant
term. Handle the empty family explicitly.

Give bounded bilinear and module versions of Cauchy products and double
sums, assuming summability of the input families. Prove joint decay before
exchanging sums. Summation is norm-decreasing in the coefficient sup norm.
A family of null families is summable in the sup-norm space if its sup
norms tend to zero; pointwise decay alone is insufficient.

### 0.2 Normed rings and multiplicative units

Construct the closed unit-ball subring and its open-ball ideal. Elements
of the former are power-bounded and of the latter topologically nilpotent.
For multiplicative norms, topological nilpotence is equivalent to norm `<1`;
comparison of topological ring-boundedness with norm-boundedness uses
the multiplicative-unit scaling supplied by a Tate norm. Do not infer this
comparison from a merely non-discrete ring topology. General submultiplicative
norms do not give the converses.

Prove the ultrametric Neumann estimates for `‖x‖<1`, including
`‖(1−x)⁻¹‖=1` and `‖(1−x)⁻¹−1‖=‖x‖` in a complete norm-one ring.
Deduce unit lifting and the inclusion of the open-ball ideal in the
Jacobson radical of the unit ball. Over a field the reduction is a field;
over `ℚ_p⟨X⟩` it is `𝔽_p[X]`.

For multiplicative units prove the inverse norm formula and exact scaling
on every module with bounded action. These supply all shell arguments.

### 0.3 Modules and norm comparisons

Use `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [Module R E] [IsBoundedSMul R E]
[IsUltrametricDist E] [CompleteSpace E]` for a Banach module with contractive
action. Over a field retain `NormedSpace K E` and its existing consequences.
State results with only the components they use: completeness belongs to
convergence and extension results, not finite-sum norm estimates. A convenience
abbreviation may shorten local hypotheses, but must not introduce another norm,
module action, completeness API or cycle of instances reconstructing the same
properties. A new bundled category of Banach modules is outside this roadmap.

For consumers allowing `‖a • x‖≤C‖a‖‖x‖` with `C≥1`, retain the explicit action bound.
Over a norm-one coefficient ring the adapted norm
`‖x‖'=sup_{a≠0} ‖a • x‖/‖a‖` satisfies `‖x‖≤‖x‖'≤C‖x‖` and makes the
action contractive. Supply this comparison where used, including the
zero-module case. Transport completeness, continuity and potential ONability;
exact isometries and norm-one bounds must refer to the selected norm.

Develop closed submodules, quotients by closed submodules, finite max-norm
products and completeness. Quotient norms are infima; approximating lifts
suffice without a norm-minimising representative.

Bounded-equivalent norms give the same bounded maps and completeness.
For ring norms inducing the same topology retain the corrected power
comparisons of [JN] Lemmas 2.1.6–2.1.7. With a common multiplicative unit,
the exponent is determined by its two norms. Equal topology alone does
not imply a linear comparison of ring norms.

For `c=‖π‖∈(0,1)`, round a module norm upwards to `c^ℤ∪{0}`. Prove
`‖m‖≤‖m‖'` and `c‖m‖'<‖m‖` for `m≠0`, with both zero at zero.
This is a module norm for the original scalar norm when that scalar norm
takes values in `c^ℤ∪{0}`. Otherwise retain the additive norm and exact
`π`-scaling. Construct `M̃=M⁰/πM⁰` over `R̃=R⁰/πR⁰`; for the discrete
module norm the denominator is precisely the open unit ball.

### 0.4 Tate norms and topological gauges

Distinguish the three interfaces: existence of a topological Tate structure,
the Tate property of a specified norm, and a chosen multiplicative
pseudo-uniformiser. For an ultrametric norm-one commutative ring, map the
normed pseudo-uniformiser to the native `TauCeti.Huber.IsPseudoUniformizer`.
Construct the unit-ball pair of definition described below, and use its
`IsHuberRing` instance and the chosen unit to obtain `TauCeti.Huber.IsTateRing`.
This bridge needs neither completeness nor multiplicativity of every scalar.
Reuse `IsTateRing.of_isUnit_norm_lt_one` when that native comparison is
available; exact multiplication by the chosen unit remains the additional
input for the quantitative results below.

Prove the shell `‖ϖ‖<‖ϖ^n m‖≤1` with unique integer `n` for `m≠0`.
Norm-one algebras over nontrivially normed fields give Tate examples by a
small nonzero scalar. The logarithmic gauge
`v_ϖ(x)=log‖x‖/log‖ϖ‖`, with infinity at zero, is superadditive on
products; it is an additive valuation only for a multiplicative norm.
Compare its field specialisation with NewtonPolygons' normalisation.

The unit ball and `(ϖ)` give a Huber pair of definition. Conversely suppose
a topological commutative ring `A` has a subring `A₀`, a topologically
nilpotent unit `ϖ∈A₀`, and neighbourhood basis `ϖ^n A₀`, `n≥0`. For `a>1` set

```text
tateGauge A₀ ϖ a x = inf { a^(−n) | n∈ℤ, ϖ^(−n)x∈A₀ }.
```

Obtain this input from `Huber.IsTateRing.exists_hasBasis_nhds_zero`, replacing
the pseudo-uniformiser by a positive power if needed to put it in the ring of
definition. This is an explicit choice of gauge data. A topologically
nilpotent unit need not satisfy the multiplicative scaling identity for an
arbitrarily given compatible norm.

Prove the seminorm, ultrametric inequality, exact `ϖ`-scaling and recovery
of the topology. Its kernel is the closure of zero. It separates points
exactly when `A` is Hausdorff, and takes value one at one in the nonzero
Hausdorff case. Changing `A₀` with fixed `ϖ,a` gives bounded-equivalent
gauges. Replacing `a` by `b>1` raises the gauge to `log b/log a`.
Retain the consumer names `tateGauge`, `exists_tateSeminorm`,
`tateGauge_eq_zero_iff`, `tateGauge_equiv`, `tateGauge_rpow`.
In the nonzero Hausdorff case promote the gauge to a normed Tate structure
on a compatible model of `A`; completeness is transferred only when the
original topological ring is complete. Going from a Tate norm to its unit-ball
gauge with `a=‖ϖ‖⁻¹` generally returns a bounded-equivalent discrete rounding,
not literal equality of norms. Other choices of `a` involve the power comparison
above. Keep the normed-to-topological implication and the
topological-to-chosen-gauge construction separate; do not install them as
mutually inverse global instances.

**Checks.** `(ℤ_p,p,p)` gives the norm on `ℚ_p`; `(ℤ_p,p²,p)` gives
values `1,p⁻¹` at `p,p²` and is not multiplicative. The zero ring has zero
gauge. Membership `ϖ∈A₀` is essential: in `ℚ_p²`, take
`A₀={(x,y)∈ℤ_p² : x−y∈p²ℤ_p}` and `ϖ=(p,p²)`; the formula gives
`g(1)=1`, `g(ϖ)=a⁻¹`, `g(1+ϖ)=a²`, violating ultrametricity.
Rounding `ℂ_p` to `p^ℤ` does not preserve its original scalar inequality.
On `ℚ_p`, the norm `N(x)=max(|x|_p,|x|_p²)` is ultrametric,
submultiplicative and norm-one, and induces the usual Tate topology. For
every `0<|ϖ|_p=r<1`, however, `N(ϖ)N(ϖ⁻¹)=r⁻¹>1=N(1)`.
Thus this specified norm has no multiplicative pseudo-uniformiser: the
topological Tate condition does not imply the normed one for an arbitrary
compatible norm.

**Dependencies.** Mathlib sums, quotients and topological groups; AdicSpaces
for the Huber comparison. Sources: [JN] §2.1, [Sch] §§3–4, [KL] §2.4.

## Layer 1 Bounded operators and finite modules

### 1.1 Operator norms over rings

For a linear map with a uniform bound, use
`inf{C≥0 : ∀x, ‖u x‖≤C‖x‖}`. Prove the bound at the infimum, the norm
and composition laws. Over Tate scalars prove continuity implies a bound,
then extend the normed-space API on `ContinuousLinearMap` in the shape of
Mathlib #42865. Use its general `Norm` instance when available and scoped
instances for additional ring-scalar structures, agreeing with the field API.
The operator norm is a supremum of ratios, not generally the supremum of values on the unit ball.

The operator space is complete and ultrametric when the target is. Supply
evaluation, operator-norm sums and the endomorphism Banach ring. Neumann
inversion for `‖1−u‖<1` agrees with `ContinuousLinearEquiv`; the inverse
norm is one for a nonzero module and zero for the zero module.

### 1.2 Mapping theorems

For Banach modules over a Banach–Tate ring, a continuous surjection has
preimages with `‖m‖≤C‖n‖` for some `C>0`. Derive this from topological
open mapping and shell scaling. Prove bounded inverse, closed graph,
strictness of closed-range maps and Banach–Steinhaus. A pointwise convergent sequence of
continuous linear maps on a Banach source has a continuous limit. For a
general net, retain the pointwise-bounded-family hypothesis; convergence
of a net alone does not bound its whole range. Give finite-free
operator bounds from the coordinate vectors.

### 1.3 Finite-dimensional spaces

Reuse Mathlib's continuity, completeness, equivalent-norm and closed-subspace
theorems over complete nontrivially normed fields. Supply ultrametric
max-norm coordinates and `t`-orthogonal bases for `0<t<1`. Under discrete
valuation prove the orthogonal version using finite-dimensional distance
attainment. No spherical completeness is assumed for the general field case.

### 1.4 Finite Banach modules

For a commutative Noetherian Banach–Tate ring, prove the canonical complete
Hausdorff quotient topology on finite modules, independent of presentation.
Maps between them are continuous and strict; submodules are closed. Any
compatible Banach module norms are bounded-equivalent. Consume existing
topological finite-module results and supply their normed comparison.

## Layer 3 Continuous functions, Mahler coordinates and bounded measures

### 3.1 Profinite functions

For a profinite space `X` and a complete ultrametric module `E`, use the
sup norm on `C(X,E)`. Locally constant functions are dense: compactness

### 3.2 Mahler's theorem

C₀(ℕ,E) ≃ₗᵢ C(ℤ_p,E),   (a_n) ↦ (x ↦ Σ_n binom(x,n) • a_n).

coefficients as `(χ(1)−1)^n`. Conversely a topologically nilpotent `t`
gives the character `x↦(1+t)^x`. Require a complete normed `ℤ_p`-algebra
with bounded structural map. In a multiplicatively normed field the
parameter condition is exactly `‖t‖<1`; keep topological nilpotence over

to obtain `n⁻`, and use coefficient `f(n)−f(n⁻)`. Thus for `f(x)=x` it is
the leading digit times `p^(ℓ−1)`. Identify the finite expansions for locally
constant functions, and give the bounded changes between these coordinates
and Mahler coordinates. Their columns are null; they need not be finite.

arbitrary `E`. The unnormalised monomials `(x−a)^j` do not give an

Put `m_h(n)=⌊n/p^h⌋!` and `e_(h,n)(x)=m_h(n)binom(x,n)`.

their disc expansions induce an isometry

C₀(ℕ,E) ≃ₗᵢ LA_h(E),      (c_n) ↦ Σ_n e_(h,n) • c_n.

### 5.4 Analytic levels of weights

For `h≥v_p(q)`, a field-valued weight is analytic on unit discs modulo
`p^h` exactly when

```text
‖κ(exp(p^h))−1‖ < r_p,
equivalently ‖T_κ‖ < p^(−q/(p^h(p−1))).
```

Prove this by reducing to §4.6 through `log(x/ω(x))/q`.
Every continuous field-valued weight satisfies it for some `h`.
Give the locally algebraic conductor bound, handling the minimum allowed
level and trivial finite-order character separately: for `κ(x)=x^kψ(x)`
with conductor dividing `p^m`, every `h≥max(m,v_p(q))` suffices.
For Banach-algebra
coefficients use sufficient convergence conditions and an explicit bound
on the resulting expansion; compactness alone does not give norm one.

### 5.5 Scalar analytic factors for automorphic applications

For a field-valued weight satisfying §5.4 at level `h`, extend its
principal-unit part analytically to `1+p^h𝒪_K`. For
`d∈ℤ_pˣ(1+p^h𝒪_K)` and `‖c‖≤‖p^h‖`, expand `κ(cz+d)`
on the closed unit disc and prove its Gauss norm is one. Put
`t_h=κ(exp(p^h))−1`. A radius `r>0` satisfying

```text
r‖c‖ < r_p,       r‖c‖‖t_h‖ < ‖p^h‖ r_p
```

gives convergence on that radius, Gauss norm at most one, and coefficient
bounds `‖a_n‖≤r^(−n)`. State the corresponding Banach-algebra version
with the actual bound on the constant factor and on the analytic character.
Use RestrictedPowerSeries for composition and coefficient estimates.
For nonnegative algebraic weight the expansion agrees with `(cz+d)^k`.
Matrix actions and the ordering convention in their cocycle identity are
owned by quaternionic modular-form theory;
this section supplies only scalar expansions.

### 5.6 An annular coefficient ring

Construct the specific integral coefficient ring with normal forms

```text
H = {Σ_(m∈ℤ) d_m T^m : d_m∈ℤ_p, v_p(d_m)≥max(0,−m)}.
```

Prove convergence of each convolution coefficient, the algebra operations,
and the algebraic identification `H≃ℤ_p[[T,U]]/(TU−p)` with `U=p/T`.
This includes arbitrary formal tails in `U`. It is not the `p`-adic
completion of the polynomial algebra `ℤ_p[[T]][p/T]`: that completion
requires additional decay of the `U`-coefficients. Do not conflate the
formal `(T,U)` topology with the gauge used below.

On `H[1/T]`, establish the coefficient criterion
`v_p(d_m)≥max(0,−m−k)` for some `k≥0`, allowing `d_m∈ℤ_p`.
For a fixed `α∈(0,1)`, construct the complete multiplicative-`T` gauge
whose unit ball is `H` and `‖T‖=α`, and prove that it is a
nonarchimedean Banach–Tate ring. State completeness for this gauge topology.
In particular `‖U‖=1`; the partial sums of `Σ_(j≥0) U^j` do not
converge in this topology even though the formal sum is an element of `H`.

At every `t∈ℂ_p` with `p⁻¹<|t|<1`, construct the evaluation
`T↦t, U↦p/t` and prove continuity using divisibility bounds. The
evaluations over this annulus in `ℂ_p` are jointly injective. There may
be no such points over the ground field `ℚ_p`; that field alone cannot
test injectivity. A general gauge-continuous specialisation need not be
Lipschitz for arbitrary choices of `α`.

Adjoin the finite factor by `H[Δ]`, compare it with the halo coefficient
construction in [LWX] §3.15, and track the ideal `(p,T)=(T)` of the
principal coefficient ring. At `p=2`, the full finite-factor maximal ideal
also contains `δ−1`; retain the integral group ring. Annular geometry,
Fredholm series and slope bounds remain downstream.

**Checks.** At `p=2`, test both sign characters and `γ=exp(4)`.
Specialise the universal character at the trivial weight and at an
algebraic weight. Verify `T↦0`, the finite-character components, and

δ_x κ=κ(x)`. Test the halo normal forms `T`, `U`, `p=TU` and

For universal specialisation also check `(1+T)^n` and the infinite series

dual-number algebra, `s↦1+sε` has `‖T_κ‖=1` and evaluation

The coordinate `p` gives evaluation into both `ℤ_p` and `ℚ_p`, although

does not give continuous evaluation into `ℚ_p`.

measures and additivity on their sum. If `a≠b`, the measure `δ_a−δ_b`
vanishes at the trivial weight but has value `a−b≠0` at `κ(x)=x`.
Every Dirac measure attains the bound: its extended norm and every
`|κ(a)|` are one.

## Dependency order and completion

Layers 0–2 precede the bounded duality in Layer 3; Layer 4 consumes the
restricted-series supplier and Layer 3; Layer 5 consumes both. Two apparent
cycles must be resolved at the stated interfaces:

* LocallyAnalyticDistributions §0.0 supplies the general completed tensor
  construction and its functoriality. Only the last corollary of §2.4
  consumes it. Countable-type splitting itself is independent of tensors
  and of the later distribution layers.
* PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras §1.7 supplies the general measure/group-algebra
  comparison without Amice. Section 5.3 then proves coordinate compatibility.
  The consumer's later Amice and weight-space layers may use that result.

A layer is complete when its definitions use native structures, its targets
and comparison maps are proved, its stated checks are formalised, and its
supplier/consumer hypotheses agree. Test zero objects and empty indices,
non-Noetherian versus Noetherian coefficients, all primes, and the strict
radius boundaries. Admitted roadmap signatures are not completed results.
Integration must not introduce `sorry`-based instances or silently change
the topology of an imported object.

# Roadmap: p-adic measures, completed group algebras, and characteristic ideals

**Summary.** This roadmap builds the common language of Iwasawa theory and p-adic L-functions:
bounded measures on profinite spaces and their duals, completed group algebras with the Mahler–Amice
identification of measures on ℤ_p with power series, pseudo-measures and their values at characters
and on the weight space, Weierstrass preparation, the structure theory of finitely generated Iwasawa
modules with the invariants μ and λ, characteristic and Fitting ideals and how they behave under
specialisation and exact sequences. It supplies the bounded/ordinary measure and pseudo-measure
foundation for p-adic L-functions and their characteristic-ideal comparisons;
LocallyAnalyticDistributions extends this foundation to the distributions used in nonordinary
constructions. Fixing the measure algebra and the module theory once lets those later roadmaps
state their theorems against shared, pinned objects.

This roadmap builds the analytic and algebraic language that Iwasawa theory shares with the theory
of p-adic L-functions: bounded measures on profinite spaces and their duals, completed group
algebras and the comparison between measures and the Iwasawa algebra, the Mahler–Amice dictionary
between measures on ℤ_p and power series with its operator calculus (weighting, translation,
dilation, φ, ψ, restriction to residue classes and to the units), pseudo-measures and their
evaluation at characters, the Weierstrass theory of O⟦T⟧ and the structure of finitely generated
Λ-modules with their characteristic ideals and μ/λ-invariants, determinant lines and specialization,
and the ring theory of coefficient orders (character group rings, quadratic presentations, Fitting
ideals of all indices, transposes) that integral Euler-system and Brumer–Stark arguments use. It
continues the Tau Ceti roadmap ProfiniteProPGroups, whose layer 9 builds the completed group algebra
`TauCeti.completedGroupAlgebra ℤ_p Γ` with its power-series coordinate; everything here is stated on
that carrier and on Mathlib's `AbstractMeasure`, `PowerSeries` and localization carriers. Its end
theorems are the comparison of integral measures with the completed group algebra (§1.7) and its
reading in the power-series coordinate (§4.5), the Mahler–Amice calculus using ψφ = 1 and φψ the
restriction to pℤ_p from PadicFunctionalAnalysis §3.4, clause 5 (§2.2), the evaluation of
pseudo-measures at characters and its continuity
(§3.3, §3a.1), the structure theorem for Iwasawa modules with the growth formula over any
mixed-characteristic coefficient ring (§4.2, §4.7), the rational trivialization of the determinant
of a perfect complex by the alternating product of characteristic ideals (§5.1), and the
Fitting-ideal identities for character group rings and transposes (§6.2, §6.6).

`README.md` is normative. [`Suggested.lean`](Suggested.lean) records the end theorems and layer
milestones that can be stated against the pinned libraries, with the few light definitions they need
and checks that fix the conventions; it is not exhaustive, and the docstrings there cite the
subsections of this file as §k.n. Every target below states its hypotheses and source; a closing
*Lean:* note names the declaration of `Suggested.lean` that carries it, and a target without that
note is specified here only. The names written inside a target (definitions, API lemmas,
intermediate results) are the proposed names for the library; a declaration of `Suggested.lean` is
cited as such, in a *Lean:* note or with an explicit mention of the file. New declarations live in
the namespaces of `Suggested.lean` (`AbstractMeasure`, `PowerSeries`, `Iwasawa`,
`TauCeti.Iwasawa`, `TauCeti`, `Matrix`) or under `TauCeti.` in the library;
the namespaces named in each subsection are the proposed ones. Every definition comes with the API
it needs and with checks that a plausible wrong definition fails; every theorem carries its exact
hypotheses, its source, and the earlier statements or library declarations it rests on. Nothing here
is optional.

## Scope and ownership

The roadmap owns:

- bounded measures on compact spaces and their operator calculus: clopen restriction, extension by
  zero, the weak and strong topologies, the Dirac measures (Layer 0), the Mahler–Amice dictionary on
  ℤ_p with weighting, translation, root-of-unity averaging, residue projections, the unit-domain
  comparisons and the Cartier operators, using PadicFunctionalAnalysis §3.4 for the bounded
  Mahler dual, dilation, φ, ψ, the bounded Amice norm and the rational integral lattice (Layer 2);
- finite coefficients and joint coordinates of measures, the finite measure algebras, the finite
  quotients and coordinates of ℤ_pˣ, and the comparison of integral measures on a profinite group
  with `TauCeti.completedGroupAlgebra ℤ_p Γ`, with coefficient extension (Layer 1);
- pseudo-measures on a commutative completed group algebra, admissible evaluation at characters, the
  characters of ℤ_pˣ and their integrals, and the evaluation at varying characters (Layer 3),
  together with meromorphic functions on the character space of ℤ_pˣ supplied by
  PadicFunctionalAnalysis §§5.1–5.3 (Layer 3a);
- ring theory of O⟦T⟧ using NewtonPolygons §6.3, clause 3 for preparation, pseudo-null modules and
  pseudo-isomorphisms, the structure theorem for finitely generated Λ-modules, the invariants μ and
  λ, the Iwasawa coordinate over O, characteristic divisors and ideals with their base change and
  change of generator, isotypic decompositions and Galois-orbit components, the cyclotomic
  polynomials and the growth formulas (Layer 4);
- line modules and determinant lines of perfect complexes, their rational trivialization and
  specialization, and topological Nakayama (Layer 5);
- the coefficient-order algebra of Dasgupta–Kakde: character group rings with their lattices, units,
  locality and completeness, the sharp involution, the contragredient dual and the transpose of a
  presentation, quadratic presentations, compound matrices and higher adjugates, the Fitting ideals
  of extensions and fibre products, and the exterior-power annihilation lemma (Layer 6).

It does not construct any p-adic L-function (no Bernoulli, Eisenstein or zeta arithmetic, no
Kubota–Leopoldt measure), no Coleman norm or trace operator and no Coleman map, no locally analytic
distributions beyond the bounded theory, no Galois cohomology, Selmer group or main conjecture, no
Euler- or Kolyvagin-system contraction, and no eigenvariety. It states no Gorenstein property and no
duality for the character group rings: the Gorenstein-order theory of Dasgupta–Kakde and the exact
duality it feeds (the lattice dual Hom_R(M, R) of a module over an order R, and the finite-module
dual Hom_O(M, K/O), which differ already for M = O/ϖ, whose lattice dual is 0 and whose finite dual
is O/ϖ again; the dualizing object, exactness, biduality and the compatibility with the
involution #) are left to the roadmap that proves the Brumer–Stark integrality statements, which
will state them with the generic lemmas on orders shared with GlobalNumberFields. Those
subjects consume the statements here through the interfaces named in each layer.

It leaves to named roadmaps:

- the bounded Mahler dual and integral unit-ball identification, dilation and Frobenius/psi
  calculus, characters and their universal property, bounded measure functions and the agreement
  of the integral Amice and completed-group-algebra coordinates, to **PadicFunctionalAnalysis**
  §§3.4 and 5.1–5.3; uniformizer-power Weierstrass preparation to **NewtonPolygons** §6.3, clause 3;
  these are roadmaps of W. Coram, to be contributed to TauCetiRoadmap ahead of this one;
- the completed group algebra itself, its inverse-limit topology, the ℤ_p power-series coordinate
  for a procyclic pro-p group, the continuity of that coordinate and the change of generator, to Tau

  image"); they are consumed, never restated;
- the Fitting ideals of finitely presented quasi-coherent modules as far as the relative singular

- the determinant of a finite locally free sheaf and its pullback comparisons on schemes, to Tau

## Conventions

Write p for the prime, including p = 2 unless a statement says otherwise; ℤ_p for `PadicInt`, k =
𝔽_p for `ZMod p`; O for the valuation ring of a finite extension K of ℚ_p, ϖ for a uniformizer, and
𝔽 for the residue field. D(X,R) is Mathlib's `AbstractMeasure` on a compact space X with
coefficients in a normed commutative ring R; it carries two topologies, the weak topology of
pointwise convergence on test functions and the operator-norm (strong) topology, and the two are
never identified: integral measures are compact for the weak topology, while a field-valued unit
ball on an infinite domain is not norm compact. Clopen restriction, extension by zero, pushforward
and convolution are operators on D(X,R); none introduces a second measure carrier. Convolution is
right-handed and written μ ⋆ ν; on a profinite abelian monoid it is commutative.

The Amice transform A_μ ∈ ℤ_p⟦T⟧ of a measure μ on ℤ_p has n-th coefficient μ(x ↦ binom(x,n)); Y =
1 + T, so that δ_a ↦ Y^a. `Suggested.lean` fixes this normalisation by `example`s: A(δ₁) = 1 + T,
A(δ₀) = 1, and the n-th coefficient of A(δ₋₁) is (−1)^n. The operators on power series are: the
Mahler derivation ∂ = (1+T)·d/dT (multiplication of the measure by x), translation (multiplication
by the character x ↦ ζ^x or by Y^a), dilation (pushforward along x ↦ ax), φ(F)(T) = F((1+T)^p − 1)
(pushforward along multiplication by p), ψ with ψ∘φ = id and φ∘ψ = restriction to pℤ_p, and 1 − φψ =
restriction to the units. Root-of-unity averages require the stated coefficient extension and
descent hypotheses. The inclusion of measures on ℤ_pˣ into measures on ℤ_p is linear and not
multiplicative for the two convolutions.

The completed group algebra of a profinite group over an adic coefficient ring carries the joint
topology of coefficient-ideal powers and open normal subgroups. For a procyclic Γ with coordinate
T = γ − 1, the kernel of the projection to level n is generated by ω_n = (1+T)^{p^n} − 1. In
characteristic p this is T^{p^n}; over ℤ_p at n > 0 it is not the ideal (T^{p^n}). At p = 2 the
units are {±1} × (1 + 4ℤ_2) and the integral theory keeps the order-two group-ring factor; no
integral division by 2 occurs.

Pseudo-measures on a commutative completed group algebra R are the elements λ of the localization at
the non-zero-divisors with ([g] − 1)λ ∈ R for every g. A character is evaluated on a pseudo-measure
only after clearing a denominator [g] − 1 whose image under the character is a unit; there is no
character map on the whole total quotient ring.

Λ = O⟦T⟧ with O a complete discrete valuation ring with finite residue field. Finitely generated
Λ-modules carry an explicit Λ-action. Pseudo-null means finitely generated with zero localization at
every prime of height at most one; for Λ it means finite. Pseudo-isomorphism is a map with
pseudo-null kernel and cokernel; it is symmetric on finitely generated torsion modules and is not
asserted to be an equivalence relation in general. The characteristic divisor of a finite torsion
module is the finitely supported function on height-one primes giving the local lengths; the
characteristic ideal is the corresponding product of primes, principal when the ring is factorial. μ
is the length of the ϖ-primary part, F_{M,γ} the distinguished polynomial of the horizontal factors
and λ its degree; the elementary factors are retained as a multiset. A finite Λ-module has
characteristic ideal Λ and, in general, a nonunit initial Fitting ideal.

Coefficient scope. The hypotheses stated in each subsection are part of this specification, and the
suggested Lean signatures express them. Coefficient extension uses the complete normed source and
isometric unit-ball embedding of §1.7; coordinates use the complete noetherian local coefficient
ring of §4.5; Galois-orbit factors use the unramified Galois splitting extension of §4.6;
determinants allow arbitrary finite projectives as in §5.1. Where a statement is made for O = ℤ_p
(Iwasawa's growth formula, the minimal resolution with 𝔽_p-dimensions) the form over a general O is
registered separately, with k and ϖ in place of 𝔽_p and p, and its residue degree f and ramification
index e in the exponents; the two are not conflated, because the ℤ_p formulas are false over a
ramified or unramified O ≠ ℤ_p (§4.2, §4.7). Vertical invariants are normalised by ϖ, never by p:
the μ-part of the structure theorem is built from powers of ϖ, μ is the length at (ϖ), and
restriction of scalars from Λ_O to ℤ_p⟦T⟧ multiplies μ by the residue degree f = [k : 𝔽_p] and λ by
[O : ℤ_p] (Λ_O/(ϖ) = k⟦T⟧ is f copies of 𝔽_p⟦T⟧ over ℤ_p⟦T⟧, and Λ_O/(F) has ℤ_p-rank [O : ℤ_p]·deg
F), while base change along an extension multiplies μ by its ramification index e (§4.6). The
equal-characteristic case O = k⟦ϖ⟧ is excluded from the growth formula, where it is false.

For a finite abelian H of order invertible in O, e_ω = (1/#H)Σ_a ω(a)⁻¹[a] after adjoining the
character values, where 1/#H is `Ring.inverse (#H)`; every statement about e_ω carries the
hypothesis that #H is invertible in O, and for p-torsion in H nothing is divided by #H. In Layer 6
characters are homomorphisms G →* Oˣ and the Pontryagin dual of a finite module uses the
contragredient action.

Determinants. The determinant of a finite projective module P of constant rank r placed in degree 0
is (⋀^r P, r mod 2), so a rank-one module in degree 0 has odd parity; the determinant of a perfect
complex is the alternating tensor product ⊗_i det(P^i)^{⊗(−1)^i} with parity function x ↦ Σ_i (−1)^i
rank(P^i_x) mod 2; the symmetry of graded lines carries the Koszul sign (−1)^{|L||L′|}, so that
exchanging two rank-one summands of a module acts by −1 on its determinant; shifting by one inverts
the line and negates the integer degree, which does not change the parity. The two-term witness
fixing every sign and direction: for the complex [Λ --a--> Λ] in degrees −1, 0 with a a
non-zero-divisor, det is Λ with even parity, H⁰ = Λ/(a), the trivialization det(P)[a^{−1}] →
Λ[a^{−1}] sends 1 to a^{−1} and the canonical section of Stacks 0FJI sends 1 to a, so the image of
det P in the fraction field is a^{−1}Λ = char(H⁰)^{−1}, not aΛ; the same complex in degrees 0, 1 has
image aΛ (§5.1).

Standing assumptions shared by several layers: p is any prime, including p = 2, and the indices n,
m, r range over all natural numbers, including 0. ℤ_p is `PadicInt p`, k = `ZMod p`, Z⟦T⟧ =
`PowerSeries ℤ_p`, k⟦T⟧ = `PowerSeries k`, and Y = 1 + T. R is a normed commutative ring unless a
statement says more. U = ℤ_pˣ has the subspace topology of the units, A_n = (ℤ/p^nℤ)ˣ is finite and
discrete (A_0 is the trivial group), red_n : U → A_n is the unit reduction `PadicInt.unitsToZModPow
n` (§1.3), π_n(μ) = π_{red_n}(μ) is the finite projection of §1.1 and π_{(r,n)}(μ) its reduction
modulo p^r (the joint projection of §1.1). Products of coordinates carry the product topology,
p-adic on ℤ_p and discrete on each ZMod(p^r). M = D(U, ℤ_p). A topology on a measure carrier is
never an instance: where one is used it is named, `AbstractMeasure.WeakTopology` or
`AbstractMeasure.StrongTopology`. ψ on integral measures is supplied by PadicFunctionalAnalysis
§3.4, clause 5,
transported to power series through the Amice transform.
