## Layer 0 Coefficients and series algebras

### 0.1 Native restricted-series algebra

Use the native coefficient predicates and build any missing coefficientwise API:
extensionality, constants, variables, monomials, polynomial inclusion, sums, products,
scalar multiplication, and compatible ring and algebra maps. The coefficients of a
product are the usual finite antidiagonal sums. Prove compatibility with the ambient
formal-series operations, including the zero-variable algebra equivalence with `R`
and the one-variable comparison.

Reindexing by an equivalence of variable sets induces an algebra equivalence with
the correspondingly reindexed radii. Include its values on coefficients, constants
and variables and its identity/composition laws. Polynomial embeddings are injective.
These are extensions of the native objects, not a replacement ring implementation.

### 0.2 Maps of coefficients

For a ring homomorphism `φ : R →+* S` with
`‖φ a‖ ≤ C ‖a‖` for all `a`, where `C ≥ 0`, coefficientwise mapping preserves
restrictedness at the same radii. Prove the coefficient formula, identity and
composition laws, compatibility with polynomial inclusion and reindexing, and
injectivity when `φ` is injective. After Layer 1, prove the Gauss-norm bound by `C`
and equality when `φ` preserves norms.

For a surjective bounded `φ`, require a uniform lifting bound before asserting
surjectivity on restricted series: there is `L > 0` such that every `b : S` has a
lift `a : R` with `‖a‖ ≤ L ‖b‖`. Choose coefficient lifts, prove their
restrictedness, and obtain the same bound for the lifted series. Describe the
kernel coefficientwise. With the norm topologies this yields a quotient map.
An isometric quotient statement requires the corresponding sharp lifting/quotient
norm hypothesis; mere algebraic surjectivity is not such a hypothesis.

### 0.3 Module-valued coefficients

For an ultrametric normed additive group `E`, construct the additive group of
coefficient families `a : (σ →₀ ℕ) → E` satisfying the weighted decay condition.
Give coefficient maps, extensionality and finite-support inclusions. For an ultrametric normed
`R`-module with `‖a • e‖ ≤ ‖a‖ ‖e‖`, construct the coefficientwise
`R`-module and bounded maps induced by bounded linear maps of coefficient modules.
Construct multiplication by scalar restricted series through convolution and prove
the module laws and norm inequality of Layer 1.

Use the native coefficient-family carrier whenever available. A function-valued
realisation of this module is a comparison in §2.4, not its definition.

**Checks.** Zero variables recover the coefficient ring or module. The variable
`X i` has exactly one nonzero coefficient. Coefficient mapping sends it to `X i`.
Zero coefficient rings and zero modules are allowed here. Over `ℚ_p`, the series
`Σ p^n X^n` is restricted at radius one and fails to be restricted at radius `p`.

**Dependencies.** Mathlib formal series, restrictedness, finite antidiagonals and
ultrametric norm inequalities. Sources: [BGR] §5.1; [Martin] §1.3 for Banach-ring radii.

## Layer 1 Gauss norms and radius calculus

### 1.1 Norms, completeness and approximation

On restricted series the Gauss supremum is finite, and for a nonzero series is
attained. Its attaining indices form a finite nonempty set. Prove the coefficient
bound, definiteness, the ultrametric triangle inequality and submultiplicativity.
The norms of constants and monomials are
`‖C a‖ = ‖a‖` and `‖a X^ν‖ = ‖a‖ r^ν`; in a norm-one ring, `‖X i‖ = r i`.
When the coefficient norm is multiplicative the Gauss norm is multiplicative.
Consume the existing attainment and dominant-antidiagonal proofs.

Complete coefficients give a complete restricted algebra/module. Coefficient
functionals are continuous with bound `(r^ν)⁻¹`. Finite-support truncations converge
in norm; in finitely many variables, total-degree truncations suffice. A dense
coefficient subset gives dense polynomials with coefficients in that subset.
Record the completion of the polynomial algebra with its Gauss norm as this
restricted algebra, compatibly with constants, variables and coefficient maps.

### 1.2 Changing the radii

If `0 < r i ≤ s i` for every `i`, there is a contractive injective map
`R⟨s⁻¹X⟩ → R⟨r⁻¹X⟩`, coefficientwise the identity. It has dense image because
it contains the polynomials. Prove identity and composition laws and compatibility
with coefficient maps and variable permutations.

For finite variables over a normed field, scaling by nonzero `u_i` gives the
isometry `f(X) ↦ f(u_i X_i)` from radii `r` to radii `s` when
`‖u_i‖ s_i = r_i`. Give the inverse and coefficient formula. Over a normed ring,
use multiplicative units and the same norm equation. Radius theorems themselves
hold at every positive real radius; this rescaling theorem cannot replace them.

### 1.3 The coefficient model and iteration

At unit radii the coefficient map is an additive isometry, and an `R`-linear
isometry for the normed modules of §0.3, between restricted `E`-valued series and `C₀(σ →₀ ℕ, E)`, with the exponent set discrete. It sends
monomials to the standard single-coordinate vectors. For general radii use the
weighted coefficient norm. Obtain an unweighted `c₀` isometry by scalar rescaling
when scalars realising the weights act norm-multiplicatively on `E`; do not assert
that isometry for arbitrary real radii without this hypothesis.

For disjoint variable sets and positive radii, splitting coefficients gives an
isometric algebra equivalence
`R⟨r⁻¹X, s⁻¹Y⟩ ≃ R⟨r⁻¹X⟩⟨s⁻¹Y⟩`.
The outer coefficient condition is decay of the **Gauss norms of the slices**.
Prove both directions, coefficient formulas, compatibility with polynomials,
reassociation, permutations and coefficient maps. State the analogous module
equivalence. The `Fin (n + 1)` specialisation is the input for multivariate division.

**Checks.** `X^n` tends coefficientwise to zero but does not tend to zero in the
unit Gauss norm. At radius `r`, `‖X‖ = r`; use `r = √p` over `ℚ_p` to check that
the construction requires no scalar of norm `r`. Each row of the array
`a_ij = 1` if `i = j`, zero otherwise, is a restricted coefficient family, but the
array is not jointly restricted at unit radii: its row norms do not tend to zero.

**Dependencies.** Layer 0; native Gauss norms, `C₀` and completeness.
Sources: [BGR] §§5.1.1–5.1.2; the arbitrary-radius estimates follow directly from
weighted coefficients, as in [Martin] §1.3.

## Layer 2 Evaluation, substitution and functions

### 2.1 Evaluation and its universal property

Let `R` and `B` be ultrametric normed commutative rings, with `B` complete, and
let `φ : R →+* B` be contractive. For finitely many `b_i` satisfying
`‖b_i‖ ≤ r_i`, evaluation is the convergent monomial sum
`Σ_ν φ(a_ν) b^ν`. It is a contractive ring homomorphism, agrees with polynomial
evaluation, sends constants through `φ`, and sends each variable to `b_i`.
It is the unique continuous ring homomorphism with these values. Supply its
functoriality and algebra/module forms on the native restricted carrier, and
compare it with the topological evaluation supplied by AdicSpaces §0.5. State the version for a coefficient map bounded by `C`, with norm bound `C`.

For a complete normed `R`-algebra `B` which can be noncommutative, include the
one-variable evaluation at `b : B`, under the same bound on the coefficient map
and `‖b‖ ≤ r`. The image of `R` is central; this makes the sum a ring homomorphism.
In particular it applies to a complete normed algebra of bounded operators when
that algebra structure has been supplied by functional analysis. Construct no
operator algebra or Fredholm determinant in this layer.

### 2.2 Analytic substitution and translation

Take `g_i ∈ R⟨s⁻¹Y⟩` with `‖g_i‖_s ≤ r_i`, for finitely many source variables,
over a complete coefficient ring. Evaluation in the target restricted algebra
defines a contractive substitution `R⟨r⁻¹X⟩ → R⟨s⁻¹Y⟩`.
Prove the coefficient sum formula, identity and composition laws, compatibility
with evaluation and coefficient mapping, and comparison with formal substitution
whenever the latter's hypotheses hold.

For `‖a_i‖ ≤ r_i`, translation `X_i ↦ X_i + a_i` is an isometric automorphism
of the algebra at radii `r`, with inverse translation by `-a_i`. Give its
binomial coefficient formula. Affine maps `X_i ↦ a_i + u_i Y_i` with
`‖a_i‖ ≤ r_i` and `‖u_i‖ s_i ≤ r_i` are contractive, with composition and
evaluation laws. These maps supply the changes of disc coordinates used by
locally analytic functions and automorphic forms.

### 2.3 Derivatives and Hasse derivatives

Use the formal derivative and coefficient-defined Hasse derivatives. In one
variable, `coeff n (D^[k] f) = (n+k choose k) • coeff (n+k) f`.
They preserve restrictedness at radius `r` and satisfy
`‖D^[k] f‖_r ≤ r^(-k) ‖f‖_r`. Include the several-variable multi-index form,
Leibniz, the Hasse composition identity, commutation of different variables,
coefficient maps, and compatibility with polynomial Hasse derivatives.
Prove the chain rule for the ordinary derivative under analytic substitution.

The one-variable coefficient construction is available over any semiring,
including a noncommutative operator algebra: natural-number multiplication in
the formula does not require commutative coefficients. Supply identity,
additivity, left scalar compatibility and the ordered Leibniz rule, then
compare with the commutative Hasse derivative. The semiring construction is
the common definition; the commutative theory is its specialisation. Test `Δ²(T²)=1` in characteristic
two, where the second ordinary derivative is zero. Normed and analytic
statements retain their completeness, ultrametric and radius hypotheses.

The translated coefficients are `D^[ν] f(a)`, and the corresponding Taylor
expansion converges in the allowed closed polydisc. Ordinary iterated derivatives
equal the relevant factorial times Hasse derivatives. Do not divide by those
factorials in positive characteristic.

### 2.4 Identity and maximum principles

For one-variable restricted series over `K`, prove Strassmann's bound: if `f ≠ 0`
and `s` is the greatest index attaining its radius-`r` Gauss norm, it has at most
`s` distinct zeros in the radius-`r` closed ball in any complete isometrically
normed field extension. Derive it from §4.3 and the field unit criterion of §3.2.
A series vanishing on an infinite subset of that ball is zero.

For a Banach `ℚ_p`-module `E` with a specified jointly injective family of bounded
`ℚ_p`-linear maps to complete normed extension fields of `ℚ_p`, prove injectivity
of evaluation of unit-radius `E`-valued series on `ℤ_p`. Obtain the finite-variable
version on `ℤ_p^n` by iteration. The family of functionals is a hypothesis, not
asserted to exist for every Banach module.

For `f ∈ T_n = K⟨X₁,…,X_n⟩`, there is a finite normed field extension `L/K`
and a tuple `x ∈ (L°)^n` such that `‖f(x)‖ = ‖f‖`. Combine evaluation with
the reduction of §3.3: a nonzero reduction can be evaluated nontrivially after a
finite residue-field extension, realised by suitable prime-to-residue-characteristic
roots of unity. Include the finite-extension and residue-separation lemmas this
argument needs. No general affinoid Nullstellensatz is an input. Deduce that the
Gauss norm is the supremum over such extension-valued points.

**Checks.** Translation by `1` is allowed at radius one although its constant
term is nonzero. Over `ℚ_p`, `X^p - X` has Gauss norm one but takes values of norm
at most `p⁻¹` on `ℤ_p`; maximum modulus cannot use only `K`-rational points.
Over `𝔽_p`, the same nonzero polynomial vanishes at all points of the unit ball;
unqualified coefficient recovery for arbitrary coefficient rings is false.

**Dependencies.** §§2.1–2.3 use Layers 0–1. The Strassmann and coefficient-recovery
parts of §2.4 use §§3.2 and 4.3; maximum modulus uses §3.3. Sources: [BGR] §§5.1.3–5.1.4;
[Martin] §1.3; [Colmez] §I.4 for the disc realisation.

## Layer 3 Multiplicative units and reduction

### 3.1 Multiplicative units over Banach rings

Develop the multiplicative-unit predicate of Convention 7. In a norm-one ring,
prove closure under products and inverses and the equivalence, for `u : Rˣ`, with
`‖u⁻¹‖ = ‖u‖⁻¹`. In a complete ultrametric norm-one ring, `1 + a` is a
multiplicative unit when `‖a‖ < 1`. Every unit is multiplicative when the
coefficient norm is multiplicative. Constants and isometric algebra equivalences
preserve multiplicative units. These statements are prerequisites of §4, with no
field or reducedness assumption.

### 3.2 Units of restricted algebras

Here `R` is complete, ultrametric and norm-one.

For `f ∈ R⟨r⁻¹X⟩`, if `a_0` is a multiplicative unit and
`‖f - C a_0‖_r < ‖a_0‖`, construct its inverse by a Neumann series and prove
that `f` is a multiplicative unit. Include the resulting inverse norm and
compatibility with evaluation.

When the coefficient ring is nontrivial and its norm is multiplicative, prove the
converse: `f` is a unit if and only if `a_0` is a unit and every nonconstant weighted coefficient norm
is strictly smaller than `‖a_0‖`. Restrictedness upgrades the pointwise strict
inequalities to a uniform strict bound. This includes arbitrary positive
polyradii. In particular, a nonzero field-valued series is invertible exactly
when the constant coefficient is its unique Gauss-norm-attaining coefficient.

### 3.3 Integral structure at unit radii

For a complete nontrivially normed ultrametric field `K`, construct the coefficient
comparison `K°⟨X⟩ ≃ T_n°`, where `T_n°` is the Gauss unit ball, and prove it is
the topologically power-bounded subring. Its topologically nilpotent ideal is
`{f | ‖f‖ < 1}`. Give the coefficient criteria and prove that coefficient
reduction induces
`T_n° / T_n°° ≃ K̃[X₁,…,X_n]`.
The reduced series is a polynomial because its nonzero coefficients are finite
in number. Prove surjectivity, the kernel formula, compatibility with constants,
variables, coefficient maps of valued fields, and evaluation at integral points.

Prove that a unit of `T_n°` reduces to a unit, that a unit reduction lifts to a
unit, and that nonzero reduction is equivalent to norm one. Distinguish units of
`T_n°` from units of `T_n`: a nonzero constant of norm less than one is a unit
of `T_n` but not of `T_n°`. General normed rings do not inherit the identification
of their power-bounded elements with a chosen norm unit ball without a theorem.

**Checks.** `1 - pX` is a unit in `ℚ_p⟨X⟩`; `1 - X` is not. In
`R = K[ε]/(ε²)` with the coefficient maximum norm, `1 + εX` is a unit with
inverse `1 - εX` although its nonconstant coefficient can have norm one. This
rules out extending the field unit criterion to all Banach rings. Reduction of
`Σ p^n X^n` is the constant polynomial one.

**Dependencies.** Layers 0–1 and existing topological power-boundedness vocabulary.
Sources: [Martin] Definitions 1.20 and 1.24, Lemma 1.21 and Remark 1.22;
[BGR] §§5.1.2–5.1.3. The arbitrary-radius converse uses dominant exponents in §1.1.

## Layer 4 Weierstrass theory over Banach rings

### 4.1 Distinguished series and the multiplication estimate

Let `R` be a complete ultrametric normed commutative ring with `‖1‖ = 1`, let
`r > 0`, and let `g ∈ R⟨r⁻¹T⟩` be distinguished of degree `s` as in
Convention 7. Prove `g ≠ 0` and `‖g‖_r > 0`. Multiplication by `g` is
norm-multiplicative: `‖gq‖_r = ‖g‖_r ‖q‖_r`.
If `k` is the greatest attaining index of a nonzero `q`, the corresponding
greatest attaining index of `gq` is `s + k`. Include the strict estimates for
the other contributions to that product coefficient.

For any polynomial `b` of degree less than `s`, prove
`‖gq + b‖_r = max (‖g‖_r ‖q‖_r) ‖b‖_r`.
This estimate supplies uniqueness and the bounds; a global `NormMulClass R`
must not appear in its hypotheses.

### 4.2 Division with bounded quotient and remainder

For every `f ∈ R⟨r⁻¹T⟩`, construct unique
`q ∈ R⟨r⁻¹T⟩` and `b ∈ R[T]` with
`deg b < s` and `f = gq + b`. State uniqueness for the pair, including `s = 0`
and `f = 0`. Prove
`‖q‖_r ≤ ‖f‖_r / ‖g‖_r`, `‖b‖_r ≤ ‖f‖_r`, and the norm identity of §4.1.
For fixed `g`, quotient and remainder are bounded `R`-linear maps; give their
values on `gq`, on lower-degree polynomials and on sums and scalar multiples.

The construction truncates the divisor, divides by its polynomial part after
normalising the leading coefficient, and iterates the tail error with a uniform
contraction factor less than one. Supply the convergence and uniqueness argument
inside the complete restricted algebra. It applies at every real `r > 0`.

### 4.3 Preparation and normalisation

Construct unique `w ∈ R[T]` and `e ∈ R⟨r⁻¹T⟩` such that `w` is monic of
degree `s`, `‖w‖_r = r^s`, `e` is a multiplicative unit, and `g = e w`.
Prove uniqueness under these normalisations and the compatibility with division.
Give the polynomial case and recover the existing field/multiplicative-norm
theorems by comparison with their distinguishedness predicates.

A bounded coefficient homomorphism transports division and preparation whenever
the original and image divisors satisfy distinguishedness at the stated radius
and degree. Prove naturality from uniqueness, including the norm-preserving
field-extension case. Do not assume that an arbitrary bounded map preserves
distinguishedness or a particular distinguished degree.

### 4.4 Several variables

Apply §§4.1–4.3 over the coefficient ring in the other variables, using the
isometric iteration of §1.3. The distinguished coefficient is a multiplicative
unit of that **coefficient restricted algebra**. Obtain division with remainder
a polynomial of degree less than `s` in the chosen variable and restricted
coefficients in the others. Include preparation, uniqueness, the full norm
estimates, naturality, and compatibility with reindexing.

**Checks.** `X - 1` is distinguished at radius one and is its own Weierstrass
polynomial; lower coefficients need not have norm strictly less than one. Degree
zero division has zero remainder. Work at a radius outside `|ℚ_p×|`. Over the
dual-number ring of §3.2, divide `T⁴` by `T² - ε`; quotient `T² + ε` and
remainder zero give a test with nonreduced coefficients.

**Dependencies.** Layers 0–1 and §3.1. Neither Newton polygons nor affinoid geometry
is needed. Sources: [Martin] Definition 1.24, Lemma 1.26, Proposition 1.27,
Corollary 1.28 and the several-variable remark following it; [BGR] §§5.2.1–5.2.2
for the field specialisation.

## Layer 5 Algebraic structure of Tate algebras

Here `T_n = K⟨X₁,…,X_n⟩` at unit polyradius. All results hold for the field
generality of Convention 1. Unit-radius noetherianity is supplied by AdicSpaces
§0.5; the remaining Tate-specific algebraic and normed interfaces are targets here.

### 5.1 Weierstrass polynomials and distinguished coordinates

A Weierstrass polynomial in the chosen variable is monic with Gauss norm one.
Its nonleading coefficients have norms at most one. Monic factors of a
Weierstrass polynomial are Weierstrass polynomials. For such a polynomial `w`
of degree `s`, identify `T_n/(w)` with a finite free module over `T_(n-1)`
on `1, X, …, X^(s-1)`. Give the reduction-to-remainder map and multiplication
in these coordinates. A finite `T_n`-module killed by `w` is finite over
`T_(n-1)`.

For each nonzero `f ∈ T_n`, with `n > 0`, construct an isometric triangular
change of variables making `f` distinguished in a specified variable. Choose
the exponents from a bound on the finite set of dominant monomials; one change
works for a finite family of nonzero series. Prove the polynomial statement
first and lift it through reduction. The substitutions and their inverses are
the analytic maps of §2.2.

### 5.2 Noetherian, factorial and dimension theory

Consume noetherianity of `T_n` from AdicSpaces §0.5. Prove that it is a unique
factorisation domain, integrally closed and Jacobson, and has Krull dimension `n`.
The induction uses §5.1 and preparation.

The auxiliary Rückert interface of [BGR] §5.2.5 consists of an injective ring
map `φ : A[X] → B` and a family `W` of monic polynomials, closed under taking
monic factors, such that `A[X]/(w) → B/(φ(w))` is an isomorphism for each
`w ∈ W`, and every nonzero `b ∈ B` satisfies `u · α(b) = φ(w)` for some
ring automorphism `α`, unit `u` and `w ∈ W`. Build its finite-quotient descent
and the transfer of unique factorisation over domains. For the Jacobson
criterion, assume that `A` is Jacobson and the Jacobson radical of `B` is zero;
the latter condition is essential. Prove it for `T_n` using the finite-extension
points of §2.4: evaluation has field image and separates nonzero series. The
Rückert hypotheses then make each nonzero prime the intersection of the maximal
ideals above it. For `T_(n+1)` over `T_n`, use the Weierstrass polynomials of
§5.1 as `W`. These algebraic lemmas are targets here on native ring, ideal and
polynomial carriers.

Prove that maximal ideals of `T_n` are generated by polynomials and that their
residue fields are finite over `K`. Use the finite-quotient induction; no geometry
of general affinoids is an input. For the dimension calculation include the
coordinate prime chain and the upper bound from finite descent. Export these
results on both the Gauss-normed carrier and the completed Huber carrier of §6.2.

### 5.3 Closed ideals and finite-module subobjects

For a submodule `N ≤ T_n^m` with the maximum norm, prove closedness and strict
closedness: every coset has a representative of least norm. Give finite
generators of norm one for nonzero `N` such that each `x ∈ N` has an expression
in them with coefficient norms at most `‖x‖`. Treat `N = 0` with an empty
generating family. Ideals are the case `m = 1`.

The quotient norm on `T_n^m/N` is complete and its values lie in `|K|`.
For finite modules, prove equivalence of the complete quotient topologies from
different finite presentations and continuity/strictness of linear maps in
these topologies. Here strictness means that the quotient by the kernel maps
homeomorphically to the image with its subspace topology; record that the image
is closed. These Tate-specific conclusions are exposed to the general
finite-module topology API of functional analysis.

Include the supporting bald-subring and orthonormal-lifting lemmas of [Bosch]
§1.3, Proposition 3, Theorem 6 and Corollaries 7–10, unless already supplied by a cited module. Do not assume spherical
completeness of `K` or a general nearest-point theorem for Banach spaces.

### 5.4 Positive polyradii and finite presentations

Retain the Banach algebra at every positive polyradius. When
`r_i ∈ √|K×|`, choose `s_i ≥ 1` and `c_i ∈ K×` with `‖c_i‖ r_i^s_i = 1`.
The map from the unit Tate algebra sending `Y_i` to `c_i X_i^s_i` is injective
and finite. Construct the finite monomial module generators
`X^ν`, `0 ≤ ν_i < s_i`, with their coefficient/norm estimates, and prove
noetherianity in this case. This is an algebraic input to the classical
strict-affinoid criterion. The converse criterion belongs to rigid geometry,
where the required general affinoid maximum-modulus theorem is available.

**Checks.** `T_0 = K`, `dim T_1 = 1`, and `T_1/(X-a) ≃ K` for `‖a‖ ≤ 1`.
The quotient by `X - 1` has rank one; the quotient by the degree-zero polynomial
one is zero. For the polynomial `X²-p` over `ℚ_p`, the quotient has basis
`1, X`, with `X² = p`. Include the finite presentation at radius `√p`.

**Dependencies.** §§2.1–2.3, the maximum principle of §2.4, Layer 3 and Layer 4;
Mathlib polynomial, finite-module,
integrality and dimension APIs. Sources: [BGR] §§5.2.3–5.2.7 and 7.1.1;
[Bosch] §§1.2–1.3. The radius presentation is a weighted coefficient construction.

## Layer 6 Topological and adic series comparisons

### 6.1 Topological and subset-weighted restricted series

**Supplier contract: AdicSpaces §§0.4–0.5.** Consume the plain and subset-weighted
series on Tau Ceti's existing carriers, together with its §§0.1–0.3 topological-ring
notions and separated completion. In finitely many variables the required
interface is as follows. Retain Wedhorn's admissibility hypothesis
on each weight set `M_i`: the ideal generated by `M_i` is open. Include the
weighted polynomial topology, the coefficient description, density, completion,
renaming and iteration.

For complete Hausdorff coefficient rings and bounded admissible weight sets,
state the universal property for a continuous coefficient homomorphism `φ` to a
complete Hausdorff nonarchimedean target ring, with the set `⋃ᵢ {φ(m) b_i | m ∈ M_i}` power-bounded.
For finitely many variables in a commutative ring this is equivalent to
power-boundedness of each indicated set; pointwise power-boundedness alone is
not the hypothesis.
Consume uniqueness, naturality and compatibility with polynomial evaluation. In
the trivial-weight case this requires power-bounded variable images. General
topological localisation and its denominators remain in AdicSpaces §0.4.

### 6.2 Normed and completed comparisons

At unit polyradius, the normed and topological coefficient conditions agree.
Consume and extend the native ring and algebra equivalences; prove agreement
of their topologies, coefficients, polynomial embeddings and variables. For
complete coefficients, compare the separated completion as well. These
comparisons commute with evaluation, coefficient maps and iteration.

Give the weighted comparison when the chosen subsets encode radii through
multiplicative units, stating the conversion of weight bounds to norm bounds.
Arbitrary real polyradii remain the normed construction; a set of arbitrary
real numbers is not a Huber weight family. Transport the supplied Tate-algebra
noetherianity theorem along the unit-radius comparison, and identify the result
with AdicSpaces' field instance of strong noetherianness.

### 6.3 Series over an adic noetherian ring

**Supplier contract: AdicSpaces Part III §F0.1, `restricted-power-series-adic`.**
The following adic algebra is consumed, not reassigned. This roadmap proves
compatibility of its reductions and continuous maps with §6.2 wherever both
constructions apply.

For a commutative noetherian ring `A`, complete and separated for a finitely
generated ideal `I`, the supplier gives the native restricted-series carrier
`A{X₁,…,X_n}`, complete and separated for the ideals `I^m A{X}`, and
`A{X}/I^m A{X} ≃ (A/I^m)[X₁,…,X_n]` for `m ≥ 1`.
Its compatible reductions give the inverse-limit description, and its adic
completion theorem gives noetherianity. Consume the comparison of completed
and coefficient-subring carriers when proving the compatibility above.

For a complete separated linearly topologised commutative `A`-algebra with a
continuous structure map, arbitrary choices of the variables define a unique
continuous map out of `A{X}`. Explain the distinction from §6.1: ideal
neighbourhoods make every element of this target power-bounded. Include
coefficient base change and reduction compatibility wherever the stated
continuous map and completion hypotheses apply, without a flatness assertion.

### 6.4 Quotient and tensor interfaces

Expose coefficientwise kernels and bounded lifts from §0.2 as continuous maps
on the compared series carriers. For a finite free coefficient module, prove
that forming restricted series commutes with its finite-coordinate presentation;
for finite modules over `T_n`, use the strict finite presentations of §5.3.
Explicitly, a presentation `T_n^a → T_n^b → M → 0` induces
`T_n⟨Y⟩^a → T_n⟨Y⟩^b → M⟨Y⟩ → 0`, with the same presentation matrix,
where `M⟨Y⟩` is the module-valued construction of §0.3 with a complete quotient
norm on `M`. Prove exactness, the quotient topology and independence from the
chosen presentation. Use bounded lifts to establish surjectivity on restricted
coefficient families, rather than inferring it from algebraic surjectivity alone.

The general completed tensor product of Huber pairs and the theorem
`B ⊗̂_A A⟨X⟩_M ≃ B⟨X⟩_φ(M)` along an adic coefficient map are owned by
AdicSpaces Part II §R0.3, target `completed-tensor-restricted-power-series`.
The interfaces supplied here are the coefficient map, continuity, the series
universal property and the compatibility with constants, variables and
iteration. Consumers apply that theorem with its admissibility and adicness
hypotheses; this roadmap does not assume a completed-tensor comparison for an
arbitrary continuous map or construct the general tensor product itself.

**Checks.** For discrete `A`, restricted series are polynomials. For `A = ℤ_p`
with its `p`-adic topology, reduction of `ℤ_p⟨X⟩` modulo `p^m` is
`(ℤ/p^m)[X]`. The series `Σ X^n` lies in the full formal ring `ℤ_p⟦X⟧`
but not in `ℤ_p⟨X⟩`. The completion in zero variables is `Â`, and is
identified with `A` only under completeness and separatedness.

**Dependencies.** §6.1 consumes AdicSpaces §§0.1–0.3 and its existing weighted

## Layer 7 Open-disc, entire and overconvergent series

### 7.1 Series on an open disc

For `R₀ > 0`, define a series on the open disc of radius `R₀` by restrictedness
at every `0 < r < R₀`. It is a subring of the native formal series and carries
the topology generated by those Gauss norms. For complete coefficients it is
complete; give its description as compatible restricted series along a countable
sequence of radii increasing to `R₀`. Prove independence of that sequence,
polynomial density, coefficient continuity and evaluation at `‖x‖ < R₀`.

Bounded coefficient series lie in the open unit-disc algebra. Give the inclusion
of the bounded-coefficient algebra and its continuous evaluations at strict
unit-ball points. Surjectivity of this inclusion is not asserted. Translation,
derivatives, coefficient maps and substitution carry the radius conditions
obtained in Layers 1–2. The bounded and algebraic locally analytic Amice
transforms belong to functional analysis and the
[locally analytic distributions roadmap](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/854).
Measure theory, distribution topologies and geometric Mellin transforms are
consumers of the coefficient algebra, not inputs to its construction.

### 7.2 Entire series and polynomial division

A series is entire when it is restricted at every real radius `r > 0`. Define
the subring on native `PowerSeries`, prove closure under the algebraic operations,
rescaling and Hasse derivatives, and give evaluation in every complete normed
coefficient algebra as in §2.1. Prove completeness and polynomial density for
the topology of all Gauss norms, equivalently those of a sequence tending to
infinity. No single Banach norm represents this topology.

For a polynomial `P` with invertible leading coefficient and an entire `F`
over a complete ultrametric norm-one commutative ring, prove unique division
`F = P Q + B`, with `Q` entire and `B` a polynomial of degree less than
`deg P`. Normalise `P` to be monic, apply §4.2 at every sufficiently large
radius, and use uniqueness to identify the quotients and remainders. Recover
the norm identity when the leading coefficient is a multiplicative unit and
the radius makes the polynomial distinguished. Include the zero remainder
case, division by `T-a`, and `F(a)=0` if and only if `F=(T-a)Q` for an entire `Q`.

Prove that coefficient maps commute with entire division and with evaluation
under their boundedness hypotheses. The associated coprimality notion uses
`IsCoprime` in the entire-series ring; provide its basic algebraic consequences.

**Explicit monic division.** For monic `P` of degree `d`, if
`Σ b_k T^k = (P.reverse)⁻¹`, prove that the quotient has coefficients
`Σ_k coeff (n+d+k) F · b_k`. Establish convergence and agreement with the
unique quotient above, including `P=1`. Export the quotient, its entireness,
the division identity and the evaluation/linear-factor criterion as a common API.
For `F(0)=1` and `F(a)=0`, prove `a` a unit with inverse
`−Σ_n coeff (n+1) F · a^n` (`IsEntire.isUnit_of_evalAt_eq_zero`).

**Monic entire resultant.** Define `entireResultant P F` as the determinant
of multiplication by the remainder on the finite free algebra `R[T]/(P)`.
Prove invariance modulo `P`, multiplicativity in `F`, bounded base change,
agreement with the degree-bounded polynomial resultant, and
`Res(T−a,F)=F(a)`. Supply `Res(P,F)=PG+HF` with `G` entire and `H` a
polynomial of degree less than `deg P`. Deduce that the resultant is a unit
exactly when `P,F` are coprime in the entire ring. These identities form the
public API for entire reduction, multiplication and Bézout arguments.
For degree zero the quotient algebra has rank zero: `Res(1,F)=1`, even for
`F=0`. For positive-degree monic `P`, `Res(P,0)=Res(P,P)=0`.
Test `Res(T²,a+bT)=a²` over rings with nilpotents, and the quotient `T−a`
and remainder `(a²−b)T+ab` in division of `T³` by `T²+aT+b`.

**Normalised entire preparation.** If `F(0)=1` and `F` is distinguished at
radius `r` of degree `d` as in §4.3, deduce `F=PG`, where `P(0)=G(0)=1`,
`deg P=d`, the leading coefficient of `P` is a unit, and `G` is entire and
invertible in the radius-`r` restricted algebra. Specify that the monic
normalisation of `P` is the distinguished polynomial of §4.3. Prove
uniqueness with this normalisation, entire coprimality of `P,G`, and
compatibility at nested radii where the hypotheses hold. Obtain entirety of
`G` by entire polynomial division and uniqueness after restricted preparation.
The monic polynomial from dividing `T^d` by `F` is `T^d` minus its remainder;
it is not its reciprocal. A zero series is excluded by `F(0)=1`.

These generic interfaces supply compact-operator and Fredholm theory.
Coleman's spectral transform, Fredholm resolvents and projectors are operator
constructions and remain outside this roadmap.

### 7.3 Overconvergent series

**Supplier contract: AdicSpaces Part IV §F1.1.** For finite variables over `K`,
consume its algebra
`W_n = ⋃_{ρ>1} K⟨ρ⁻¹X₁,…,ρ⁻¹X_n⟩`
inside the native formal-series ring, its ring/algebra structure, inclusion
in `T_n`, polynomial density and completion for the restricted unit Gauss norm.
This roadmap proves the comparison with the condition using a positive
polyradius whose coordinates are all greater than one, and compatibility of
the derivative and substitution operations with that inclusion.

Give the correct radius control for substitution: for overconvergent `f` and
overconvergent inner series of unit Gauss norm at most one, choose a common
radius slightly greater than one on which substitution satisfies §2.2.
Prove compatibility of the resulting substitutions with inclusion in `T_n`.
Radii in `√|K×|` suffice in the union; radii in `|K×|` alone need not suffice
for a discretely valued field. General dagger algebras and their locally convex
fringe topology are supplied by AdicSpaces Part IV §F1.

**Checks.** `Σ X^n` is open-unit-disc analytic and not unit-radius restricted.
`Σ p^n X^n` is overconvergent over `ℚ_p` but is not entire: its boundary radius
is `p`. `Σ p^(n²) X^n` is entire. Polynomials belong to all three constructions.
Over `ℚ_p`, the exponential `Σ X^n/n!` has a finite convergence radius and
must not be used as an example of an entire series.

**Dependencies.** §§7.1 and 7.3 use Layers 0–2; §7.3 also consumes the
`W_n` contract of AdicSpaces Part IV §F1.1. Entire division also uses Layer 4.
Sources: [Colmez] §§I.4 and II for open-disc coefficient analysis;
[Coleman] Appendix A3 for entire division; [GK] §1 for overconvergent series.
The stated radius-limit and coefficient-map compatibilities are explicit
consequences of the radius estimates and completeness in Layers 0–2.

## Dependency order

The normed construction and its Weierstrass theory have this order:

```text
Mathlib coefficients and ultrametric analysis
  → Layer 0 → Layer 1 → evaluation and substitution in §§2.1–2.3
                   ↘ Layer 3 → Layer 4 → Layer 5
                        ↘          ↘
                        maximum    Strassmann and coefficient recovery in §2.4
                        modulus

Layers 0–2 → open-disc series
Layers 0–2 and Part IV §F1.1 → overconvergent analytic comparisons
Layers 0–2 and 4 → entire series and polynomial division

AdicSpaces topological algebra → §6.1
§6.1 and normed Layers 0–2 → §6.2
Part III §F0.1 adic restricted series and §6.2 → §6.3 comparisons
§0.2 and §5.3 → §6.4
```

The arrows to §2.4 are deliberate: none of Layers 3–5 uses Strassmann's theorem.
Layer 5 uses only its maximum principle, which follows from Layer 3 without
division. Thus this dependence introduces no cycle.
General affinoid geometry, Newton polygons and Fredholm theory consume the
results; they are not prerequisites. A dependency on a subsection does not
require completing the rest of that consumer's roadmap.

## Completion criteria

The roadmap is complete when the following interfaces agree on the specified
carriers and all layer checks are proved, using the named suppliers for the
contracts they own. This criterion does not require separate proofs of supplied
theorems.

1. Polynomial approximation, coefficient maps, normed restricted series and
   topological completions commute through the named comparisons.
2. Evaluation and analytic substitution have the stated universal properties,
   radius bounds, coefficient formulas and compatibility with formal operations.
3. Division and preparation work at arbitrary positive radii with general
   Banach-ring coefficients and a multiplicatively distinguished divisor;
   the existing multiplicative-norm and field versions are recovered.
4. The several-variable Tate-algebra structure and finite-module results are
   available in all characteristics on the common unit-radius carrier.
5. Adic restricted series reduce to polynomial rings, and the hypotheses
   distinguishing the topological and normed universal properties are explicit.
6. Open-disc, entire and overconvergent series share the radius/evaluation API
   while retaining their distinct defining conditions and topologies.

An implementation should exercise these through actual consumers: Newton
factorisation uses §4; the locally analytic disc model uses §§1.3 and 2;
radius-improving operators use §1.2; entire Fredholm algebra uses §7.2;
classical affinoid presentations use Layer 5; and Huber and dagger constructions
use Layers 6–7. Those applications do not become additional targets here.

# Rigid analytic geometry

Develop classical affinoid algebra and its comparison with rigid and adic
geometry over a complete nontrivially valued nonarchimedean field. The algebraic
milestones are Noether normalisation, the maximum modulus principle, integral
reduction and the Banach function algebra theorem. The geometric milestones
construct the classical G-site, rigid spaces and analytification, and compare
them with the shared adic-space programme. Coherent cohomology and proper
GAGA are transported from their named suppliers. Applications include proper
cohomology, analytic families and the geometry underlying eigenvarieties.

This README is the mathematical specification. Every target and check is
required. [Suggested.lean](Suggested.lean) fixes representative interfaces on
existing carriers; its admitted theorems are specifications, not proofs. It is
not an exhaustive checklist. Production modules import library mathematics,
not another roadmap's prototype.

## Conventions and foundations

1. Use `[NontriviallyNormedField K] [IsUltrametricDist K] [CompleteSpace K]`.
   Characteristic zero, discrete valuation and spherical completeness are
   additional hypotheses only where stated. Put
   `√|K×| = {r>0 : ∃ n≥1, ∃ c∈K×, r^n=|c|}`.
2. `Tₙ=K⟨X₁,…,Xₙ⟩` is the shared native restricted-series algebra at unit
   polyradius. Use coefficient-preserving equivalences for alternative
   presentations. Distinguished-variable conventions must agree with the
   supplier's iteration map, including the choice of first or last variable.
3. `IsAffinoidAlgebra K A` is a proposition: there is a surjective algebra
   map `Tₙ→A`. It does not select a norm or a topology. Quotient Gauss norms
   give complete algebra norms; §1 proves independence of their topology.
   Equivalent norms need not be equal or isometric.
4. Classical points are `MaximalSpectrum A`. The value `|f(x)|` uses the
   unique extension of `|·|` to the finite residue field `A/x`; no embedding
   into a chosen algebraic closure enters its definition. Define
   `|f|sup = sup_x |f(x)|`, with value zero for the zero algebra. Prove
   boundedness before using a real supremum.
5. Use `TauCeti.Huber.powerBoundedSubring` for `A°`, its native
   `topologicallyNilpotentIdeal` for `A°°`, and `Ã=A°/A°°`. Keep a presentation
   ring `A₀=π(Tₙ°)` separate from `A°`.
   Nilpotents remain in all algebra and sheaf carriers. Reduced affinoids
   are uniform; nonreduced affinoids use strong noetherianness for sheafiness.
6. Rational fractions are `A⟨f/g⟩=A⟨T⟩/(gTᵢ−fᵢ)` with `(g,f₁,…,fₘ)=A`.
   Rational domains require `|g(x)|≠0` and `|fᵢ(x)|≤|g(x)|`.
   All localisation and tensor comparisons commute with structure maps.
7. Use native `Ideal`, `Submodule`, `Module.Finite`, `Module.Projective`,
   tensor products, continuous linear maps, schemes, sites, sheaves and
   sheaf cohomology. An arbitrary module has an algebraic Čech complex;
   Banach topologies and strictness are asserted for finite modules.
8. Classical points and adic points are different carriers. The comparison
   preserves rational traces and ringed sites, not all underlying points.
   In particular, a higher-rank condition `v(T)<1` is not by itself a
   description of the adic image of the rigid open unit disc.

in finite extensions: include all finite residue fields and their finite
splitting extensions. A decomposition is continuously split and
operator-stable; its first summand is finite projective and annihilated
by a monic such `Q` with unit constant term. Every polynomial satisfying
the same conditions acts invertibly on the complementary summand. Its
continuous projector has the specified image and kernel and commutes with
the operator. Construct it from the continuous complementary-submodule
projection, independently of Fredholm theory. CompactOperators supplies
Riesz summands; LAD §4.16 proves the numerical comparison for a separated
Fredholm factor. Existence at every cutoff over an arbitrary affinoid
family is not asserted.

For `r=|p|^h` this means eigenvalue valuation `≤h`, including equality.
It concerns annihilator roots; the roots of `det(1−TU)` are reciprocals.
LAD §4.16 owns `slopeCriterion_classical_iff_geometric`, numerical
normalisation, functoriality and uniqueness, using §2's supremum theorem.
Its coefficient test for monic `Q=ΣaⱼXʲ` with unit `a₀` is
`|aⱼ/a₀|sup rʲ≤1` for every `j`; do not reprove that comparison here.
Sources: [Urban] §2.3; LAD §4.16; CompactOperators Layer 3.

**Checks.** For `c∈K×` and a finite projective Banach module, `c·id` with `|c|=r`
belongs wholly to the first summand; the zero operator has zero first
summand. For `0<|c|<1`, `X−c` fails the `r=1`
condition, whereas `1−cT` passes its root test. Actual polynomial
annihilation is required even over a nonreduced base; pointwise tests alone
cannot detect nilpotent endomorphisms.

### 7.3 Coherence, identity principle and quasi-Stein spaces

**Supplier contracts: Part III R3.2–R3.4.** Finite modules
and coherent sheaves on `Sp A` are equivalent via the associated-module
functor and global sections, compatibly with restriction, tensor products
and exact sequences. Include coherent ideals/closed subspaces, finite
algebras/finite morphisms and affinoid acyclicity.

**Classical identity principle (supplied to Part II R1.9).** On a connected
normal rigid space, any nonempty admissible open is
analytically Zariski dense. Restriction is injective for functions and
finite locally free sheaves. Do not assert this for arbitrary coherent
sheaves supported away from the open, or omit normality.

**Supplier contract: Part III R3.4.** A quasi-Stein exhaustion is countable,
increasing, admissible and affinoid,
with dense restrictions of coordinate rings. Prove density for coherent
sections, generation on each member by global sections and vanishing of
higher coherent cohomology. No relative-compactness condition or global
finite generating set is implicit. Include the relative version when
inverse images of affinoid opens are quasi-Stein. Sources: [Kiehl-AB];
[Conrad] §§1–2; Part III R3.4.

### 7.4 Proper mapping, strictness and base change

**Supplier contract: Part III R3.6.** For Kiehl-proper `f:X→Sp A` and
coherent `F`, prove `M^i=H^i(X,F)` finite over `A`, all higher direct
images coherent, and closed-range differentials for finite affinoid Čech
complexes computing this cohomology. Use the finite inner-cover definition
of properness, with its separatedness and base-change properties. Neither
smoothness nor reducedness is assumed.

For an affinoid subdomain `Sp B→Sp A` or a finite flat affinoid map,
prove the canonical base-change isomorphism
`B⊗_A M^i ≃ H^i(X_B,F_B)`. For every complete isometric `L/K`, prove
the same with `B=A_L`; compare its algebraic tensor with the completed
field tensor using §1.3. Maps are induced by pullback and scalar action
and commute with connecting homomorphisms. Arbitrary nonflat base change
does not follow. Source: [Kiehl-E] Satz 2.6, Satz 3.5 and §3;
Part III R3.6.

### 7.5 Principal filtrations and formal functions

For the same `f,F`, `a∈A`, and `i≥0`, let

`R_n=ker(M^i→H^i(X,F/a^nF))`, for `n≥0`.

Require `R_0=M^i`, decreasingness, `a^nM^i⊆R_n`,
`aR_n⊆R_(n+1)`, and equality in the last inclusion for all sufficiently
large `n`. Prove a uniform shift `d` with `R_(n+d)⊆a^nM^i` for every
`n`. Also prove a uniform shift `e` such that the transition

`H^i(X,F/a^(n+e)F)→H^i(X,F/a^nF)`

has image in the image of `M^i`. Thus both the kernel and cokernel systems
of `M^i/a^nM^i→H^i(X,F/a^nF)` are pro-zero; the two shifts need not
coincide. Include the transition maps, not just abstract isomorphic limits.
Source: [Kiehl-E] Theorem 3.4 and the argument preceding Theorem 3.7.

For every ideal `J⊆A`, prove the canonical formal-functions isomorphism
`(M^i)^∧_J ≃ lim_n H^i(X,F/J^nF)`, with naturality. The general-ideal
argument is required and uses the noetherian filtration/Artin–Rees inputs;
it is not obtained by merely relabelling `a` as `J`. This is ideal-adic
completion, not Banach completion. The proof and its classical/adic forms
share Part III's cohomology implementation.

**Checks.** For `a=0`, `R_0=M^i` and `R_n=0` for `n≥1`; for `a=1`,
`R_n=M^i` and quotient cohomology is zero. For the identity of `Sp A` in
degree zero, `R_n=a^nM`. On `ℙ¹`, compute `H⁰(𝒪)=K`, `H¹(𝒪)=0`
and compare the Čech, sheaf and base-change maps.

## Layer 8: analytification and rigid–adic comparison

### 8.1 Analytification, local rings and components

Construct the classical rigid analytification consumed by Part II R1.
Construct absolute
analytification and relative analytification over `Sp A` for schemes
locally of finite type over `Spec A`. The latter schemes need not be
locally of finite type over `K`. Include the universal property, points,
fibre products, immersions and finite maps, with their canonical comparison
maps. Build relative affine charts using completed presentations and glue
them. The flat local comparison gives exact pullback; the coherent-sheaf
and proper GAGA comparisons are Part III R3.7's targets.

For a classical analytic point `x` over a closed point `x₀`, identify
the completed local rings, compatibly with their local map. Prove that
`𝒪_{X,x₀}` is reduced, respectively normal, iff `𝒪_{X^an,x}` is.
Use §1.2 and Layers 3–4 for affinoid and analytic excellence, the shared
permanence theorems for finite-type schemes over affinoids, and the
completion criteria; normal here means an integrally closed local
domain. Deduce the global equivalences for reducedness and normality.
Also retain connectedness and irreducible-component comparisons, with
components carrying their reduced induced structures. Sources: [Conrad]
§1 and Appendix A; SchemeAndStackFoundations' excellence input.

**Checks.** The affine line at zero and the dual-number thickening. Over
a field of characteristic different from two, the origin on
`y²=x²(x+1)` has an algebraic local domain but an analytic germ with two
branches, using a convergent square root of `1+x` on a small disc.
Local integrality is therefore not an additional equivalence. Completion
isomorphisms do not alone justify a local-domain assertion.

### 8.2 Classical points and constructible density

Construct `Max A→Spa(A,A°)`, prove injectivity, and identify rational
traces and their coordinate rings. In `Spv A`, let `L_A` consist of the
valuations at most one on `A°` and strictly less than one on `A°°`.
Prove its equality with the constructible closure of the classical points;
deduce their constructible density in `Spa(A,A°)`. Constructible subsets
are determined by their classical traces. Prove the finite rational-cover
criterion through this comparison. Sources: [Huber-CV] Theorem 4.1,
Corollary 4.2; Part II R1.7's classical-point contract.

**Checks.** Classical points of the disc, the nonclassical Gauss point,
and `|T|≤|ϖ|`. A rank-two point just below the Gauss point can have
`v(T)<1` but `v(T)^n>|ϖ|` for every `n≥1`; it is outside the adic
open `⋃_n{|T|^n≤|ϖ|}` corresponding to the rigid open disc. Its
singleton is proconstructible, not constructible: density does not say
arbitrary subsets are determined by classical points.

### 8.3 The image of the rigid–adic functor

Construct the shared functor `r(Sp A)=Spa(A,A°)` and prove compatibility with
gluing, products, the structure sheaf and its ringed topos. It is fully
faithful on rigid spaces. Adic spaces locally of finite type over
`Spa(K,K°)` are locally images of affinoids. Restricted to quasi-separated
objects, `r` is an equivalence with quasi-separated adic spaces locally of
finite type. Prove `r(X)` affinoid iff `X` affinoid. Source: [Huber-FR]
Proposition 4.5; Part II R1.7.

**Checks.** Two rigid closed discs glued along the rigid open disc give
a non-quasi-separated example: in its adic image the two rank-two boundary
points from §8.2 remain distinct. Over algebraically closed `K`, also
construct the example of two adic discs glued along the complement
of the closure of the Gauss point; it is locally of finite type but is
not in the global image. These distinguish local image, full faithfulness
and essential surjectivity. Check the affinoid case and empty space.

Part II owns the further separatedness, properness and partial-properness
comparisons with its adic morphism classes, using §6.3's classical notions
and `r`. Consume its converses with their discrete-valuation hypotheses
and its separately stated locally quasi-finite exception; do not infer
an unqualified converse from the forward comparison.

### 8.4 Proper GAGA

**Supplier contract: Part III R3.7.** For a scheme proper over an
affinoid base, require the exact tensor-compatible equivalence of coherent
sheaves under analytification and the canonical `A`-linear cohomology
comparison in every degree. Include compatibility of higher direct images
with analytification for a proper morphism, even if the target is not
proper. Degree-zero maps are pullback/adjunction maps and the higher ones
extend them functorially.

**Checks.** `ℙ¹`, its line bundles and finite schemes including nilpotent
thickenings. Nonproper affine-line analytification has nonpolynomial global
functions and does not satisfy an unrestricted GAGA statement. Étale and
pro-étale comparisons are owned by Part IV and AdicEtaleGeometry; this
roadmap asserts no additional equivalence of those topoi.

## Dependency order and completion

1. Import the shared Tate and Banach foundations; prove characteristic-free
   weak stability and its Japanese application.
2. Prove affinoid normalisation and topology independently of geometry,
   then supremum and integral theory. The polyradius converse follows
   the value-group theorem; it is not needed to prove that theorem.
3. Compare the algebra with Part II's carriers, localisations, tensors
   and spectral data. General G-site theory is independent of this step.
4. Construct classical subdomains, Tate acyclicity, the G-site and rigid
   category, then rigid analytification and the rigid–adic functor. Use
   foundational adic results, not Part II's consumers of these classical
   constructions. Establish the classical properness predicates.
5. Transport Part III's coherent, quasi-Stein, proper-cohomology and GAGA
   results through the ringed-site equivalence. Prove the elementary
   numerical decomposition and projection of §7.2 independently; LAD then
   supplies the geometric and Fredholm-window comparisons.

Completion requires all stated generalities, all canonical-map compatibility
theorems and every check above. There must be one production definition of
each shared series, operator, tensor and geometric object. Compile the
actual modules and audit the transitive axioms of their capstone theorems;
only `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound` are accepted. An
elaborating roadmap prototype is not a proof or an implementation milestone.

# Roadmap: scheme, stack, cohomology and intersection foundations

**Summary.** This roadmap is the general algebraic geometry that the arithmetic roadmaps stand on: relative Proj, henselian pairs and excellent rings; descent, algebraic spaces, torsors and algebraic stacks; cohomology on the Zariski, Nisnevich, étale, fppf and pro-étale sites with coherent duality and Brauer groups; curves, divisors and Picard functors; deformations, formal schemes, algebraization and de Jong's alterations; and Chow groups with Chern classes, Riemann–Roch and the Hodge index theorem. We want it because Mathlib provides schemes, their morphisms and much of the abstract categorical infrastructure, but the stacks, site cohomology, duality and alterations needed for Shimura varieties, moduli of curves and abelian varieties, Galois representations in étale cohomology and the comparison theorems of p-adic Hodge theory still require substantial shared development. Rather than let each arithmetic roadmap rebuild a private version, this roadmap fixes one set of carriers and statements that the others import and cite.

This roadmap builds the general algebraic geometry that the arithmetic roadmaps of Tau Ceti stand
on and that neither Mathlib nor another Tau Ceti roadmap owns. From Mathlib's `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme`,
its morphism classes and its big and small sites, and from the Tau Ceti library's quasi-coherent
algebras, line-bundle classes, divisors and models of curves, it builds six layers: the
scheme-theoretic base (relative Proj, extension of coherent sheaves, the local structure of morphisms
locally of finite type, henselization of pairs, excellent rings, perfect schemes, ideal sheaves);
descent, algebraic spaces, torsors, quotients and algebraic stacks; sheaf cohomology on sites with
the comparison of the Zariski, Nisnevich, étale, fppf and pro-étale topologies, coherent Grothendieck
duality, Brauer groups and equivariant cohomology; the curve, divisor and Picard theory that glues the
existing curve roadmaps together; infinitesimal deformations, formal schemes and algebraization,
modifications, the moduli stack of stable pointed curves and de Jong's alterations; and Chow groups
with Chern classes, intersection products, Riemann–Roch and the Hodge index theorem. Its end theorems
are the henselization of a pair with its universal property (Layer 0), Artin's bootstrap theorem and
the Keel–Mori theorem (Layer 1), coherent Grothendieck duality and the Brauer class of an Azumaya
algebra (Layer 2), the Picard torsors of a curve without a rational point (Layer 3), Schlessinger's
theorem, Grothendieck's existence theorem for coherent modules, algebraization of compatible
morphisms and de Jong's alteration theorems
(Layer 4), and Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch, the Hodge index theorem and the Weil bound for curves over
finite fields (Layer 5). Every object is defined on Mathlib's `Scheme`; every theorem names its
hypotheses.

| Layer | Title | What it delivers |
|---|---|---|
| [0](#layer-0-schemes-and-morphisms) | Schemes and morphisms | direct-image algebras and relative Proj, coherent extension and Hartogs, dimension theory and limits, henselization of pairs, catenary, Cohen–Macaulay, Nagata and excellent rings, perfect schemes and universal homeomorphisms, étale topological invariance (§0.23a), scheme Frobenius (§0.29), ideal-sheaf comparisons |
| [1](#layer-1-descent-algebraic-spaces-and-stacks) | Descent, algebraic spaces and stacks | fpqc/fppf descent, algebraic spaces, group spaces, groupoids, torsors and quotients, algebraic and Deligne–Mumford stacks, moduli spaces, Galois gerbs |
| [2](#layer-2-sites-and-scheme-cohomology) | Sites and scheme cohomology | site cohomology and torsors, quasi-coherent cohomology and supports, topology comparisons, the Nisnevich site, pro-étale site foundations, coherent duality, Brauer groups, equivariant cohomology |
| [3](#layer-3-curves-divisors-and-picard-objects) | Curves, divisors and Picard objects | genus checks, degrees and duality for vector bundles on curves, Picard groups, groupoids, norms and torsors, Picard stacks and Abel maps |
| [4](#layer-4-deformations-formal-schemes-models-and-alterations) | Deformations, formal schemes, models and alterations | thickenings and lifting, deformation functors, hulls and obstruction theories, adic thickening systems and algebraization, modifications and strict transforms, stable pointed curves, alterations |
| 5 | Intersection theory and Riemann–Roch | Chow groups, pushforward and pullback, Chern classes, Gysin maps and intersection products, K-theoretic pushforward and Riemann–Roch, surfaces and the Weil bound |

Construction follows the `*Needs:*` clauses rather than subsection numbers. The prerequisite
stages include §0.17 before §0.6 and the Cohen–Macaulay theorem of §0.16;
§0.21 before §§0.15,0.19; §0.29 before §§0.24–0.26; and §1.3 before §1.2.
Build the site and cohomology inputs §§2.1–2.3,2.6,2.9,2.12,2.10–2.11 before
§1.15's torsor-class and Picard comparisons. In §4.11, construct modification predicates
and their elementary API before §4.12's Chow lemma; its strict-transform package uses
supported sections and the existing blow-up API. In Layer 5, build pushforward, flat
pullback and localization (§5.2), then projective bundles (§5.4), then the affine-bundle
isomorphism of §5.2, then Gysin maps and products (§§5.5–5.6). The blow-up decomposition
of §5.7 precedes GRR (§5.8).

## Scope and ownership

The geometric Chow groups and all operations graded by absolute closure dimension
are restricted to schemes locally of finite type over a fixed field, with maps over
that field (§5). General bases, including DVRs, need a different grading and are
outside this API. Section 4.6 uses Mathlib's two-term cotangent complex for algebra
lift classes with an existing flat lift. The non-affine Brauer comparison of §2.22 includes
the construction of the gerbe of local splittings.


**This roadmap owns** the shared scheme-, space-, site- and coherent-sheaf foundations: the general
relative Proj and its comparison with the finitely generated case, extension of coherent modules,
henselization of pairs, the catenary, Cohen–Macaulay, Nagata and excellent packages, perfect schemes
and perfection, the universal-homeomorphism equivalence of small étale sites (§0.23a),
absolute, relative, iterated and finite-field scheme Frobenius with coherent twists (§0.29),
the ideal-sheaf comparison API, algebraic spaces with their small étale sites,
group algebraic spaces, groupoids, torsors and their classes, categorical and geometric quotient predicates,
projective quotients by finite groups, algebraic stacks, moduli spaces, Galois gerbs, the
functoriality of sheaf cohomology on sites, the comparison of the topologies of a scheme with the coefficient sheaves `𝔾_a`, `𝔾_m`, `μ_n`, the
Nisnevich site, the pro-étale site foundations (replete topoi, w-contractible covers,
left-completeness), coherent Grothendieck duality in the generality of the Stacks Project, the Brauer
group of a scheme, abelian-extension boundaries, equivariant sheaf cohomology, the curve and Picard theory that no curve roadmap
states, formal deformation theory with elementary obstruction theories, adic thickening systems, coherent existence and algebraization of compatible morphisms, modifications,
strict transforms and alterations, the moduli stack of stable pointed curves, Chow groups,
Chern classes, refined Gysin maps, intersection products, a K-theoretic pushforward for
Riemann–Roch, and surfaces. Formal geometry here uses chosen ideals and level-preserving adic thickening
systems. Comparison with the category of topologically locally ringed formal schemes and
independence from ideals of definition are outside this scope. Polarized algebraization of
formal schemes and a category equivalence for polarized systems are also outside this scope.

**Owned elsewhere and consumed here.** The following objects have one owner; this roadmap states
comparisons to them and never a second carrier.

- *Sheaves of modules, locally free sheaves, tensor, dual, determinant, symmetric and exterior
  powers, quasi-coherent algebras, relative Spec and its anti-equivalence, graded algebras and the
  symmetric algebra*: Tau Ceti `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.QuasicoherentAlgebra`,
  `CategoryTheory.CommMon.relativeSpec`, `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.relativeSpec`,
  `SheafOfModules.dual`, `SheafOfModules.monoidalClosed`, and
  [AlgebraicVectorBundles](../AlgebraicVectorBundles/README.md) Layers L0A–L2B. A finite locally
  free sheaf of rank `r` is Mathlib's `SheafOfModules.IsLocallyFree` together with
  AlgebraicVectorBundles L0B's rank predicate `isFiniteLocallyFreeOfRank`; the degree theory of
  Layer 3 and the Chern classes of Layer 5 are stated on that predicate. AlgebraicVectorBundles
  leaves projective bundles and Chern classes to successors; they are Layer 5 here.
- *Relative Proj of a finitely generated graded quasi-coherent algebra, projective morphisms,
  relative ampleness, the relative dualising sheaf of a proper flat finitely presented Gorenstein
  curve (contract J-B / SR-2), the curve-family specialisations of coherent higher direct images and
  base change (the general proper-coherence API is JacobianChallenge Layer C), finite
  extensions of discrete valuation rings (`TauCeti.FiniteDVRExtension`), models over a discrete
  valuation ring, nodal local models over a discrete valuation ring, prestable, semistable and
  stable families, blow-ups, admissible blow-ups, strict transforms of closed subschemes along
  blow-ups and intersection numbers on regular arithmetic surfaces, effective étale descent of
  polarised schemes*: [StableReduction](../StableReduction/README.md) Layers 0–4. Layer 0 here
  states relative Proj for an arbitrary graded quasi-coherent algebra with the comparison to
  StableReduction's; Layer 4 states strict transforms along arbitrary modifications with the
  comparison to StableReduction's along blow-ups, and the Noetherian-base nodal local structure with
  the comparison to StableReduction's over a discrete valuation ring.
- *Group objects* (the convention `GrpObj (Over.mk f)` in `Over S`), *finite locally free group
  schemes, finite affine invariant quotients (`TauCeti.AffineInvariantQuotient.quotient` and
  `.projection`), finite étale schemes and Galois sets, effective descent of affine schemes and
  of finite locally free schemes along a faithfully flat morphism, polarised descent of projective
  curves, Weil restriction, the
  relative Grassmannian, strict henselization and the openness of the regular locus of a finite-type

The sites, the coefficient sheaves `𝔾_a`, `𝔾_m`, `μ_n`, Hilbert 90, the Kummer and Artin–Schreier
sequences, `𝔾_m` on curves, Tsen and Brauer groups remain owned here, together with the Galois,
limit, Hochschild–Serre, Gabber and hypercovering theorems for arbitrary abelian sheaves and the
pro-étale site foundations. In particular, §§2.1–2.2 own `Sheaf.derivedPushforward`,
`Sheaf.higherDirectImage` and `leray_spectral_sequence` for generic sites and abelian D⁺ complexes.
Scheme compactifications, Nagata existence and common refinements are constructed downstream
in EtaleCohomologyFoundations. The full cotangent complex, polynomial resolutions, general
square-zero obstruction API and derived module algebra are constructed downstream in
DerivedModuleAlgebra. These are client developments of the foundations here, not inputs to
this roadmap. Section 2.19 constructs coherent upper shriek locally and compares it with
any given open-proper factorization.
Finite-module twists, finite and adic étale comparisons, trace formulas, complex comparison,
Tate modules and étale cycle classes are downstream applications of these foundations;
they are not prerequisites for any target here. Section 2.9 exports `muEtale`, and §2.11
exports its Kummer sequence. The downstream twist owner identifies its degree-one twist
with this sheaf for invertible order.

**Interfaces consumed by the arithmetic roadmaps.** The crystalline, prismatic, analytic and ℓ-adic
roadmaps consume this roadmap through comparison maps whose theorems they own; this roadmap fixes only
its side of each interface. (i) Cohomology is Mathlib's `Sheaf.H` on the named site; the pro-étale
ℓ-adic coefficient is `Scheme.ellAdicSheaf`, not a discrete constant sheaf; `Br′(X)` is the torsion of
`H²_ét(X, 𝔾_m)`, distinct from the Azumaya Brauer group until §2.22's comparison applies
(Bhatt–Scholze 2014, Def. 6.8.1, Lemma 6.8.2). (ii) Over `ℂ`, algebraic de Rham to Betti cohomology
(Grothendieck 1966, Thm. 1′) and finite-coefficient étale to Betti cohomology with its relative form
(SGA 4 XVI, Thm. 4.1) are taken on Layer 2's sites; over `ℝ` the Galois-equivariant Betti groups carry
the sign twist (Benoist–Wittenberg 2020, §1.1; Benoist 2019, (1.1) and (2.16)). (iii) Let `A` be an adic space, `S` a scheme and
`A → S` a morphism of locally ringed spaces. For schemes `X, Y` locally of finite type over `S`,
a proper `S`-morphism `f : X → Y`, a torsion ring `Λ` and `K ∈ D⁺(X_ét, Λ)`, form
`X^ad = X ×_S A`, `Y^ad = Y ×_S A` with site maps `φ_X, φ_Y`. The canonical map
`φ_Y^* Rf_* K → Rf^ad_* φ_X^* K` is an isomorphism (R. Huber, *Étale Cohomology of Rigid Analytic
Varieties and Adic Spaces*, setup 3.7.1, p. 225, Theorem 3.7.2, p. 226). This proper comparison
allows arbitrary torsion coefficients, including residue-characteristic torsion; the bounded-below
condition on `K` is part of the statement. The scheme–adic fibre products and site maps belong to
the analytic roadmap, so this is a README-only interface here. Comparisons with diamonds in
characteristic `p` are separate (Scholze 2017, §§26–27). (iv) `R lim_n RΓ_ét(X, ℤ/ℓⁿ)` with its Galois action is compared
with pro-étale `ℤ_ℓ`-cohomology by derived completeness, and `lim H^q` replaces `H^q R lim` only under a
stated `lim¹` vanishing (Bhatt–Scholze 2014, Def. 3.4.1, Prop. 3.4.2, Cor. 5.1.6). (v) Prismatic,
crystalline and `A_inf` specializations (Bhatt–Scholze 2022, Thm. 1.8; Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze 2018,
Thms. 14.3–14.5) and the `B_dR` comparison with its trace-normalized period line (Betts–Stix,
Props. 3.19–3.21) are consumed with derived tensor products and Frobenius twists written out.
(vi) Cycle classes `cl^r : CH^r(X) → H^{2r}_ét(X, Λ(r))`, `X` smooth over a perfect field and `n`
invertible, are defined by the ℓ-adic roadmaps on §5.1 and §5.6 (Milne LEC, §23, Thm. 23.4), compatible
with products, proper pushforward and Gysin maps.

## Conventions

1. Rings are commutative with identity; the zero ring is allowed unless a target excludes it.
   Schemes, morphisms and opens are Mathlib's `Scheme`, `Scheme.Hom`, `Scheme.Opens` in a fixed
   universe `u`; "Noetherian", "separated", "proper" and "smooth" are hypotheses written on the
   target that needs them, never folded into a definition.
2. Big sites are Mathlib's `zariskiTopology ≤ etaleTopology ≤ fppfTopology ≤ fpqcTopology` on the
   category of schemes (slices `Over S` for a base); small sites are `X.Etale` with
   `Scheme.smallEtaleTopology`, and `X.ProEt` with `Scheme.ProEt.topology`. Cohomology is Mathlib's
   `Sheaf.H`; for `O_X`-modules it is Tau Ceti's `Scheme.Modules.Cohomology`. Every cohomological
   statement says which coefficient regime it is in (`𝔾_m` and smooth groups, `p`-torsion in
   characteristic `p`, quasi-coherent, arbitrary abelian sheaves) and never transports a result across
   regimes without a named comparison. Finite and adic coefficient extensions are downstream
   consumers; their comparisons retain finite Tor amplitude and coherent derived reductions.
3. Stacks are pseudofunctors with Mathlib's `IsStack`; representability of a morphism of presheaves
   means by schemes, of stacks by algebraic spaces; torsors are fppf torsors; group actions are on the
   left; group objects are `GrpObj` in the cartesian monoidal categories `Over S` (schemes, the
   ModularCurves convention) and `Over h_S` (algebraic spaces).
4. The genus of a proper curve is `dim H¹(X, O_X)`; the degree of a locally free sheaf of rank `r` is
   `χ(E) − r·χ(O_X)`. Thickenings are closed immersions surjective on points; modifications are
   proper birational, alterations proper dominant and generically finite. Chow groups are graded by
   dimension, measured by `Order.height x` for the closure of a scheme point `x`;
   `Order.coheight x` measures codimension. Intersection products on smooth varieties are graded
   by codimension.
5. Names live under `TauCetiRoadmap.SchemeAndStackFoundations`, in namespaces named after the
   strand (`Henselization`, `Excellence`, `IdealPullback`, `Spaces`, `Groups`, `Torsor`,
   `Nisnevich`, `Coherent`, `Brauer`, `Curve`, `Picard`, `Formal`, `Deformation`, `IsAlteration`,
   `Chow`, among others); the names proposed for the library are the ones in the subsections
   below, under `AlgebraicGeometry` for direct extensions of Mathlib objects (relative Proj,
   thickenings, adic thickening systems, alterations) and under `TauCeti` for the ring-theoretic
   and curve strands. `Suggested.lean` contains the key definitions with real bodies and the
   headline theorems that are statable at the pins, with some Checks as `example`s; each
   subsection lists its declarations there on a *Lean:* line. This document names every API item
   and every test; every target or test named here and absent from `Suggested.lean` is specified
   in this README only and is equally required. Proposed names of such README-only items inside
   the strands of `Suggested.lean` are set in italics (for example *Torsor.hom_isIso*), so that
   they are not mistaken for declarations of that file.
6. Every definition subsection lists its unit tests under **Checks**: a genuine construction that
   satisfies the definition, a degenerate or edge case, a false positive obtained by dropping one
   essential clause of the definition, and, where a carrier is shared with a library or another
   roadmap, a compatibility test against that carrier. A wrong definition fails at least one of them.

## How to read the build

The layer numbers organize the subject; the prerequisite stages above and each `*Needs:*`
clause give the construction order. Layer 0 is scheme theory and commutative algebra on
Mathlib's carriers and supplies every later layer. Layer 1 builds algebraic spaces on the big
fppf site, then group spaces, torsors,
quotients and stacks; it needs Layer 0 only for the henselian and excellent packages used in its
examples. Layer 2 is the cohomology layer: its first half (§§2.1–2.17) is site-theoretic and needs
Layer 1 only through the torsor carrier, its second half (§§2.18–2.23) is coherent and needs Layer 0's
Cohen–Macaulay package. Layer 3 assembles the curve roadmaps and adds what they lack; it needs
Layer 2's Hilbert 90 and duality. Layer 4 needs Layer 0 (excellence, henselian pairs), Layer 1
(stacks, for the moduli of stable curves), Layer 2 (Ext groups and torsors of lifts) and Layer 3
(Picard schemes of curves). Layer 5 needs Layer 0's relative Proj, Layer 2's coherent duality,
Layer 3's degrees and Layer 4's blow-ups and deformation to the normal cone. Construction
prerequisites can have higher subsection numbers; comparison-only references are identified
as comparisons. In particular, construct groupoids before quotients, the Nisnevich site
before topology comparisons, and homotopy invariance before refined Gysin maps.

## Layer 0: schemes and morphisms

The scheme-theoretic base of the roadmap, following the Stacks Project's chapters on constructions,
morphisms and commutative algebra. Mathlib provides schemes, affine schemes, quasi-coherent modules,
gluing, fibre products and the named morphism classes with their base-change stability; Tau Ceti and
AlgebraicVectorBundles provide quasi-coherent algebras, the relative spectrum and graded algebras.
Layer 0 adds the sheaf comparison and direct-image algebras, the general relative Proj compared with
StableReduction's finitely generated case, extension of coherent sheaves and Hartogs statements, the
dimension theory and limit theory of morphisms locally of finite type, henselization of pairs as a
small colimit of étale neighbourhoods, the catenary, Cohen–Macaulay, Nagata and excellent packages,
perfect schemes and perfection, flat base change of annihilators and cokernels, and the ideal-sheaf
comparison API that closed immersions need.

**Conventions of this layer.** `S_aff` is Mathlib's small affine Zariski site `S.AffineZariskiSite`.
A quasi-coherent algebra is Tau Ceti's `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.QuasicoherentAlgebra` (a commutative
monoid in `S.Modules` with quasi-coherent underlying module), a graded one is AlgebraicVectorBundles
L2A's `GradedQuasicoherentAlgebra`; gradings are indexed by `ℕ` with `O_S` in degree zero. Henselian
pairs are Mathlib's `HenselianRing R I`; regular rings are `IsRegularRing`; regular sequences are
`RingTheory.Sequence.IsRegular`. Perfection of an `𝔽_p`-algebra is Mathlib's colimit-along-Frobenius
`PerfectClosure`, never the inverse-limit `Perfection`. Weil restriction is ModularCurves 0F; strict
henselization, miracle flatness and the openness of the regular locus are ModularCurves 4D; coherent
sheaves are JacobianChallenge Layer B's `FinitelyPresentedSheaf`.

### 0.1 Quasi-coherent algebras as sheaves of algebras, and direct-image algebras

Construct, for a quasi-coherent `O_S`-algebra `A`, the coequifibered presheaf of rings on `S_aff`
that Mathlib's relative gluing consumes, `U ↦ A(U)` with the localisation maps
`CommMon.isLocalization_basicOpen`, and prove the comparison `sectionsPresheaf_iso`: the sheaf of
algebras it generates is `A` itself as a sheaf of `O_S`-algebras, naturally in `A` (Stacks, Situation
27.3.1 (01LM), Lemma 27.3.2 (01LN)). Define `pushforwardAlgebra f`, the direct image `f_* O_X` for
`f : X → S` quasi-compact and quasi-separated, as a quasi-coherent `O_S`-algebra (the direct image of
a quasi-coherent module along such an `f` is quasi-coherent by Stacks, Lemma 26.24.1 (01LC)), and
prove `pushforwardAlgebra_affine`: for `f` affine it is AlgebraicVectorBundles L1A's
`affineFunctions`, and `pushforwardAlgebra_baseChange`: for a flat `g : S' → S` with base change
`f' : X' → S'`, the base change map `g^* f_* O_X → f'_* O_{X'}` is an isomorphism of
`O_{S'}`-algebras (Stacks, Lemma 30.5.2 (02KH), the case `i = 0`).
*Needs:* Tau Ceti `QuasicoherentAlgebra`, `CommMon.sectionsPresheaf`; AlgebraicVectorBundles L1A;
Mathlib `QuasiCompact`, `QuasiSeparated`.

**Checks.**
- `sectionsPresheaf_structureSheaf`: for `A = O_S` the presheaf is `U ↦ Γ(U, O_S)` and the
  comparison is the identity.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_id`: `(𝟙 S)_* O_S = O_S` as algebras.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_hartogs`: for the open immersion `𝔸² ∖ {0} → 𝔸²` over a field,
  the direct image is `O_{𝔸²}` by Hartogs and hence is quasi-coherent.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_reduced_points_isQuasicoherent`: over every field `k`, let
  `f : ⨿_{n≥0} Spec k → Spec k[t]` send `t` to `n`. Its direct image is quasi-coherent:
  the global module is `M = ∏_n k`, with `t` acting by `(n)_n`, and on each `D(g)` the
  canonical localization map `M_g → ∏_{g(n)≠0} k` is an isomorphism, compatible with
  restriction. Extend a tuple by zero to obtain surjectivity; a tuple supported on
  `g(n)=0` is killed by one multiplication by `g`, giving injectivity.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_unbounded_thickenings_not_quasicoherent`: over every field `k`,
  put `A = k[t]` and take `f : ⨿_{n≥1} Spec(A/(t^n)) → Spec A`. Its global module is
  `M = ∏_{n≥1} A/(t^n)`, whereas `f⁻¹D(t)` is empty and the sections there are zero.
  In `M_t` the unit tuple survives: for every `r`, the coordinate `n=r+1` of
  `t^r · (1)_n` is nonzero. Thus `M_t ≠ 0` and `f_*O` is not quasi-coherent.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_finite_thickenings_isQuasicoherent`: for the finite family
  `1 ≤ n ≤ N`, `f_*O` is quasi-coherent and `t^N` kills the whole global product,
  whose localization at `t` is zero, agreeing with the sections on `D(t)`.
  This includes the empty family `N=0`.

These localization comparisons use the affine quasi-coherence criterion
([Stacks, §26.7 (01I6)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01I6)); the qcqs
pushforward theorem is [Lemma 26.24.1 (01LC)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01LC).
